0.title: The Acts of the Apostles
0.overview:
Acts is not primarily a history of the early church — it is the history of the risen Christ continuing his work through the Spirit he promised and poured out. Luke begins with a deliberate hinge: the “former book” (his Gospel) recorded all that Jesus “began to do and to teach.” The operative word is began. What follows in Acts is what Jesus continued — not in the flesh now, but in the power of the Spirit, through the mouths and feet and wounds of his witnesses.

Luke wrote for Theophilus (“lover of God”), likely a Roman official being catechised in the faith. But the scope of the narrative exceeds any single reader. Luke traces the gospel’s movement along the spine of the Roman Empire — Jerusalem to Rome, Jewish synagogue to Gentile household, from a frightened upper room to Caesar’s capital. This is not accident; it is Providence. The same God who told Abraham “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” is the God who compels a tentmaker from Tarsus to stand in the Areopagus and announce that the Unknown God has a name.

The Holy Spirit is the true protagonist of Acts. He falls at Pentecost like a sovereign flame. He speaks through Philip on a desert road. He stops Paul from entering Asia. He binds Paul to go to Jerusalem though chains await. He is not a vague presence but a Person with a will — the third Person of the Trinity, sent by the risen Son at the command of the Father, to accomplish the Father’s eternal purpose: a people for his name drawn from every tongue and tribe and nation.

Reformed readers will find in Acts not an argument for the faith but something far more bracing: the sovereignty of God in mission. The gates of hell do not hold. Persecution only scatters the seed further. Imprisonment opens courts to preach. Shipwreck lands an apostle on the right island. Nothing is accidental; everything is appointed. The book ends with Paul in Rome, under house arrest, “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.” The final word is unhindered. The empire could chain the man but not the Word.

Read Acts with your eyes open to the God who is always working — in the upper room, in the council chambers, in the storm, in the jail at midnight. He is the same God today.

1.title: The Promise and the Wait
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, <sup>2</sup>until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen. <sup>3</sup>He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. <sup>4</sup>And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, “you heard from me; <sup>5</sup>for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” <sup>6</sup>So when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” <sup>7</sup>He said to them, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority. <sup>8</sup>But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.” <sup>9</sup>And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. <sup>10</sup>And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes, <sup>11</sup>and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” <sup>12</sup>Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. <sup>13</sup>And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James. <sup>14</sup>All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. <sup>15</sup>In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about one hundred and twenty) and said, <sup>16</sup>“Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. <sup>17</sup>For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry.” <sup>18</sup>(Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. <sup>19</sup>And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.) <sup>20</sup>“For it is written in the Book of Psalms, ‘May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it’; and ‘Let another take his office.’ <sup>21</sup>So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, <sup>22</sup>beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us—one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.” <sup>23</sup>And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias. <sup>24</sup>And they prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen <sup>25</sup>to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.” <sup>26</sup>And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
1.overview:
After the resurrection, Jesus spent forty days with his disciples — not hiding, not ascending immediately, but teaching. Teaching about the kingdom of God. There is something deliberate about those forty days. The same God who spent forty years preparing Israel in the wilderness, forty days preparing Moses on the mountain, forty days testing his Son in the desert, now spends forty days confirming to his apostles that the one who died is the one who lives — and that the one who lives will send what the Father promised. The disciples’ question — “will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” — is not stupid. It is premature. God’s timetable is always larger than ours.

The ascension is not absence — it is exaltation. The cloud that receives Jesus is the cloud of divine glory, the Shekinah, the same cloud that led Israel through the wilderness and filled the tabernacle and settled on Sinai. He goes up not to disappear but to reign. And the two men in white robes say what angels always say when humans stare too long at the sky: why do you stand looking into heaven? There is work to do. There is a promise to wait for. There is a world to witness to. The wait in the upper room is not passivity; it is obedience — and it is prayer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Risen Lord Sends His Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Acts opens not with a new beginning but with a continuation. Luke's second volume picks up exactly where the first left off, and its opening sentence sets the terms for everything that follows: the Gospel recorded what Jesus began to do and teach, which means this book records what he went on doing. The forty days between resurrection and ascension are not a footnote. They are the foundation. The men who will turn the world upside down do so not on the strength of a memory but on the strength of an encounter, and Luke insists on the evidence: many proofs, over weeks, with meals.

Two commands and one refusal shape the section. They are told to wait — which is grace, not delay, because the promise had to arrive before the mission could. They are told where the mission will go, in a sentence that turns out to be the table of contents of the whole book: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and the end of the earth. And their own question, whether the kingdom is now to be restored to Israel, is answered by being redirected: the Father keeps times and seasons inside his own authority, and the disciples are given a task instead of a timetable. They asked when; he told them where.

Then the cloud. The ascension is not the removal of Jesus but his enthronement, and the two men in white robes are there to stop the church misreading it as a loss. Their question — why do you stand looking into heaven? — is the first pastoral correction in the history of the church, and their promise is its first creed in miniature: this same Jesus will come back in the same way you watched him go. Personally, bodily, visibly. Between those two clouds lies everything Acts is about.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascension and the Reign of Christ

The ascension is not the absence of Jesus but the exaltation of Jesus. He who died and rose now reigns at the right hand of the Father (Psalm 110:1), exercising all authority in heaven and on earth. The church does not act in the absence of its king; it acts under the authority of its enthroned king. The cloud that received him is the glory-cloud of the Old Testament, and Daniel had already described the scene from the other side: one like a son of man coming with the clouds to the Ancient of Days, to receive a kingdom that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13-14). The Reformed churches have insisted that the ascension is essential to the gospel and not an epilogue to it: without it Christ does not send the Spirit (John 16:7), does not intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25), and does not carry our nature into the presence of God, where it now permanently is.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Eleven men were given a promise with no date, a mission far beyond their means, and an order to stay put until God moved. They obeyed the hardest part first, which was the waiting.

Now: The church lives in the same interval, between the cloud that took him and the cloud that brings him back. The temptations at either end are unchanged: to stand looking into heaven, absorbed in timetables the Father reserved to himself, or to rush at the work in a strength that was never promised. The command is the same as it was on the hillside — receive, and then witness.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ancient books came with a dedication, and the dedication was usually a patron — the man whose money paid for the papyrus and the copying. Luke has written two volumes and put the same name at the head of both. In the Gospel he calls him most excellent Theophilus (Luke 1:3), and that is not a courtesy Luke scatters about: the only other men in his writing who receive it are the Roman governors Felix and Festus (23:26; 26:25). So Theophilus was in all likelihood a real man of rank, with the means to underwrite a work this long and the standing to be addressed like a magistrate. Here, at the head of the second volume, the honorific has quietly gone. He is simply Theophilus. That proves nothing on its own, but it reads like a friendship that has moved indoors.

Then comes the sentence that gives the whole book its shape. Luke says his first volume dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach. Began. A man summarising a completed biography does not reach for that verb. He reaches for it because he does not think the story finished at the tomb, or at the cloud. Volume one was the beginning of the works and words of Jesus; volume two is their continuation — and it is still Jesus doing them. Read on and Luke will say it in so many words. It is the Lord who adds to the church day by day (2:47). It is Jesus who asks why do you persecute me when the man actually being hunted is a Christian in Damascus (9:4). It is the Lord who opens Lydia's heart while Paul is talking by a river (16:14). The apostles are the instruments. The agent has not changed.

Notice, too, how this book ends — or rather how it does not. Paul is in a rented house in Rome, preaching to whoever comes up the stairs, and Luke simply stops. No verdict, no execution, no farewell, not even a closing benediction. A dozen theories have been offered for the abruptness. The simplest is that a book about what Jesus continues to do has no natural last page, because the work has not stopped. If you want to know what the risen Christ is occupied with this morning, the title of this book is the answer.

One clause here is easy to read straight past: he gave his commands through the Holy Spirit. The risen Son, standing in a resurrection body, with all authority in heaven and on earth already granted him, still speaks and acts by the Spirit. Whatever else that means, it means the Spirit who is about to fall at Pentecost is not a replacement brought in to cover an absence. He is the same Spirit by whom Jesus was conceived, at whose descent he was anointed at the Jordan, in whose power he drove out demons, and by whom he now issues his last orders. The church is not handed a substitute for Christ. It is given the Spirit of Christ, and therefore Christ.

And there is a difficulty here worth meeting head-on before it ambushes anyone. Luke's Gospel appears to run from the empty tomb to the ascension in one unbroken stretch, so that a reader closes Luke 24 with the impression that Jesus went up on Easter evening — while Acts 1 says forty days. But it is the same man writing, with his own first volume at his elbow, quoting its opening line in his second sentence. He is not correcting himself; he is filling in. Luke 24 names events in order without dating them, which is what compressed endings do in every language; the close of a scroll contracts and the opening of the sequel expands. If the two accounts genuinely cancelled each other, the author would have to have forgotten his own ending within a paragraph of citing it.

verseByVerse.quote: He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, "you heard from me;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke chooses a technical word for the evidence. Many proofs renders tekmeria, a term the ancient world used in the law courts and in medicine for the kind of evidence that settles a matter — not a hint pointing somewhere, but a demonstration closing a case. It occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. The man who opened volume one by telling his patron he had investigated everything carefully (Luke 1:3) reaches here for the strongest word available to him, and then says what it consisted of: not one apparition in a dim room, but appearances spread across forty days, to individuals and to crowds, on roads and beside a lake and behind locked doors, with conversation, and with food.

That last detail carries more weight than it looks. The margin of most Bibles notes that 'staying with them' may equally be rendered eating with them — the verb is built on the word for salt, and to share salt with a man is to sit at his table. Either way the point holds, because Luke has already shown us the risen Jesus asking whether there is anything in the house and eating a piece of broiled fish while they watched (Luke 24:41–43). Ghosts do not get hungry. Visions do not chew. Whatever happened on the third day happened to a body, and the men who are about to be flogged for saying so had eaten breakfast with the evidence.

Then an arresting silence. Forty days of teaching about the kingdom of God, and Luke reproduces not one sentence of it. No transcript, no outline, no lost book. But he does not need to reproduce it, because the rest of the volume is the exposition. Everything the apostles preach from Pentecost onward — that the crucified Nazarene is Lord and Christ, that the promises made to the fathers have landed in him, that the door stands open to Gentiles who were never inside it — is not something they pieced together afterwards in committee. It is what he told them in those six weeks. Acts is the transcript, in the only form that finally proves anything: men living on it, and dying on it.

It is worth adding, before anyone builds too much on the word proofs, that evidence and surrender are not the same thing. In this very book men will hear the apostolic testimony, find nothing in it they can refute, and stroll away amused (17:32). Others will hear it and tremble and still do nothing but postpone (24:25). Good evidence removes an excuse; it does not manufacture a will. So the honest thing to say to a friend who insists he would believe if only the case were stronger is that the case is already stronger than he thinks, and that the obstacle has probably never been in the case at all.

And then the order, which is the strangest element in the paragraph. A man with a message that is going to remake the world tells eleven of them to go nowhere. Not to plan, not to organise, not to begin — to wait. That is the command that costs a willing person more than any other, because it looks exactly like doing nothing, and it spends the one asset a new movement has, which is momentum. But the promise had to arrive before the mission did. And notice where he made them wait: Jerusalem. The city where they had failed, where they had run for the dark, where Peter had sworn on the pavement that he had never met the man. To send them out from there in their own strength would have been cruelty wearing the clothes of a commission. He kept them still until what they needed was inside them.

verseByVerse.quote: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John the Baptist had drawn this contrast himself, standing in the Jordan with the water running off his hands: I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming — he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit (Luke 3:16). Now the mightier one stands on the far side of an empty tomb and says the promise is days away. Water was the picture; the Spirit is the thing pictured. Water goes over a man. The Spirit goes into him.

'Not many days from now' turns out to mean ten, and they did not know that. They knew only that it was near. This is very often the shape of Christian waiting: a promise that is certain, a nearness that is real, and a date that is withheld. Nobody in that upper room could have marked a calendar. They could only stay where they had been put and keep asking. Ten days is long enough for a man to wonder whether he misheard.

But the phrase baptized with the Holy Spirit has become one of the most contested in the New Testament, and a reader deserves to know why before he meets the argument somewhere less careful. A large and sincere part of the church teaches that this is a second work of grace, distinct from and later than conversion — that a man is born again when he trusts Christ and then, perhaps years afterwards, is baptized in the Spirit and enters power, usually with a sign to mark it. The case is built almost entirely from this book, and it is not built out of nothing: in Acts the Spirit does sometimes come visibly and later, and Luke plainly regards those moments as significant.

The difficulty is that Acts is narrative, and narrative tells you what happened, not what must always happen. When the letters take up the phrase directly, they define it the other way: in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13) — all, not the advanced; and the effect is membership, not promotion. And the four occasions in Acts where the Spirit comes with visible drama are not four random Christians. They are the four boundary-crossings of the mission: Jews at Pentecost (2), Samaritans (8), Gentiles in a Roman officer's house (10), and men still living inside John's baptism who had not heard the story finished (19). Each is a first. Each has apostles present as witnesses. Luke is not laying down a pattern for private experience; he is recording how the door was opened, one hinge at a time, and how heaven certified it in public so that nobody could later say the wrong people had been let in.

Two guards belong on that, one on each side. The first is for the believer who has never had an experience he could point to and has begun to suspect he is a second-class Christian. If the Spirit is what makes a man belong to Christ at all (Romans 8:9), then a person who trusts Christ, hates his sin, and loves the brethren has the Spirit, whatever his emotional weather has been. There is no unbaptized remainder in the body of Christ. The second guard runs the other way, against the temptation to answer all this with a shrug. This same book will describe men already filled at Pentecost being filled again in a shaken room (4:31), which means fresh and powerful visitations of God are a thoroughly biblical category and not an embarrassment. To want more of God is right. The label may be wrong; the hunger is not. It would be a poor result if a reader finished a careful paragraph about the Spirit with his doctrine tidied and his longing cooled.

Set the two baptisms side by side one last time and see what is being offered. John could get a man wet and send him home to try harder. What is promised here is God himself, taking up residence in people who a few weeks earlier had scattered like birds. It is a staggering thing that the Holy One should choose such lodgings, and stranger still that he should call it a promise rather than a condescension.

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had come together, they asked him, "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" He said to them, "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the last question the apostles ever put to Jesus on earth, and it is about politics. After three years of teaching, a crucifixion, a resurrection and six weeks of instruction on the kingdom of God, what they want to know is whether the occupation is about to end. It is easy to be lofty about that. It is harder once you notice what they were living in: a foreign garrison in the temple city, a governor who had already executed their master to keep the peace, taxes flowing to a Caesar who took divine titles. Their Scriptures had promised a son of David on a real throne. They were not inventing the expectation. They were asking when the book would come true.

And Jesus does not tell them the expectation is wrong. That is the first thing to see, and it is easily missed by readers who assume he brushed a crude hope aside. He has just spent forty days on the kingdom; if the question rested on a false premise, this was the moment to say so, and he does not. He corrects one thing only: the timing, and their assumed right to know it. It is not for you to know times or seasons. The two words are not decoration — one is duration, the stretch of time that has to run, and the other is the decisive moment when it arrives. Both are fixed, and both are fixed by the Father's own authority, which in the Greek has the flavour of a matter kept inside his own jurisdiction. Not unknowable in principle. Not theirs.

Christians have divided over what he left standing. Some read the silence as leaving room for a future national restoration of Israel, with the promises to the fathers finding a literal fulfilment still ahead. Others read the next verse as the answer itself: the kingdom is being restored, beginning at Jerusalem and moving outward, and the Israel being gathered is the one defined by the Messiah rather than by the map. The second reading has the stronger claim on this paragraph, since verse 8 begins with but and plainly offers itself as what they should have asked about. It does not follow, though, that God is finished with the Jewish people, and the New Testament will not let that conclusion stand (Romans 11:1, 25–26). A reader can hold the mission of verse 8 with both hands and still expect God to keep every promise he ever made, without needing a chart to show him how.

What is not negotiable is the practical edge of the rebuke, and it has cut every generation since. There has never been a decade without someone announcing the date. Farms have been sold, careers abandoned, children taken out of school, and the morning after has always come, with the faithful poorer and the watching world confirmed in its suspicion. Every one of those movements had to begin by contradicting this sentence. When a teacher tells you he has worked out what the Father reserved to his own authority, you have all the information you need about him, and you need not examine his arithmetic.

But notice what Jesus did not say, because the comfort is in the difference. He did not say there is no date. He said the date is not yours. Somewhere in the counsel of God there is a day already fixed, as fixed as any day in the diary, on which every wrong currently running unchecked will be stopped where it stands. That is not a vagueness offered to keep people quiet; it is a certainty withheld to keep them free. A man who knew the date would spend his life either presuming on the time remaining or paralysed by its shortness. Not knowing, he is left to do the only sane thing, which is to be found faithful whenever it comes. There is a considerable difference between a secret and an evasion, and this is the first kind. The Father is not being coy with his children. He is keeping his own counsel, which is one of the things it means to be God.

verseByVerse.quote: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answers a question about the calendar with a sentence about a map. They asked when; he tells them where, and how far. And the first word out of his mouth is not an instruction but a gift: you will receive power. Not summon it, not generate it, not work up to it. Receive it. Everything the church is about to do in this book runs downhill from a verb they have no part in except to hold out their hands.

It is worth being exact about what the power turned out to be, because the word invites daydreams. Within three chapters these men are in custody. Within seven, one of them is dead under a pile of stones. The power promised here did not make them untouchable; it made them unstoppable, which is a different and better thing. What Luke actually records after Pentecost is boldness where there had been hiding, clarity where there had been confusion, and joy in places where joy has no business being — a flogging that ends in rejoicing (5:41), a midnight hymn from a prison floor (16:25). If a Christian is waiting for power to arrive as a feeling of invincibility, he may miss it entirely when it comes as the ability to open his mouth in a room where it costs him something.

And what they are made is not preachers, not apologists, not strategists, but witnesses. The word is martyres, and English took it over as 'martyr' — not because the word means dying, but because of what kept happening to the people it described. Luke himself watches the shift begin: by the time Paul is telling his story he speaks of Stephen as your witness, and every reader knows what happened to Stephen (22:20). But keep the courtroom sense first, because it is the one that sets a nervous believer free. A witness is not the barrister. He is not asked to win the case, construct the argument, or hold his own against a hostile expert. He is asked one thing: say what you saw. He may be interrupted, disbelieved, and cross-examined by people cleverer than he is, and none of that touches his qualification, because he was there and they were not. Anyone who has been dealt with by Jesus Christ has standing in that witness box, and nobody without a testimony of his own can take it away.

Then the geography, and it doubles as the table of contents. Jerusalem fills chapters 1 to 7; Judea and Samaria, chapters 8 to 12; the end of the earth, chapters 13 to 28. Luke is writing to a plan, and the plan was dictated in this sentence before a word of the story had happened. Notice where Samaria sits. Not last, where it could be indefinitely deferred, but second — the people a Judean would cross a river to avoid, placed in the middle of the itinerary so that no one could reach the ends of the earth while stepping over the neighbours he despised. And the end of the earth is a quotation waiting to be identified; it comes from Isaiah's servant, appointed as a light for the nations that salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6), which Paul will one day pick up and apply to himself as his own marching orders (13:47).

One guard, because this verse is preached wrongly more often than almost any other. It is regularly turned into a method — reach your Jerusalem first, then your Judea, then the world — as though local outreach must be completed before anyone may go abroad. That is not what the sentence is. It is Luke's map of one historical expansion, not a sequence of permissions, and the book itself refuses the reading: the gospel reaches Samaria because a persecution scattered people who had no strategy at all (8:1–4), and Antioch is evangelised by men whose names nobody bothered to record (11:20). God has never waited for a city to be finished before starting on another one.

And it is worth sitting with the sheer improbability of the sentence before moving on. Eleven provincials on a hillside outside a minor city in an occupied province are told that their testimony will reach the end of the earth. Every visible fact contradicted it. They had no money, no institution, no standing, and no member of their number who could have got a hearing at any court in the world. It happened anyway, and it happened along exactly the lines laid down here. That is not a tribute to the eleven. It is what it looks like when the risen Christ says a thing will be so.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke's care as a reporter shows in five words: as they were looking on. This is not something they inferred the next morning from an empty hillside. They watched it happen. And what they watched was not a fading, not a dissolving, not a body becoming gradually transparent. He was lifted, and then a cloud came between, and the hillside was one man emptier than it had been a minute before.

The cloud is the detail everything turns on, and it is not weather. All through Israel's Scriptures the cloud is where God is pleased to be visible without being looked at: it goes ahead of the people through the wilderness, it fills the tabernacle so thickly that Moses cannot get in (Exodus 40:34–35), it comes down on the temple so that the priests have to stop the service and stand there (1 Kings 8:10–11). When a cloud takes a man out of sight in this literature, he has not gone behind a weather front. He has gone inside the glory.

Which means the scene has to be read from both ends to be read at all. From the hillside it is a departure, and it looks like loss. From the other side of the cloud it is an arrival, and Daniel had described it centuries before: one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, presented before the Ancient of Days, and given dominion and glory and a kingdom that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). Notice the direction of travel in Daniel. He is not coming down to earth in that vision; he is coming up to the throne. The disciples are watching the underside of a coronation. And the psalm the apostles will quote more than any other text in their Scriptures is about what happens when he gets there: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool (Psalm 110:1). Peter will preach it within a fortnight (2:34–35).

Someone will ask, reasonably, whether heaven is really up. It is not, in the sense of being a distance measurable in miles above Jerusalem; a man who kept rising would run out of air long before he ran out of sky. But the question mistakes a sign for a map. He went up because a body must leave visibly if witnesses are to testify that it left, and because upward is what exaltation looks like to creatures who walk about on the ground. The direction was for their eyes. The destination was the throne.

There is something else here that is rarely said and ought to be. Jesus did not shed his body at the cloud. He took it with him. There is at this moment, in the presence of God, a human being — with hands, with a voice, with a memory of Nazareth and of nails — and he is not visiting. The nature he assumed in the womb of a Galilean girl he has never laid down and never will. This is where the Reformed churches have insisted on being careful, and the care is worth understanding: a real body is somewhere, and being somewhere means not being everywhere, so when Christ promises to be with his people always he is with them by his Spirit and in his deity, not by his flesh being spread thin across the world. Lutheran Christians have taken a different line on that last point and have not been foolish to do so; the disagreement is old and serious and is not about whether Christ is truly present with his church. But the pastoral weight of it belongs to everyone. Our nature is not a costume he wore for thirty-three years. It has been carried into the immediate presence of God and seated there.

Stand back from it and the wonder is not that they gazed. It is that heaven received him. The One by whom all things were made had been spat at by soldiers who were too bored to look him in the face, and had let them; and now the glory that Moses was not permitted to see closes over him like a door opening. He did not ascend to become glorious. He ascended because he always was, and because the work he came to finish was finished. Every knee in that hidden place bent as he came in, and the marks in his hands went in with him and are there still.

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Angels have a way of asking questions that are really instructions. Why do you stand looking into heaven? There is no unkindness in it, and there is no patience with it either. The men are not doing anything wrong; they are doing something finished. He has gone. The sky has nothing further to show them, and the next thing God has for them is at the bottom of the hill.

They are addressed as men of Galilee, which is not a compliment in Jerusalem. It is the label that will be thrown at Peter beside a fire and at the whole company at Pentecost (2:7). Provincials with an accent. Heaven uses the word without a flicker of apology, and then tells these particular provincials that the next act of world history runs through them.

The promise itself is four words long and it is the anchor of Christian hope: in the same way. Whatever the ascension was, the return will match it. He left personally, and a person will come back — not an influence, not a movement, not an era of improved conditions. He left bodily, and a body will return; the same body, the same man, the same face. He left visibly, in front of witnesses, and the return will be public: the world will not be informed of it, it will see it. And he left in a cloud, which is where Daniel had said the Son of Man belonged.

That phrase quietly rules out a good deal. It rules out the teaching that Christ already returned invisibly, whether in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 or at some private date since. Something did happen in AD 70, and Jesus had said it would; but the angels are not describing a change in the spiritual climate. They are standing beside men whose eyes still hurt from watching, and they say: like that. It equally rules out the reduction of the second coming to a figure of speech for death, or for progress, or for the gradual improvement of the human race. The Christian expectation is not that things will get better. It is that a particular man will arrive.

And it rules out, by the plain force of the rebuke, the religion of the raised binoculars. There has always been a kind of believer whose whole interest in the future is diagrams — who can tell you the sequence of the last seven years but has not spoken to his neighbour in nine of them. The first men ever tempted to that were interrupted mid-stare by angels, and the interruption is in the Bible. The correct response to he is coming back has never been to stand still and calculate. It is to be found doing something he asked for when he arrives.

But the promise deserves better than to be used only as a corrective, because it is not primarily a rebuke; it is the sentence a great many Christians have died holding. Measure it against what is actually wrong with the world. Somewhere today a woman is being told the results were not what anyone hoped. A father is going through his son's room a year after the funeral and cannot yet move the football boots. Someone who was harmed as a child has watched the man who did it live comfortably into old age and die unaccused. Injustices are not merely unpunished; whole categories of them are now unrecoverable, the witnesses dead, the record lost. To all of it this sentence says: there is a date, and on that date the one who was in the room the whole time will come back in the open, and nothing will be left buried. That is not a poetic way of saying things will feel better eventually. It is a man on a cloud, and a docket that has been kept.

They walked down the hill. There is no record of any of them looking back up, and the next thing Luke tells us is that they went to pray.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — The Waiting Church and the Reconstituted Twelve
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Ten days separate the ascension from Pentecost, and Luke fills them with a portrait of the waiting church. The eleven walk back down Olivet into the city that had killed their master, because that is where they were told to be, and go up to a borrowed room. Luke names every one of them — a movement built on eyewitness testimony has to be able to say who its witnesses are. With them are the women, and Mary, who appears here for the last time in the New Testament praying alongside everyone else, and the brothers of Jesus, who a few years earlier had thought he was out of his mind. About a hundred and twenty people in an upstairs room: the entire visible result of the ministry of Jesus of Nazareth, devoting themselves to prayer because it is the only work a waiting church can do.

Then Peter stands up, and the man who denied Christ at a fire handles the church's first crisis from the Scriptures. Judas had been one of the Twelve, numbered and allotted his share, and his treachery was foreseen without being excused — the Spirit had spoken of it by David's mouth in Psalms 69 and 109. Luke breaks in with a parenthesis for his Greek-speaking reader, explaining the field bought with the betrayal money and the name the city gave it, Akeldama, which people were still using when he wrote. The horror is left undecorated, and the account is closed: a plot of ground and a nickname.

The office, however, outlives the man who disgraced it. Let another take his office is read as a mandate, and Peter sets out the narrowest job description in the New Testament: accompaniment from John's baptism to the ascension, and eyewitness testimony to the resurrection. Two men qualify, Barsabbas and Matthias — and one of them, having been found fit in public, is publicly not chosen, and stays. The church prays to the one who knows all hearts because it has run out of anything it can see, casts lots as God had appointed for exactly such a decision, and the Twelve stand complete on the last morning before everything changes.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Apostolic College and Its Significance

The reconstitution of the Twelve before Pentecost is deliberate. The Twelve answer to the twelve tribes and represent the reconstituted people of God (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30); an incomplete Twelve would be a broken sign at the moment the sign was about to be needed. The qualifications Peter states (v. 22) mark the apostolic circle as a closed and historically anchored group — the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and foundations are laid once. The New Testament does use apostle more widely of sent ones and church messengers, but no one alive can meet the terms stated here, which is why the church has no further foundational word to wait for. Judas, meanwhile, stands as the sober warning at the door of the book: he was numbered among them, sent out with them, and trusted with the money, and nearness to Jesus did not save him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A hundred and twenty people with no money, no standing and no strategy prayed together for ten days, settled a painful question from Scripture rather than by argument, and appointed a man who is never mentioned again.

Now: The church's preparation for anything God intends to do has not changed shape: gathered, praying, working from the text, willing to be led, and made up very largely of people whose names will appear nowhere. Barsabbas, qualified and passed over in front of everyone, was still in the room when the Spirit fell.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's journey away. And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They walk back. That is the first thing, and it is an act of obedience with a cost, because Jerusalem was the last place on earth a follower of the executed Nazarene had any business being. It was the city with the arrest warrants, the city with the council that had already shown what it would do, the city where every one of them could be identified by half a dozen people in the temple courts. Jesus had told them to stay there (v. 4), and so they went back into it.

Luke measures the walk in a way that tells you something about his sources. A Sabbath day's journey was the distance the rabbis permitted on the day of rest — about two thousand cubits, something under a mile — reasoned out from the command that no one should leave his place on the seventh day (Exodus 16:29) and from the pasture-land measured around the Levitical towns (Numbers 35:5). It is the only appearance of the phrase in the New Testament. Luke is writing for a Greek-speaking patron who would not have known the rule and did not need it; he keeps it because it is how the people who were there described the distance. Small untranslated habits like that are what a report looks like when it comes from inside.

Then the roll-call, and it deserves more attention than it usually gets. Luke could have written 'the eleven' and moved on. He writes out every name. A movement staking everything on the claim that certain men saw a dead man alive has to be able to say who they were, and Luke names them, in a city where any one of them could be found and questioned within the hour. Anonymous testimony is worth nothing anywhere, and he knows it. Notice also the order, which is not the order in his own Gospel (Luke 6:14–16). Andrew has moved down and John has moved up to stand beside Peter at the head of the list — because those two are about to work as a pair through the opening chapters of this book, at the temple gate, before the council, and on the road into Samaria. Luke is arranging the names for the story he is about to tell.

Two of them need a word. 'Judas the son of James' is not Iscariot, and Luke says so by naming the father; he is the apostle who appears as Thaddaeus in the other lists, and the awkwardness of the double naming is itself a mark of honesty. A church inventing its own records does not saddle itself with a second Judas. And 'Simon the Zealot' had belonged to the party of armed resistance, men who believed the answer to Rome was a knife. Sitting in the same small room is Matthew, who had made his living collecting Rome's money from his own people. In any village in Galilee those two men were natural enemies of the sharpest kind — the collaborator and the man sworn to cut collaborators' throats. They are now praying together, and will shortly be arrested together. Nothing in politics does that. It is what happens when two men discover that the thing they had each been trying to save the nation from is smaller than the thing they have both been saved from.

The room is called an upper room, a rented or borrowed space up the outside stairs of a Jerusalem house. Christian tradition has long linked it with the room where the Passover was eaten, and it may be right, though Luke uses a different word here from the one in his Gospel and does not press the point. What matters is the scale. The risen Lord of heaven and earth has been enthroned at the right hand of God, and his entire visible operation on earth is a borrowed room upstairs with about a hundred and twenty people in it, most of whom have no money and one of whom is still living down the worst night of his life. Everything in this book grows from that room.

verseByVerse.quote: All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke gives the waiting church one adverb and it becomes a signature: homothumadon, with one accord, of one mind and one impulse together. He will use it again and again in the early chapters — in the temple courts (2:46), in a prayer meeting after an arrest (4:24), in Solomon's portico (5:12) — until it is almost the church's second name. And the prayer is not occasional. The construction is continuous: they were devoting themselves to it, keeping at it, the way a man keeps at something he cannot do without. They had been given a promise with no date attached and the only work available to them was asking.

Look at who is in the room. The women are there, and Luke is the writer who always says so. In a world where a woman's word carried no weight in a court, women had been the last at the cross, the first at the tomb, and are now in the founding prayer meeting of the Christian church. Nobody constructing a respectable origin story in the first century would have arranged it that way.

Mary is there too, and this is the last time she appears in the New Testament. It is worth pausing on where Scripture chooses to leave her, because a great deal has been built on her since. She is not on a platform. She is not being asked for anything. She is on her knees in a crowded room with a hundred and nineteen other people, waiting for the Holy Spirit like everyone else. She is honoured — blessed among women, and the church should not be so nervous of the abuse that it forgets the text — but she is honoured as one of the redeemed, not as a channel of redemption. Her son had said as much when a woman in a crowd blessed the womb that bore him and he answered, rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it (Luke 11:27–28). Here she is doing exactly that, and the New Testament closes the door on her with her hands together and her face down, which is the most honourable place she could possibly be left.

But the phrase that should stop a reader is the last one: and his brothers. These are the men who a few years earlier had come to collect him because they had decided he was out of his mind. These are the brothers of whom John flatly records that not even they believed in him (John 7:5). They had grown up in the same four-room house, eaten at the same table, watched him work in the same trade, and concluded he was deluded. And now they are in the prayer meeting. One of them, James, will be leading the Jerusalem church within fifteen years, presiding over the council that decides the Gentile question (15:13). He will write a letter, and it will open by calling his own elder brother Lord and himself his servant. Another, Jude, will do the same. Whatever else happened in the forty days, this happened: then he appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7). Paul mentions it in a single clause and does not elaborate, and it is one of the most eloquent clauses in the Bible.

Anyone praying for a relative who will not believe should not be handed a formula here, and should be handed this. It took years. Mary lived a long time in a house where her other sons thought her firstborn was mad, and there is no indication she was given any assurance in the meantime. What she was given, eventually, was a room with all of them in it. The case is never closed while a man is alive, and the people who know you best and have the most reason to dismiss you are not out of reach; the risen Christ went looking for one of them personally. That is not a promise that every son and every brother will come. It is a plain fact that the hardest cases in the New Testament include the ones who had shared a childhood with him, and they came.

And then Peter stands up. Luke slips the crowd size in as an aside — about a hundred and twenty — and it is a strikingly modest number to set against the promise of the end of the earth. It is also, some have noted, the number the rabbis required before a community could constitute its own council; whether or not Luke intends the echo, the point is that the entire visible harvest of the ministry of Jesus of Nazareth could sit down together in one upstairs room. Within a chapter it will be three thousand.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider who is speaking. The last time Peter opened his mouth in Jerusalem about Jesus of Nazareth, he was standing at a charcoal fire in a courtyard swearing he had never met the man, and then he went out and wept. Now he is on his feet in front of a hundred and twenty people, opening the Scriptures, handling the hardest subject the young church has — the treachery of one of their own — and doing it with composure. Nobody voted him into that. Something was restored on a beach in Galilee, and this is what restoration looks like a few weeks later: not a man excused, but a man working.

His first move is to reach for a text. The Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David. Notice the double authorship stated without any awkwardness: the Spirit spoke, and he spoke by the mouth of David. Not instead of David's mouth, and not merely through it as a hollow pipe — David's vocabulary, David's grief, David's own experience of a friend at his table who turned on him, and the Holy Spirit speaking in all of it. That is how these men understood the book they were reading, and it is why Peter can treat a thousand-year-old lament as an instruction for a decision this week.

But had to be raises the question that has troubled thoughtful readers ever since, and it should be met plainly: if Scripture had to be fulfilled, was Judas ever free to do otherwise, and is God then the author of the worst act in human history? Luke does not dodge this, and he will state both halves of the answer twice more in the next few chapters, more starkly than anyone would dare to invent. At Pentecost Peter says Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and in the same breath says you crucified and killed him (2:23). In a prayer meeting a few weeks later the church says that Herod and Pilate and the nations gathered to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place (4:27–28). The Bible never treats these as two positions to be chosen between. It puts them in one sentence.

What it never says is that God put the greed there. Judas was not overpowered. He was a thief with his hand in the common purse long before he went to the priests (John 12:6), and what he did in the end was exactly what he had been doing in small amounts for years, which is to convert Jesus into money. He was not a man forced into a role; he was a man who found a buyer. God did not implant the appetite, and he did not compel the transaction. He wove a free and filthy act into a purpose that the man committing it knew nothing about. That is not tyranny. It is something far more frightening and far more reassuring: there is no evil so deliberate that it can get outside the plan of God, and no evil so useful to that plan that the man doing it is thereby excused.

And no one may say he was never given a chance. He had three years of it. His feet were washed by the man he had already agreed to sell, in the same room, on the same night. He was warned repeatedly, and warned in a way that let him withdraw without public exposure — the others at that table had no idea who was meant, which means Jesus had shielded him even while confronting him. He was called friend in the garden with the kiss still wet on the face. Mercy was held out to Judas until the last hour available, and he walked past it every single time. Whatever mystery sits behind the word predestined, it does not sit between Judas and a door he wanted to go through.

Peter's last words here are the ones that ought to be carried out of the room: he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry. Judas was not an outsider who got in. He was on the list. He was sent out to preach with the rest and, as far as the Gospels ever indicate, things happened when he did. He was trusted with the money. And when Jesus said at the table that one of them would betray him, not one of the eleven looked at Judas; every man there suspected himself first. Three years of the closest proximity any human being has ever had to Jesus Christ, and it did not save him. Proximity is not possession.

That sentence has frightened tender consciences for centuries, so one thing must be added to it. Judas is not a mirror for the believer who is afraid he loves Christ too little. Judas was never afraid of that for a moment. He did not want Christ and fear he was failing him; he wanted what Christ could be turned into, and when the exchange rate disappointed him he cashed out. A man who is anxious because he longs to love Jesus more than he does has already given the evidence that Judas never gave in three years of standing closer than anyone.

verseByVerse.quote: (Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
These two verses are Luke talking, not Peter. The giveaway is the clause 'in their own language' — Peter is addressing a room full of Jerusalem believers who spoke that language every day and would no more need it explained than a Londoner needs Thames translated. Luke has stepped out of the speech to tell his Greek-reading patron what the field was called and why. The whole thing is a footnote, and English Bibles are right to put it in brackets.

It is also the kind of footnote that quietly does a great deal of work. A story invented at a distance does not stop to give the local name of a piece of ground, preserve it untranslated in the original dialect, and then explain it. Akeldama was a real place with a real name that people in that city were still using when Luke wrote, and any reader in Jerusalem could have gone and looked at it. Legends do not usually leave a forwarding address.

Two apparent collisions with Matthew's account have to be faced, and they come apart more easily than their reputation suggests. The first is the purchase. Matthew says the chief priests took the returned silver and bought the field, because it was blood money and could not go into the treasury; Luke says Judas acquired it with the reward of his wickedness. But that is ordinary legal speech about a dead man's money, and it always has been. The silver was legally his; the priests would not touch it for sacred use and could not simply return it to a corpse, so it was spent on his account, and the ground went down under his name. Luke is not picturing a man house-hunting between the betrayal and the rope. He is telling you whose money paid for it, which is precisely why the city attached his crime to the deed and called the place what it called it.

The second is the death itself. Matthew says he hanged himself; Luke says he fell headlong and burst open. Read as two claims about the same instant they are irreconcilable, and read as two moments in one afternoon they are not. A body left hanging does not stay hanging indefinitely, and the ravine country south of Jerusalem is rock. The rope gives, or the branch does, or the corpse comes down of its own weight in the heat, and what is found at the bottom is what Luke describes. Matthew tells you what Judas did. Luke tells you what was found, and why the field got the name it kept. Neither writer is contradicting the other; they are standing at different ends of the same terrible day.

Luke does not moralise over the corpse and neither should anyone else, but he does not tidy it either, and the refusal to tidy it is deliberate. Thirty pieces of silver was a real sum and it bought a real thing: a field nobody wanted, with his name on it forever, and a body in the middle of it. That is the whole return on the transaction. The account is closed and the balance is a plot of ground and a nickname.

One thing must be guarded here, because this passage is read by people carrying something heavy. Judas is not in Scripture as a case study in suicide, and he must not be used as one. What is said about him is said about a man who sold the Son of God for money and never once repented of the wanting, only of the outcome. The manner of his death is reported; it is not what he is condemned for. A reader who has buried someone who took their own life — a son, a wife, a friend who was in agony and could not see a morning — is not looking at that person's portrait in these verses, and anyone who hands it to them as one has misread the passage badly. Despair and treachery are not the same sin, and the God who reads hearts has never confused them.

verseByVerse.quote: "For it is written in the Book of Psalms, 'May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it'; and 'Let another take his office.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter's warrant for what he is about to propose is two lines of Hebrew poetry, and it is worth watching how he uses them, because it shows how the first Christians read their Bible. Psalm 69 is David hunted and hated, drowning in trouble, with the scorn of those who reproach God falling on him. Psalm 109 is David betrayed by a man he had loved, who repaid friendship with accusation. Neither psalm has Judas in view in any obvious sense; both are the cry of the Lord's anointed under treachery. And that is exactly why Peter reaches for them. If David's sufferings were the shadow, then the greater Son of David betrayed by a table companion is the substance, and what happened to the man who did it is written into the pattern.

He alters one thing, and he does it in the open. The psalm has their camp and their tents, plural, a whole party of enemies; Peter makes it singular — his camp, let there be no one to dwell in it. He is not misquoting. He is doing what the psalm itself invites, narrowing a corporate judgement down onto the representative case, the way a general verdict lands on the man who actually stood in the dock. And the second citation, Psalm 109:8, is the operative one: let another take his office. The word behind 'office' is the one that will later give the church its term for an overseer. Peter reads it as a mandate, not a comment. The seat is not abolished by the man who disgraced it; it is vacated, and it is to be filled.

That is the point the whole chapter has been building toward, and it is worth saying plainly because it steadies people who have watched a leader fall. Treachery at the top did not destroy the apostolate. The office outlived the man. Churches have been broken by the discovery that someone trusted was a fraud, and the temptation afterwards is always the same — to conclude that the whole thing was a fraud, or that the position itself was the problem and should quietly be left empty. Peter's answer is to open the Scriptures and appoint a successor. The work is bigger than the worst man who ever did it.

But there is a genuine difficulty in these quotations that most readers feel and few have explained to them. These are the imprecatory psalms, the prayers that ask God to ruin somebody. May his camp become desolate. And anyone who turns up Psalm 109 to check the reference will find that the line immediately after the one Peter quotes asks that the man's children be fatherless and his wife a widow. How is a Christian, who has been told to pray for those who persecute him, supposed to hold a book that contains prayers like that?

Three things make it bearable, and they are worth having. First, an imprecation is the opposite of vengeance, not an instance of it. A man who prays that God will judge his enemy is a man who has just handed the matter to a court and taken his own hands off it. The alternative to the imprecatory psalm is not gentleness; it is the knife. Second, the enemies in view are not personal irritants but the settled adversaries of God's anointed and God's purpose — which is why Peter can apply the psalm to a man who sold the Son of God and would be nonsense applied to a neighbour who is difficult about the boundary hedge. And third, these prayers are ultimately in the mouth of Christ himself, the righteous sufferer the psalms were describing all along, and he is the one who has the right to ask for judgement and the one who on a cross asked for the opposite.

So there is a real caution here, and there is also a real permission. The caution is that no Christian may use these psalms as ammunition for a grudge; the moment a man prays desolation on someone who has merely wounded his pride, he has stopped praying and started cursing. The permission is for the other reader, the one who has been genuinely and terribly wronged, who has discovered that he wants justice with an intensity that frightens him, and who has concluded that wanting it makes him a bad Christian. It does not. Scripture has given him words for that, and the words are prayers — which means the right destination for the fiercest thing in him was never the offender, and never the polite suppression of it either, but God.

verseByVerse.quote: So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us — one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter now states the job description, and it is the narrowest in the New Testament. Two things are required, and no more. The man must have been with them during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, from the baptism of John until the day he was taken up; and he must be able to testify to the resurrection as something he saw. That is the whole specification. Nothing about gifting, eloquence, education, or promise. The apostolic office is not a set of abilities. It is a position in history.

Something quietly wonderful is buried in the first requirement. Peter assumes there is more than one such man available, and he is right — two are produced within the minute. Which means that for three years there had been people following Jesus from the Jordan to Olivet, through the crowds and the opposition and the night of the arrest, whose names appear nowhere in any Gospel. They were there when the five thousand were fed and there when almost everyone walked away. They had no title and no mention. And the qualification for the highest office the church would ever have turned out to be precisely the thing they had been doing unnoticed the entire time, which was staying.

The second requirement fixes what an apostle is for. He is a witness to his resurrection — that is the office in one phrase. Not a manager, not a visionary, not the holder of a private revelation. A man under oath about an event. Everything the church has ever had to say begins with a factual claim about something that happened outside a wall in Jerusalem on a particular Sunday, and the Twelve exist to say that they were there when it was verified.

Which raises the question every reader of this passage eventually meets: are there apostles today? A good many churches say so, and some ordain men to the title. The answer has to be given in two parts, because the New Testament itself uses the word in two ways. In the wider sense an apostle is simply a sent one, and Scripture applies it freely: Barnabas is called one (14:14), Epaphroditus is his church's apostolos to Paul (Philippians 2:25), and there are men described as apostles of the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23). If a modern believer means by the word a pioneering missionary who opens new ground, he is using it in a way the New Testament allows, and the ministry he is describing is badly needed.

But the office Peter is filling in this room is not that, and it is closed by the very terms he has just read out. Nobody alive has accompanied Jesus from John's baptism to the ascension. Nobody alive saw the risen Christ in the way this qualification demands. Paul is the one apparent exception, and he is careful to present himself as exactly that — an appearance granted out of sequence, last of all, to one untimely born (1 Corinthians 15:8) — and to say last. The Twelve, with Paul beside them, are the foundation of the household of God (Ephesians 2:20), and foundations are laid once. A builder who keeps returning to lay more foundation has stopped building.

That gives an ordinary Christian a workable test, and he does not need to be rude to apply it. The question is not what a man calls himself; it is what he claims his title entitles him to. If a leader means that he plants churches and takes responsibility for regions, no harm is done and the church is the better for him. If he means that his word carries the weight the apostles' words carried — that he may add to Scripture, or bind a conscience where Scripture has not, or require obedience that is not accountable to the text — then he is claiming something Peter's own criteria exclude him from, and the humblest believer in the room has the right to say so with a Bible open at this page.

And there is a comfort in the closed door that is easy to miss. Because the apostolic office is finished, the church is not waiting on any further foundational word. Nobody is going to arrive with a revelation that changes the terms. Everything the church needs was deposited by men who could be cross-examined by people who had been in the same crowds, and it has been sitting in the open ever since.

verseByVerse.quote: And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two men step forward, and one of them is about to become the most quietly instructive figure in the chapter. Joseph carries three names — a Hebrew given name, an Aramaic patronymic, and Justus, a Roman one — which is the ordinary signature of a Jew who moved easily in the wider world of the empire. Matthias is named and nothing else is said about him. Both men clear the bar Peter has just set, and it is a high one: both had been with Jesus from the Jordan to Olivet, through everything, for three years.

Then the lot is cast and one of them is not chosen.

Everything in this passage that a modern reader actually needs is standing in that sentence, and it is almost never preached. Barsabbas did not fail to qualify. He was not passed over for a defect, or a sin, or a lack. He was found fit — publicly, on the record, by the eleven — and then he lost. In front of a hundred and twenty people. There was no private letter, no gentle word beforehand, no face-saving arrangement. The lot fell, the room saw it fall, and he had to walk home through Jerusalem knowing that the man beside him was now one of the Twelve and he was not.

Anyone who has been passed over knows the particular taste of that, and it is not the same as failure. Failure at least gives you something to work on. This is the other thing: being genuinely good enough, being told so, and watching it go elsewhere. The elder's role that went to the other man. The post you had trained for and he had not. The ministry you would plainly have done well, handed to someone whose only advantage was that God chose him. It is a specific grief and it is a lonely one, because there is nobody to blame and therefore nothing to do with it.

Scripture will not hand out a cheap comfort here, and it is important not to invent one. The text does not say God had something better in mind for Barsabbas. It does not say he was spared a burden, or that his real calling lay elsewhere, or that everything worked out. It says he was not chosen, and then it never mentions him again. Sometimes faithfulness has to be carried on without an explanation, and pretending otherwise only adds a lie to a disappointment.

But watch what the silence afterwards does and does not contain. There is no schism. No rival gathering across the city, no faction of the aggrieved, no letter of complaint preserved because it caused trouble. Barsabbas is simply in the room at Pentecost with everyone else, and one of the hundred and twenty on whom the Spirit falls a few days later is a man who has very recently had the biggest door in the world shut in his face. He stayed. Whatever it cost him, and Luke does not tell us, he stayed.

And it is worth remembering that Matthias is never mentioned again either. Both men disappear into the same silence, one of them an apostle and one of them not, and both of them spent the rest of their lives serving a Lord who had seen the whole business and kept the accounts himself. The people whose names occur once in the Bible and then never again are not the margin of the story. They are most of the church, in every generation, and the reason the story reached us at all.

verseByVerse.quote: And they prayed and said, "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They pray before they draw, and the prayer is four lines long. There is no eloquence in it and no preamble. They tell God what they cannot do, ask him to do it, and stop.

The word they use for him is unusual enough to be worth stopping on. Kardiognosta — heart-knower — is a title that appears twice in the whole Bible, here and at 15:8, and both times it is on Peter's lips, and both times the church is trying to decide who truly belongs. Here it is two candidates who look identical from the outside. There it will be a house full of Gentiles nobody expected God to accept. In each case the church has run out of evidence it can see, and reaches for the one who reads what no one else can. It is a name for God born out of the church's own helplessness, and both times it settles the matter.

Notice also who is being addressed. They say Lord, and the immediate antecedent in this passage is the one who chose the original apostles (v. 2) — Jesus. So within a few weeks of the ascension, before a single council, creed or doctrinal controversy, a room full of Jewish monotheists is praying to a man they had eaten breakfast with, addressing him by a title that in their Scriptures belongs to God alone, and attributing to him the knowledge of every human heart. Nobody argues for it. Nobody defends it. They simply do it, in the most instinctive act a religious person ever performs. The doctrine of the deity of Christ was not voted in at a later council; it was already the posture of the church before the church had a vocabulary for it.

And there is a searching mercy in what they ask him to do. He knows the hearts of all. That means, for one thing, that he was not taken in by either candidate's best behaviour in a difficult fortnight, and it means he is not taken in by anyone's now. The estimate of you that your church holds is assembled from what you have let it see. His is not. That cuts in the direction most people fear first: he has read the thing you would resign over if it were known. It also cuts the other way, and this is the side worth resting on. He has read the part of you that nobody has ever believed — the repentance that was real even though nothing changed for months, the love for him that survives in someone whose life makes it look implausible, the reason you did the thing that everyone misread. There is one person in the universe who has never once misunderstood you, and he is the one who went to a cross knowing all of it in advance.

The shape of their praying is worth copying, too. They did not ask God to reveal his choice and then sit back; they did the work first. They established the qualifications from Scripture, applied them honestly, narrowed the field to two men who genuinely met them, and only then said: show us. Guidance in the Bible almost always arrives on the far side of homework. God is not usually in the business of doing for people the part they could have done with a clear head and an open Bible.

The last clause is the darkest in the chapter and the church handles it in six words. Judas turned aside to go to his own place. They do not enlarge on it, do not speculate about it, and do not soften it. The phrase says only that he arrived somewhere that fitted him, a destination matched to a direction he had been travelling for years. The restraint is a lesson in itself. Where Scripture draws a line and stops, it is safest to stop there too — and it is telling that the men who had most cause to be bitter about Judas said less about his end than almost any preacher since.

verseByVerse.quote: And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two stones, or two marked pieces of pottery, go into a fold of cloth. Somebody shakes it, and one falls out. That is how the twelfth apostle of Jesus Christ was appointed, and a modern reader is right to find it startling. But it was not superstition and it was not a coin toss dressed up in prayer. Casting lots was a means God had himself appointed in Israel — the land was divided by it, the scapegoat on the Day of Atonement was chosen by it (Leviticus 16:8), the priests' courses were arranged by it — and the proverb that governs the practice says exactly what the eleven were counting on: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Proverbs 16:33). They were not gambling. They were using the last instrument of the old order on the last morning it existed. And then the lot disappears from the New Testament entirely. It is never used again after this chapter, because ten days later God moved in. Matthias is numbered with the eleven; the Twelve stand complete, matching the twelve tribes they were always meant to answer to; and the church is ready for what is about to happen to it.

So how does God guide you today, if not by lots? Not by dice, omens, or 'putting out a fleece,' but by the settled means he has since given in fuller measure: his completed Word ('a lamp to my feet,' Ps. 119:105), the indwelling Spirit, prayer, sanctified wisdom, and the counsel of godly friends. The lot belonged to the brief gap before Pentecost and before the New Testament was written; we stand on the far side of both, and are the richer for it.

One more question hangs over this passage and is asked more often than any other about it: did they get it wrong? A good many teachers have said so. The argument runs that the eleven acted in the flesh — using lots before the Spirit had come, jumping ahead of God — and that the real twelfth apostle was Paul, whom the Lord would choose himself a few chapters later. It is usually pressed by noting that Matthias is never mentioned again.

The evidence does not support it. Luke records the episode without a breath of disapproval, and he is not a man who hides the church's failures — he will tell us about Ananias lying to the Spirit, about the Greek-speaking widows being neglected, about Paul and Barnabas quarrelling so sharply that they parted company. Here there is no such note. On the contrary, when the Spirit falls in the next chapter Peter stands up with the eleven (2:14), which makes twelve, and Luke says nothing to suggest the number is wrong. Nor were they improvising: Peter is following a text, and the text says let another take his office (Ps. 109:8). They prayed before they drew, and they used the means God himself had appointed for exactly this purpose (Prov. 16:33). Doing the last legitimate thing of the old era, on the last morning of it, is not the same as acting in the flesh.

The silence about Matthias afterwards proves nothing either, because Acts is silent about nearly all of them. Ten of the Twelve are never heard from again in this book; only Peter and John get a narrative. By that test the whole apostolate was a mistake. And Paul cannot have been the man in view here, because he fails the stated qualification in the plainest way: the replacement had to have accompanied Jesus from John's baptism to the ascension, and Paul had done nothing of the kind. He knows it, and calls himself one untimely born. He is not the twelfth apostle to Israel; he is the apostle to the Gentiles, which is a different thing and no smaller. The Twelve had to be twelve because they answer to the twelve tribes, and Jesus had told them they would sit on twelve thrones judging them (Luke 22:30). The gap had to be closed before Pentecost, and the eleven closed it with Scripture in one hand and prayer on their lips.

1.theology: The Ascension and the Reign of Christ. The ascension is the most neglected event in the Christian calendar — and one of the most theologically freighted. It is not simply that Jesus left; it is that he was enthroned.
