Now: God is not in the habit of waiting for ideal conditions, and he has a long record of using whatever is already lying about — a borrowed upper room, a set of ritual baths, and a preacher with a provincial accent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, "Brothers, what shall we do?" And Peter said to them, "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘Cut to the heart’ — the Spirit-empowered proclamation of the crucified and risen Christ produces genuine conviction: the crowd recognizes their city’s guilt and their own implication. The question ‘What shall we do?’ is the best possible response to the gospel — the response of those who take it seriously enough to ask what it demands. Peter’s answer is two-fold: repent (a turning of the whole self) and be baptized in the name of Jesus (public incorporation into the community of the forgiven). Both produce forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

‘Baptized in the name of Jesus’ — there is an apparent tension with Matthew 28:19, where the risen Christ commands baptism ‘in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’ The two formulas are not contradictory: ‘in the name of Jesus’ is shorthand for the entire trinitarian authority invested in the risen Christ — to be baptized into Jesus is to be baptized into the God who raised him, the Spirit he poured out, the Father who sent him. The Petrine formula identifies the new covenant Lord; the Matthean formula explicates the divine identity of that Lord. Early church practice harmonized them (Didache 7), not because either was deficient, but because each illuminates different facets of the same saving act.

Oneness Pentecostals (the ‘Jesus Only’ movement, early 20th century) have used ‘in the name of Jesus’ passages to argue that trinitarian baptism is invalid and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three Persons but three manifestations of one Person — Jesus. The mainstream church, Eastern and Western Reformed traditions alike, reads the Lukan formula as abbreviation rather than contradiction: no theological reduction of the Trinity is warranted, since the same Acts 2:33 shows Jesus receiving the Spirit from the Father and pouring him out — a scene that requires three genuine divine agents. (cf. Mark 1:15; Rom. 6:3–4)

‘Be baptized... for the forgiveness of sins’ raises a question worth settling: does the water itself wash sins away? The Reformed and broadly Protestant answer is no — baptism is the God-given sign and seal of the forgiveness that is received through repentance and faith, not the cause of it. Forgiveness is by grace through faith in the blood of Christ (‘everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins,’ Acts 10:43; Eph. 1:7), which is why the dying thief was saved with no baptism at all (Luke 23:43). So we do not rest our hope in the water but in Christ, to whom the water points. (Our Roman Catholic and ‘Churches of Christ’ friends read it differently, holding that baptism actually conveys the new birth — ‘baptismal regeneration’; the difference is real, and turns on whether the rite signifies grace or effects it.)

verseByVerse.quote: "For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scope of the promise is breathtaking in its breadth: you (those present), your children (future generations), 'all who are far off' (Diaspora Jews and, by implication, Gentiles — cf. Ephesians 2:13). The boundary of the promise is not ethnic or geographic but covenantal: 'everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.' Election and invitation are held together: God calls, and the called must repent. The gospel is universal in its offer; the Spirit is sovereign in its application.

'The promise is for you and for your children' stands near the heart of a long, friendly disagreement among Bible-loving Christians over who should be baptized. The Reformed and Presbyterian (infant-baptist) reading sees an unbroken covenant pattern: God has always included the children of believers in the covenant and its sign (circumcision in the Old Testament, Gen. 17; now baptism), so believers' infants receive the sign as covenant children, awaiting their own personal faith. The Baptist (believer's-baptism) reading takes 'your children' simply as offspring who, like everyone, must themselves repent and believe to receive the promise — noting the very next clause, 'everyone whom the Lord our God calls' — and so baptizes only those who profess faith. Both honour Scripture and the gospel of grace; the difference turns on how much the old covenant sign carries over into the new. (It is held charitably even within Reformed circles, which include both convictions.) These notes are written from a Reformed vantage, but the point you must not miss is the one both sides shout together: the promise is sheer grace, and it is offered to you and yours.

verseByVerse.quote: And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, "Save yourselves from this crooked generation." So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things in these verses are usually read straight past, and both change them.

The first is that we are not being given the sermon. With many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them — Luke has handed us a digest. What survives of Peter's Pentecost sermon takes about three minutes to read aloud; he was at it a great deal longer, and the verb Luke uses for the exhorting is a continuing one. He kept going. Whatever else the first Christian preacher did, he did not stop when he had covered the material.

The second is the grammar of the famous sentence, and it turns the sentence inside out. Save yourselves from this crooked generation sounds in English like an instruction to perform a rescue: pull yourself together, extract yourself, do something. In Greek it is passive — be saved. Peter is not telling these people to save themselves. He is telling them to let themselves be saved, to stop resisting a rescue that is being carried out on them. A man in a burning building is not told to put the fire out. He is told to stop arguing and be carried down the stairs.

That is not pedantry about a tense. It is the difference between the gospel and every other religion on earth, and it happens to sit inside a verse that is regularly quoted to prove the opposite.

Notice, too, what they are being saved from. Not from hell in the abstract, and not from the world in the sense of leaving town: from this crooked generation. The phrase comes out of the Song of Moses, where God calls his own covenant people a crooked and twisted generation (Deuteronomy 32:5). Peter takes Moses' description of Israel and lays it on the Israel standing in front of him, which is an extraordinarily hard thing to say to a devout crowd on a feast day, and he says it anyway. A generation is not something a man can resign from. Nobody chooses his parents, his decade, or the assumptions he absorbed before he was old enough to examine them. He can only be taken out.

Then the number, and it carries an echo the crowd's Bible readers would not have missed. When Moses came down from Sinai and found the nation dancing round a calf, three thousand men fell that day (Exodus 32:28). The law came, and three thousand died. Here the Spirit comes, and three thousand live. Paul later reduced the principle to a sentence: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

One practical question a reader may feel too foolish to ask: where do you baptise three thousand people in a city with no river? The answer is that Jerusalem was already built for it. The southern approach to the temple was honeycombed with stepped immersion pools cut into the bedrock so that pilgrims could purify themselves before going up; dozens have been excavated and can still be walked into today. The apostles did not have to improvise a single thing. The plumbing of the old covenant was standing ready on the morning the new one needed it.

And one guard, because this verse has bruised a great many faithful people. Three thousand in a day is not the measure of a ministry. The same Spirit produced this and produced Jeremiah, who preached for forty years to a nation that never turned, and was right the whole time. Numbers are God's business and are not issued as a report card. What is asked of a preacher is what Peter did here — bear witness, keep exhorting, and leave the cutting of hearts to somebody better qualified.

verseByVerse.quote: And they devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke's word for what they did is stronger than devoted may suggest to an English ear. It means to stick at a thing, to hold on, to stay put. It is used of a boat kept standing by ready for Jesus, of the apostles refusing to be pulled off prayer and the word (6:4), and, memorably, of Simon Magus attaching himself to Philip and not going away (8:13). It is not the vocabulary of attendance. It is the vocabulary of a man who has got hold of something and will not be prised off it. And Luke puts it in a tense meaning they kept on doing it.

Then four things — and in Greek each has the definite article: the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, the prayers. Not four qualities to aspire to. Four items you could have been taken to and shown.

The apostles' teaching comes first because everything else has to be measured against it. Three thousand brand-new believers had just witnessed wind, fire and a miracle of languages — and what they were put on was a syllabus. That is a remarkable piece of pastoral judgement, and it runs against every instinct: the correction of an overwhelming experience is not more experience but more truth. What the apostles taught then is the book a reader has open in front of him now, which means there is no way to be devoted to the apostles' teaching and casual about the New Testament. They are the same devotion.

The fellowship is a word worn thin by use. In this chapter it costs money within three verses. It is not the conversation afterwards; it is a shared life, in which what belongs to one is genuinely available to another.

The breaking of bread almost certainly covers both ordinary meals and the Lord's Supper, which in this period were not separated — the table where the bread was broken in remembrance was the table where supper was eaten. It is worth stopping on the fact that Christ's chosen memorial of himself is not a monument, an annual ceremony or a pilgrimage, but the most ordinary act of a human day.

The prayers, plural and definite, very likely includes the set hours of prayer at the temple, which the apostles were still keeping a chapter later (3:1). The first Christians did not invent a devotional life from nothing. They took the one they already had and prayed it to a Lord they could now name.

Here is the use to make of this verse, and the use not to make. Any believer can run the list over his own life in half a minute and find out where he actually stands, which is a mercy, because most people's sense of how they are doing spiritually is governed by how they feel that week rather than by anything checkable. But it is a description of what the Spirit produced in a healthy church, not a set of hoops to be cleared for approval, and it is not a stick. Nobody in this verse is doing these four things in order to be accepted. They had been forgiven that morning. This is simply what forgiven people turned out to want.

verseByVerse.quote: And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. And all who believed were together and had all things in common.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Awe came upon every soul. The word is simply fear, the ordinary Greek word for being afraid, and Luke chooses it deliberately. Something was in that city which people did not handle casually. The same reaction runs through the church again in chapter 5, on a far darker morning: a community genuinely aware that God is present does not become breezy about it.

That is worth weighing, because a good deal of modern Christian atmosphere is engineered to be the opposite — to keep everyone comfortable and the temperature at room level. The first church was joyful; Luke says so explicitly three verses later. It was also afraid. It did not experience the two as being in competition, and any picture of God that has to shed one in order to keep the other has quietly lost him.

Many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles — the tense is continuous, so this is a season rather than a single burst. And the preposition is doing work: through. Luke is careful all the way through this book never to let an apostle become the source of anything.

Then the sentence that has caused more argument than any other in the chapter: all who believed were together and had all things in common. Three things need saying, and the third is the one usually skipped.

First, it was not compulsory. Peter says so outright a few chapters on, when Ananias sells a field and lies about the price: while it remained unsold, was it not your own, and after it was sold was it not at your disposal? (5:4). The property was theirs. Nobody was assessed. Luke is not describing a system imposed on a community; he is describing something a community did.

Second, it did not abolish ownership as such. They still had homes to break bread in three verses later, and Mary the mother of John Mark still has a house with a gate and a servant girl in chapter 12. This is selling as needs arose, not the founding of a commune.

Third — and this is the honest part, which people who are eager to say it was not communism often stop just short of — none of that lets the reader off. The text still says that these people held what they owned so loosely that men sold land in order to feed strangers they had met that month, and that in consequence nobody among them lacked anything. Whatever the arrangement was not, that is what it was. A church can be perfectly orthodox about private property and completely unlike this.

Which suggests a test, and it is narrower and less comfortable than the one people usually apply. The question is not whether a Christian would give if he were asked. It is whether he would know. In a congregation of any size, is there anyone quietly going without whom nobody has noticed? The Jerusalem church knew, which means somebody had asked — and the asking is where the whole thing begins.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tenses carry this verse, and English hides them. Luke does not say they sold their possessions and distributed the proceeds, as though there had been one great liquidation on a particular afternoon. He says they were selling and were distributing — continuous, repeated, going on. This is not a founding event. It is what kept happening, week after week, as needs came up: somebody's situation became known, a field or a house was sold, the money went where it was needed, and a month later it happened again.

That changes the picture, and it makes it harder rather than easier. A single dramatic act of renunciation has a certain appeal, and it has the great advantage of being over. What Luke describes is the far more expensive business of remaining permanently available.

Then the criterion, and it should be read precisely: as any had need. Not equally. Not by formula. The measure is need, which means somebody had to know what the needs were and exercise judgement about them — and that requires a community close enough that a widow's circumstances are not a private matter she has to raise herself. It also means the money did not go where it was not needed, which is worth saying to anyone who has watched generosity administered by people who never met the recipient.

And the arrangement was not perfect, which Luke does not conceal. Within four chapters the distribution has broken down along language lines — the Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked in the daily service, and the apostles had to restructure the leadership of the church to put it right (6:1). Luke could have left that out. He includes it, and a reader should notice both what that says about Luke and what it says about the church. The first congregation, filled with the Spirit and running on extraordinary generosity, still developed a problem that fell along ethnic lines within a few years. Radical love does not exempt an institution from needing structures — and the people who complained were right to complain.

This verse is often preached in a way that leaves ordinary Christians feeling vaguely guilty about owning a house, which produces a low hum of unease and no actual giving. Something more useful is available in it. These people did not resolve to become generous. They had, that spring, been forgiven an unpayable debt by a man they had helped to kill, and had been handed the Spirit of God as a free gift when what they had coming was judgement. Money went out of their hands because something enormous had come into them. Generosity here is a symptom, and symptoms are not produced by being scolded about symptoms.

verseByVerse.quote: And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two settings in one sentence, and the church has needed both ever since. Attending the temple together — the largest sacred enclosure in the ancient world, thirty-five acres of stone, where a man stands in a crowd of thousands and is one voice in it. And breaking bread in their homes — a room where the loaf has to be passed from hand to hand and everybody present is known by name. Nothing the temple does can be done in the kitchen, and nothing the kitchen does can be done in the temple. Congregations tend to be strong in one and thin in the other, and to make a virtue of whichever they happen to have.

Notice as well that the temple is still in use. These are not people who have walked out of Israel's worship. They are Jews who have found out what it was for. The break comes later, and when it comes it is forced on them.

Day by day appears twice in these two verses — once of their meeting and once of the Lord's adding. The rhythm of the thing is daily, which is not a rule to be laid on a modern week, but it is a comment on what they wanted. Nobody had instructed them to meet every day.

With glad and generous hearts — the second word is unusual and appears nowhere else in the New Testament. It means something like singleness, or simplicity: the absence of a hidden agenda. Set beside gladness, it describes a table at which nobody is angling for anything, and anyone who has sat at the other kind of table will recognise that as rarer than it sounds.

Then a phrase that has to be handled honestly: having favour with all the people. It is true, and it does not last. Within two chapters the apostles are under arrest; within five, one of their number is dead; within six, a persecution has scattered the church out of the city. Luke is describing a season, not issuing a promise. It is a mistake to read this line as though a faithful church will always be liked — Jesus said plainly that it would not be — and it is an equal mistake to treat unpopularity as evidence of faithfulness. Sometimes a church is disliked because it is faithful and sometimes because it is unpleasant, and the two are not told apart by measuring how disliked it is.

And then the last clause, which is where Luke chooses to set the chapter down. The Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved. Not the apostles added. Not the preaching added. The Lord added — and the verb is continuous, so he kept on doing it. Peter had preached the sermon of his life that morning and three thousand had come in; and when Luke comes to summarise what was actually happening, the credit goes somewhere else entirely.

Which is the fitting end to a chapter that opened with a sound nobody in the room produced. Everything in Acts 2 comes down from somewhere else: the wind, the fire, the languages, the exaltation of Christ, the Spirit poured out, the cutting of three thousand hearts, and now the daily arrival of people who were being saved. The church did not launch itself and has never once grown itself. It was given a Lord who had been raised, given a Spirit who had been promised, and given, morning after morning, the people he had decided to add. The right response to a chapter like this one is not a strategy. It is worship.

2.theology: The Sovereignty of God at the Cross. Acts 2:23 is the Reformed doctrine of divine sovereignty distilled to a sentence. The cross happened “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God.” The word translated “definite plan” means God’s eternal counsel, his settled, unalterable purpose. This is not foreknowledge in the Arminian sense of God merely looking ahead and seeing what humans would choose. This is foreordination: God planned the cross before the world began (1 Peter 1:20, Revelation 13:8). Total depravity and sovereign grace appear in one verse: the guilt is wholly human, the purpose is wholly divine. The cross is the intersection of man’s worst deed and God’s greatest gift.
2.examples:
Then: The feast of Pentecost was transformed on this day from an agricultural harvest festival into the birthday of the church. Devout Jews from fifteen regions of the empire heard the mighty works of God proclaimed in their mother tongues and were cut to the heart. The harvest that day was three thousand souls.

Now: Every Lord’s Day is a Pentecost echo. The same Spirit, the same Word, the same call to repentance — and the same Lord who adds to his church those who are being saved. The question for every preacher and every congregation is whether we are as devoted to the apostles’ teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers as that first gathering was. The form has not changed. The power has not diminished.

3.title: The Lame Man and the Living Lord
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. <sup>2</sup>And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple. <sup>3</sup>Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms. <sup>4</sup>And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.” <sup>5</sup>And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them. <sup>6</sup>But Peter said, “I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!” <sup>7</sup>And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong. <sup>8</sup>And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God. <sup>9</sup>And all the people saw him walking and praising God, <sup>10</sup>and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. <sup>11</sup>While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon’s Portico. <sup>12</sup>And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk? <sup>13</sup>The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him. <sup>14</sup>But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, <sup>15</sup>and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses. <sup>16</sup>And his name—by faith in his name—has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all. <sup>17</sup>“And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. <sup>18</sup>But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled. <sup>19</sup>Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out, <sup>20</sup>that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, <sup>21</sup>whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago. <sup>22</sup>Moses said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you. <sup>23</sup>And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people.’ <sup>24</sup>And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days. <sup>25</sup>You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.’ <sup>26</sup>God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness.”
3.overview:
Silver and gold has Peter none. This is not a confession of poverty but a declaration of what he does have: “In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk.” The man at the Beautiful Gate has been lame from birth — forty years of sitting, of watching others enter the temple he could not enter, of reaching out his hand to receive what others chose to give. In one moment, at the word of Peter and the power of the risen Christ, his ankles are strengthened, and he goes in walking and leaping and praising God. He who could not enter the temple now cannot stop praising the God of the temple.

But Luke wants us to see more than a healing. The sermon that follows is the point. Peter will not let the crowd look at him; he points them past himself to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob who has glorified his servant Jesus. The healing is a sign — what God has done in this man’s body is a picture of what God is doing in the world: the lame are walking, the guilty are forgiven, the dead are raised. All of it through the name that is above every name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Healing at the Beautiful Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two men on their way to a prayer meeting, and a beggar who wants a coin. Nothing in the opening of this chapter announces a turning point. Peter and John are keeping the three o'clock hour of prayer, as they have all their lives. The man at the gate is doing what he has done every working day for forty years. Both parties are on rails.

Then Peter stops, and the first thing he does is not a miracle. It is to look at the man, and to make the man look back — Look at us. A beggar's trade is conducted with lowered eyes on both sides: the hand goes out, the coin comes down, and neither face is seen. Peter takes that arrangement apart before he says anything at all about Jesus, and the man lifts his head expecting a better than usual donation. What he gets is the sentence the church has never found a substitute for — no silver, no gold, and the name of Jesus of Nazareth.

Then he goes into the temple, which is the detail to hold. He had been set down outside its most magnificent door every morning of his adult life, and now he walks through it on his own feet, and jumps, which is not something a man who has never walked knows how to do. And the crowd recognised him. Verses 9 and 10 carry the whole evidential weight of this chapter and of the trial that follows: he was not a stranger who might have been anybody, he was part of the furniture of the place, and everyone in Jerusalem had stepped round him. Which is why, when the council meets the next morning to decide what to do, the one thing it cannot say is that nothing happened (4:16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Signs, and What They Are Signs Of

The healings in Acts are called signs, and a sign is not the destination; it is a board at the roadside with the name of the destination written on it. These are not displays of power for their own sake, and they are certainly not the working of impersonal forces — Luke will show us in this same book what happens when men try to use the name as a technique (19:13–16). They are the personal act of a risen King through men he has authorised, and what they point to is the repair of a world that has been broken since Eden. A man's ankles are made whole in the middle of Jerusalem, and the thing being said is about everything: a day is coming when the whole creation will be put right, and here is a down payment on it, walking about in the temple courts and making a good deal of noise. Reformed theology has also read the apostolic signs as authenticating the apostolic message, which is why Scripture ties them so closely to the apostles themselves, and why the long argument over whether such things continue is an argument about their function and never about whether God is able.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The man asked for alms and got his legs. But Luke is careful about what else he got: he went into the temple, which he had never done. The gate he sat at was the boundary of his whole life, and he had spent forty years on the wrong side of it with his hand out. He received his body back, and his place with it. Now: The church still meets people asking for the small thing because it is the only thing they know how to ask for, and it still has no silver worth mentioning. What it has is a name. The temptation in every generation is to be embarrassed by that and to offer something more respectable instead.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three details in this opening sentence are doing quiet work.

The ninth hour. Three in the afternoon, when the evening lamb was killed on the great altar and the incense went up, and the whole city knew the hour by the sound of it. It is also, as any reader of Luke's first volume knows, the hour at which Jesus died (Luke 23:44–46). Peter and John are going up to pray at the hour of the sacrifice, into a building where a lamb is being killed, some months after watching the real one die at that same hour. Luke makes nothing of it. He simply tells us the time.

Peter and John. Luke keeps putting these two together — sent ahead to prepare the Passover, running to the tomb, and later sent down together to Samaria (8:14). On paper it is an odd pairing, the loud one and the quiet one, and it lasted for years. Whatever else the church is, it is not an arrangement in which everybody has to be the same shape.

Lame from birth. Not an accident, not an illness he might have recovered from; he had never taken a step. And the next chapter tells us he was over forty years old (4:22), which turns a phrase into a life. Somebody carried him out every morning and carried him home every night for something like twelve thousand days. Whoever they were, Luke does not name them. There is a family in this story doing forty years of unrecorded lifting.

And where they set him down is the point. The gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate was most likely the great bronze doorway on the eastern side, of which Josephus says that twenty men were needed to close it and that it far surpassed the gates plated with silver and gold. So he sat at the most magnificent doorway in the Jewish world, and he could not go through it. The law barred a priest with a lame leg from approaching the altar to offer (Leviticus 21:18); an old saying attached to David's capture of the city held that the blind and the lame should not come into the house (2 Samuel 5:8); the strict community at Qumran excluded the lame from its assembly outright. Whether or not any written regulation formally shut this particular man out of the inner courts, everyone in Jerusalem knew where he belonged: outside, at the door, with his hand out.

So a man is carried daily to the threshold of the place where God had promised to meet his people, and set down in the last position from which he can see in without going in. If a picture were wanted of religion at its most exquisite and least useful, it would be hard to improve on this: the most beautiful gate in the world, a man who cannot walk through it, and a system with nothing to offer him but the small change of the people who can.

One thing should be said before the miracle, because this chapter is sometimes read in a way that quietly insults people. Nothing here suggests the man's condition was a punishment, or that it revealed anything whatever about him personally, and Jesus had already refused that entire way of thinking. What the exclusion at the gate exposes is not a defect in the man. It is a limit in the arrangement — and within a few verses the arrangement is going to be walked straight through by somebody it had shut out.

verseByVerse.quote: Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A single verse, and the most ordinary sentence in the chapter. He sees two men about to go in, and he asks for money. He has asked ten thousand times; there will be a way of saying it, a pitch worn smooth with use, and the words will be out before he has properly looked at them.

Notice what he does not ask for. It does not occur to him to ask to be healed. Why would it? He was born like this, nothing in forty years has ever suggested another possibility, and the two men in front of him look poorer than most of the crowd going past. He asks for what he knows how to ask for. The request is entirely reasonable and enormously too small.

There is something here worth taking personally, and a guard to put round it first. The guard: this is not an argument for asking God for larger things on the theory that he is then obliged to produce them, a doctrine with a great deal of wreckage behind it. The thing worth taking is quieter. Scripture says plainly that we do not know what to pray for as we ought (Romans 8:26), which is not a rebuke but a mercy, because it means our prayers are not the ceiling. This man received what he had not asked for, could not have imagined, and had no faith for; he was still expecting coins when Peter took hold of his hand.

But a harder question sits in this verse, and it should not be walked past, because a suffering reader will find it whether or not the commentary points at it. This man was carried to that gate every day for decades. Jesus of Nazareth went in and out of that temple repeatedly, feast after feast, for three years. He must have passed him. And the man was still lame on the afternoon Peter came by.

There is no way of making that comfortable, and an attempt would be worse than the silence. What can be said is that Scripture never presents God's healing as a service delivered evenly, and never pretends otherwise. At a pool in this same city a multitude of sick people lay in five colonnades, and Jesus healed one man and left. Elisha cured a foreign general of leprosy and left many lepers in Israel uncured — and Jesus said so out loud in his first sermon, to a congregation that tried to throw him off a cliff for it (Luke 4:27). The pattern is not accidental and it is not concealed. It is stated, by the Lord himself, to people who did not want to hear it.

Which makes the timing here worth looking at squarely. Forty years of being carried to a gate looked, from inside those years, like forty years of nothing happening. It turns out to have been forty years of a man being kept for an afternoon when his healing would be witnessed by the whole population of the city, would be admitted as undeniable by the highest court in the nation, and would put five thousand men within hearing of the gospel (4:4). He had not been overlooked.

That is said about this man, and it is not a formula to be laid over anyone else's forty years. Luke tells us what God did here; he does not tell us what God is doing in every case, and a person who says otherwise to somebody in the middle of it is guessing. But it is worth knowing that this delay had a shape, because from inside a delay there appears to be no shape at all.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, "Look at us." And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the word of power there is a look, and Luke gives it four verbs in two verses: Peter directed his gaze, John did the same, the man was told to look, and he fixed his attention. Nothing has happened yet except that two men and a beggar are looking at each other, and Luke thought it worth the ink.

The verb he uses of Peter is a strong one — a fixed, deliberate stare, the same word used later of Stephen looking into heaven and of Paul looking straight at the council about to try him. It is not a glance. Peter stops, and locks on.

Consider what that interrupts. The transaction at a beggar's pitch is arranged so that nobody has to look at anybody. The hand goes out, the eyes go down, the coin is dropped from above, and the giver walks on having discharged something without once meeting a face. It is efficient, and both parties are protected by it — the giver from the person, and the beggar from the humiliation of being seen. Most people avoid a beggar's eye for the perfectly honest reason that they intend to give nothing, or to give a little and go.

Look at us. Peter dismantles the arrangement, and he does it before there is any healing on offer — which means that for a moment the man is simply a person being addressed, probably for the first time that day and possibly the first time that week.

It should be said that this is not a method to be copied in the hope of results; Peter is not doing a thing that works. But there is an order in it that does travel. Attention comes before help. Whatever else the church has been given to do, it cannot do any of it for people it will not look at — and a great deal of Christian charity is organised, with the best intentions in the world, so that nobody has to.

And notice what the man is doing at the end of verse 5: expecting to receive something from them. He is wrong about what and entirely right about who. He is looking at the right men with far too small a hope, which is a more promising position than the alternatives, and God has a long record of meeting people exactly there.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!" And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. A name in that world was not a label. It stood for the person and everything he was — his authority, his standing, his will — which is why a king's officer acted in the name of the king and expected to be obeyed as though the king were present in the room. Peter is not reciting an incantation. He is standing at a temple gate as the accredited representative of somebody who is not visibly there, and doing exactly what such a man does: acting on his master's authority, in his master's name, in public.

And notice which name he uses. Of Nazareth — the address, the sneer, the thing written on the board over the cross a few months earlier for the whole city to read on its way past. Peter does not reach for a dignified title. He uses the one that had been used to dismiss the man and to execute him, and it puts a cripple on his feet.

Then the touch. He took him by the right hand and raised him up — and the verb Luke chooses for raised is the one used throughout the New Testament of the resurrection. The gesture is a small enactment of the thing being announced: a man who cannot get up is pulled upright by somebody who has met the one God raised. And Luke, who was a physician, then gets more specific than anyone else in the New Testament — his feet and ankles were made strong, using a term for the ankle bones that appears nowhere else in the Greek Bible. He is telling us which joints took the weight.

Do not hurry past the first half of what Peter says, because it is the half people remember. I have no silver and gold. The leading apostle of the church, in the days of its greatest power, is standing at the temple gate without money. He is not withholding it on principle; he does not have it. And he does not brush the man's need aside either — he gives what he has, which turns out to be a great deal more than what was asked for.

There is an old story, told of a medieval pope showing a visitor the treasures of Rome, who remarked that the church could no longer say silver and gold have I none — and was answered, neither can she now say rise up and walk. Whether it happened as told or not, the point is worth keeping. Power in the church has never been carried in its purse, and the two have a way of trading places.

It is also worth setting beside the teaching that God's favour shows itself in wealth, and that a believer who lacks money is short of faith. Here is the man through whom this miracle came, and he has nothing in his pockets. On that account he was either the least favoured man in Jerusalem or the doctrine is wrong. Not that poverty is holiness — this same church will take up collections and handle money carefully. But what Peter had to give was not for sale, and no amount of silver would have bought it.

One guard, and Luke himself supplies it later in this same book. There were men at Ephesus who heard about the name and tried to work it as a formula — I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims — and it went extremely badly for them (19:13–16). The name is not a lever. It works here because Peter belongs to the one who owns it, and it has never once worked for anybody who wanted the effect without the allegiance.

And then the scale of the exchange should be allowed to land. A man asks two strangers for the price of a meal. What is given him instead is the power that raised Christ from the dead, applied to his ankle bones, at three in the afternoon, at the door of a building he had never been inside. He asked for the smallest thing anyone had ever asked those two men for, and he was answered from the throne of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke piles up the verbs, and the pile is the point: leaping up, standing, beginning to walk, entering, walking, leaping, praising. Seven actions in one sentence, from a man who had never performed any of them.

Stop on the leaping, because it is stranger than it looks. A man lame from birth has never learned to walk. Even supposing the legs were suddenly sound, balance and coordination and the whole unconscious skill of putting one foot in front of the other are learned in infancy over months of falling down. He does not fall down. He is given the legs and the use of them in the same instant, and his first instinct with a working body is to jump.

Isaiah had used that very word. Then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy (Isaiah 35:6) — and it is worth knowing what sort of chapter that comes out of, because it is not a list of medical predictions. Isaiah 35 is a poem about a desert that blossoms and a highway running through it, and the ransomed of the LORD coming home to Zion with singing and everlasting joy on their heads. The leaping man is one line in a song about the end of exile. What breaks out in the temple courts that afternoon is a fragment of that poem arriving early.

And he goes in. Set down at that gate morning after morning for forty years and never once through it, he now walks in with the two men, on his own feet, making a scene. The place of worship, which for his whole life had been the building he was carried to and not into, is the first place he goes.

What he does with the new legs is worth noticing, because it is not what most people would predict. He does not go home. He does not go looking for work, or for whoever had been carrying him, or to walk the streets of a city he had only ever seen from a sitting position. He goes into the house of God and praises, and Luke says it twice in one verse in case the reader is moving too fast.

There is something in that for anyone who has had a prayer answered and then found out how quickly an answer becomes the new normal. This man's gratitude is loud, immediate, physical and entirely undignified, and nobody in the narrative asks him to keep it down. There is a kind of praise that only comes from people who remember exactly what they were like before — and a church is generally poorer in proportion to how fast it forgets.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people saw him walking and praising God, and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These two verses look like scene-setting. They are in fact the hinge on which the next chapter turns.

All the people saw him... and recognised him. That word carries the whole evidential weight of the chapter. He was not a stranger who might have been anybody. He had been at that gate every day for decades; he was part of the furniture of the place, the way a particular tree or a particular doorway is; every worshipper going up to pray had stepped round him, and a great many had put something in his hand. There was no room for a substitution, no possibility of mistaken identity, and no scope for saying the case had been overstated.

Which is precisely what the Sanhedrin runs into the following morning. They meet, they consult, and the sentence Luke records out of that meeting is among the most remarkable in the book: we cannot deny it (4:16). The most powerful body in the nation, actively hostile, with every motive in the world to find a hole in the story, examines it and concludes that a notable sign has been done and the whole of Jerusalem knows. It then forbids the apostles to speak — which is not what men do when they have exposed a fraud. It is what men do when they have run into something true that they did not want.

Luke gives the crowd two words for their reaction. The first means a stunned, arrested wonder; the second is the word for being put out of one's own mind. Neither is faith. This is the condition a person is in when the shape of the world has just changed and nothing has yet replaced it, and it is exactly the condition Peter is about to preach into. Astonishment is not conversion, and Luke never confuses the two: a crowd can be amazed at an act of God and still need telling what it means. Which is why the miracle takes ten verses and the sermon takes sixteen.

And it is worth noticing how the whole thing was arranged. God healed the one man in Jerusalem whose condition every single person in the city was in a position to verify, at the busiest hour of the day, at the most public gate of the temple, in front of the crowd going up to pray. Nothing about it is quiet. He is perfectly capable of working where nobody sees, and does so constantly; but when he intends a thing to stand as evidence, he puts it where it cannot be filed away, and then he lets his enemies examine it at their leisure.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Peter cannot do a miracle without preaching one. The crowd runs together under Solomon's colonnade, staring at the two men who have just done something impossible, and Peter's opening words are a refusal: why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk? Everything that follows is an attempt to get the crowd's eyes off the apostles and onto a name.

The sermon is short and extraordinarily dense. Jesus is God's servant, which is Isaiah's word for the one who would be wounded for our transgressions; the Holy and Righteous One; the Author of life, whom they killed, which is a sentence with an absurdity built into it. He is the prophet Moses promised, and the offspring in whom, by the covenant with Abraham, every family on earth was to be blessed. Peter lays the whole Old Testament in front of them and says it has been about this man the entire time.

Then it turns, and verses 17 and 18 are the pivot: brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance. That is not an excuse; it is the one door the law of Moses ever left open, and Peter walks his hearers through it. Verse 19 calls for repentance and turning, so that sins may be blotted out — wiped off the page like ink off papyrus. Then a promise of times of refreshing and of a day when everything is restored, and immediately alongside it, in verse 23, the hardest sentence in the chapter: every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people. Peter offers no mercy that has not been made costly by a real warning.

And the warning is not the last word. Verse 26 closes the sermon on a definition of blessing, and it is not the definition most people use: God sent his servant to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness. In the city that had killed him, to the people who had asked for a murderer instead, the blessing comes first — and it consists of being turned round.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus as the Fulfilment of the Covenant with Abraham

Peter closes on Genesis 22:18 — in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed — and it matters a great deal where that sentence comes from. It is spoken on the mountain, after the knife is stopped and the ram is found caught in the thicket: the promise that the whole world would be blessed through Abraham's line is given at the exact moment God provides a substitute for a beloved son. Peter quotes it in a sermon about a beloved Son for whom no substitute was provided. The gospel, on this reading, is not the abandonment of God's promises to Israel but their arrival — not a second plan drawn up after the first failed, but the first plan reaching the date it had been set for. Reformed biblical theology insists that the covenant of grace runs unbroken from Genesis to Revelation and finds its definitive form in Christ, which is why Peter can preach this to Jews in the temple courts without once suggesting that they should change religion.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter preached to people who bore the most direct responsibility there was — you denied the Holy and Righteous One — and then called them brothers four verses later and told them the blessing was coming to them first. Now: The order has never changed. A gospel that cannot name what a man has actually done has nothing to forgive him for; a gospel that names it and leaves him standing there is not the gospel at all. Peter does both in one sermon, and the second half is longer than the first.

verseByVerse.quote: While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon's. And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: "Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first thing Luke tells us about the healed man is that he would not let go. While he clung to Peter and John — the verb means to grip, to hold fast. A man who has been dependent his whole life has just been made independent, and his instinct is to hang on to the two people who did it. It is a small, entirely human detail, and Luke keeps it.

The crowd runs together in the portico called Solomon's, and the location is worth knowing. It was the long colonnade running down the eastern side of the temple platform, the one part of the complex popularly believed to have survived from Solomon's original building — a sheltered walkway of columns where people gathered out of the weather. It is where Jesus was walking at the Feast of Dedication when the crowd closed round him and demanded that he tell them plainly whether he was the Christ, and where they took up stones to kill him for the answer (John 10:23–31). It is also where the church will later meet as a matter of habit (5:12). Peter is preaching Christ on the exact stones where Christ was nearly stoned for preaching himself.

Then the refusal, and it repays taking word by word. Why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk? Peter disclaims two things, and the second is the one people miss. He disclaims the power, which anybody would expect. He also disclaims the piety — the word means godliness, personal devotion — and that is the harder disclaimer, because it is the flattering one. A crowd watching a miracle will always conclude that the men involved must be unusually holy, and that is a conclusion which is extremely pleasant to leave uncorrected.

Remember who is speaking. This is the man who, a few hundred yards from where he now stands, swore to a servant girl that he had never met Jesus. If any man in Jerusalem had reason to know that his own godliness was not the operative factor in anything, it was Peter. The deflection is not modesty. It is a matter of information.

But notice what kind of deflection it is, because there is a counterfeit that looks similar and achieves the opposite. Peter does not say it was nothing, and he does not perform the shuffling embarrassment that draws quite as much attention as accepting the credit would have done. He redirects. He names somebody else, immediately and at length, and the crowd's attention goes where he sends it. False modesty keeps the light on the man by making him interesting; genuine deflection moves it. The test is simple enough — when the sentence is finished, who are people looking at?

None of which forbids ordinary gratitude to people who have helped us; Paul thanks his fellow workers by name all over his letters. What it forbids is the transfer of a debt. This crowd was about to pay Peter for something he had not done, in a currency he had no right to accept, and he would not take it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter opens with the oldest name in Israel's vocabulary: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers. It is the name God gave himself at the burning bush, and Peter chooses it deliberately. He is not announcing a new God, a new religion, or a break with anything at all. He is telling a Jewish crowd in the Jewish temple that the God they have worshipped all their lives has just acted.

Then a word a first-century congregation would have caught at once and which passes most modern readers by: God has glorified his servant Jesus. The term is not the ordinary word for a slave, and the phrase sits very close to the opening line of the last of Isaiah's Servant Songs in the Greek Old Testament — behold, my servant... he shall be glorified (Isaiah 52:13), the sentence that begins the passage running straight on into Isaiah 53: the wounds, the silence before the shearers, the grave assigned with the wicked. Peter has said one word and put the whole of Isaiah 53 into the air. His hearers knew that chapter by heart. He does not have to explain it.

Then the charge, delivered without any softening: whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him.

The comparison is deliberate and it is brutal. Pilate — a pagan governor with no covenant, no Scriptures, no promises and no particular appetite for justice — had worked out that the prisoner ought to be let go. The covenant people, standing in front of him, insisted otherwise. Peter is not scoring a rhetorical point. He is describing what happened in that courtyard, and every person listening remembered it, because it had been ten weeks.

One word in the charge deserves attention, and it changes the temperature of the whole sermon. Denied. It is the same verb Luke used, in his first volume, of Peter himself in the high priest's courtyard: he denied it, saying, Woman, I do not know him (Luke 22:57). Peter is standing in the temple accusing a crowd of a sin whose exact name is the one written against him. He is not throwing a stone from a safe distance. He knows what the word weighs because he has carried it, and he has been forgiven for it by the man he is now preaching — which is precisely why he can say this to their faces and call them brothers four verses later. The severity is not the severity of a man who has never done it. It is the severity of a man who has, and who knows what was done about it.

verseByVerse.quote: "But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter now stacks three titles, and each is chosen to make the crowd feel the shape of what was done.

The Holy and Righteous One. Both were recognised descriptions of the Messiah, and both are the opposite of what a court is supposed to condemn. You denied him — the second time Peter uses that verb in three verses, and he presses it because the denial was not an accident of a chaotic morning. It was a choice, made out loud, in a public square, in daylight.

And asked for a murderer to be granted to you. That is Barabbas, and Peter does not name him, because nobody needed reminding. Sit with the transaction a moment. A guilty man was released and an innocent man was executed in his place, at the direct request of the crowd. Barabbas is the first human being for whom Jesus of Nazareth demonstrably died in the plainest sense the words will bear: there was a cross with his name against it, and another man was nailed to it. What the crowd arranged that morning as a miscarriage of justice turned out to be a working diagram of the atonement, and they built it themselves without the faintest idea what they were making.

And you killed the Author of life. The word is one Luke likes: the founder, the originator, the one who goes first and opens a way — it turns up again at 5:31 of the Leader and Saviour. And Peter sets it directly against killed so that the absurdity cannot be missed. You murdered the source of life. It is a sentence with a contradiction built into it, like drowning water, and Peter states it flatly and lets it stand there.

Then, in six words, the reversal — whom God raised from the dead — and then the apostolic signature: to this we are witnesses.

A guard is needed here and should not be skipped, because these are among the verses that have been used to do enormous harm. You denied, you killed: sentences of this kind have been read out from pulpits in Christian Europe and followed within days by violence against Jewish neighbours. Anybody tempted to use them so should read the paragraph they sit in. The speaker is a Jew. The audience is Jewish. The setting is the Jewish temple at the hour of Jewish prayer. He calls them brothers; he says in the next breath that they acted in ignorance; he tells them God sent his servant to you first; and the entire sermon is a plea that they should be blessed. What is happening here is what has always happened when a prophet of Israel addresses Israel — Isaiah called its rulers the rulers of Sodom, and nobody has ever thought Isaiah an enemy of the Jews. Peter is not indicting a people across the centuries. He is telling the men in front of him what they did, in order to tell them what may now be done about it. And the verse that answers the misuse most completely is the one the sermon ends on: God sent his Servant to bless you.

verseByVerse.quote: "And his name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the most tangled sentence in the book of Acts, and it is worth saying so, because a reader who finds it hard to follow is not being slow. Peter doubles back on himself twice — his name, by faith in his name, has made this man strong... and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health. It reads like a man tripping over his own words in his hurry to make sure the credit lands in the right place. He gets the name in twice and the faith in twice, and the grammar takes the damage.

Underneath the tangle is a question that has to be settled, and it is a pastoral question of the first order: whose faith?

It cannot straightforwardly be the man's. Look back at verse 5. He was expecting to receive something from them — a coin. He had no expectation of healing, had not asked for it, did not know it was available, and had, as far as Luke tells us, no opinion whatever about Jesus of Nazareth. He was not healed because he believed hard enough. On the evidence of the previous paragraph, he did not believe at all.

And Peter's own phrasing points elsewhere: the faith that is through Jesus. Whatever faith is operating in this verse comes through Christ. It is not a substance the man manufactured out of himself and presented at the gate. Faith here is something handed down, not a fee paid up.

That matters far more than a point of grammar, because there is an entire style of teaching built on the opposite reading, and it wounds people badly. It tells the sick that they are not healed because their faith was insufficient; it sends them home from a meeting worse off than they came, carrying the illness and an accusation on top of it. It should be said plainly that this verse cannot be used that way. The one man in Scripture whose healing is most explicitly credited to faith in the name of Jesus had never heard the name an hour earlier.

Then the word Peter picks for the result, which appears nowhere else in the New Testament. It means wholeness — sound in every part, nothing left over, nothing half-finished. Not managed, not stabilised, not improved: whole, and in the presence of you all. The healing is complete, public and checkable, and Peter effectively dares the crowd to check it, since the man is standing there still holding on to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here the sermon turns, and it turns on one word: brothers. Two verses ago they were the people who denied the Holy One and killed the Author of life. Now they are family. Nothing has changed about the facts. Peter has simply arrived at the reason he was reciting them.

I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. This is not an acquittal, and Peter does not present it as one; he has just spent three verses establishing precisely what they did. It is something more exact, and to feel its force you have to know how Israel's law handled the distinction.

The law separated two kinds of sin very sharply. For sin committed unintentionally, through ignorance, there was a sacrifice and there was atonement: the offender brought his offering and was forgiven. For sin committed with a high hand — deliberately, in open defiance, knowing exactly what was being done — the law made no provision whatever. That man was to be cut off from among his people (Numbers 15:27–31). There was no sacrifice for it anywhere in the system.

So when Peter says you acted in ignorance, he is not being generous with the truth. He is telling a crowd who have just realised they killed the Messiah which side of that line they are standing on. It is the difference between a case with a remedy and a case without one, and he is handing them the only door the law of Moses ever left open.

He did not invent the assessment either. Paul makes the same judgement — none of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). And Luke, alone of the four evangelists, records a prayer from the cross that says it first and most simply: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34 — some of the earliest copies do not carry the sentence and most Bibles note the fact, but it is very old and it is exactly what the rest of the New Testament assumes). Peter is preaching his master's own prayer back over the heads of the men it was prayed for.

Two guards. Ignorance is not innocence. Paul says of his own persecuting years that he received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief (1 Timothy 1:13) — which is a sentence about mercy, not about acquittal; he still called himself the foremost of sinners. And Scripture is perfectly capable of condemning sincere ignorance, saying elsewhere of Israel that they have a zeal for God but not according to knowledge. Ignorance opens a door. It does not walk anybody through it.

Then verse 18 sets the other half beside it: what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled. The worst thing they ever did is the thing God had been announcing through every prophet since Samuel. Both are true at once, and Peter does not choose between them.

Which is where this passage becomes something to hold on to rather than merely to follow. A reader who is frightened that he has done the thing which cannot be forgiven should look hard at who is being addressed here. These people had, between them, arranged the judicial murder of the Son of God, and had chosen a murderer over him when they were offered the choice. And they are being called brothers, and offered forgiveness, ten weeks later, by one of his friends. Whatever the unforgivable sin may be, it is evidently not this — and the man who is afraid he has committed it is displaying the one symptom that the people who actually have never display.

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two commands, and they are not one command said twice.

Repent is a word about the mind: a change of thinking, a reversal of judgement, a man coming to see a thing the opposite way round from the way he saw it yesterday. Turn back is a word about the feet. It is the ordinary verb for turning round physically, the thing a man does in a street when he realises he has been walking the wrong way. Peter asks for both, and the order is instructive: the mind changes, and then the body goes somewhere different. A repentance that never reaches the feet has stopped halfway; and a change of direction with no change of mind is only a new set of habits, and will not last the winter.

Neither word means feeling bad. Sorrow often comes with repentance and there is nothing wrong with it, but a man can be extremely sorry and turn round nothing at all, and Scripture has a name for that. Nor is this penance, the working off of a debt by suffering something. Peter is not asking them to pay for the crucifixion. He is telling them to change their minds about the man they crucified and to walk the other way.

Then what it is for: that your sins may be blotted out.

The picture in that verb is exact. Ancient ink did not sink into papyrus and stain it the way modern ink stains paper; it sat on the surface, and a wet sponge took it off and left the sheet clean and usable. That is the word. Not the debt reduced. Not the record sealed. Not the file marked closed and filed in a drawer it can be fetched out of. Wiped off — and the page is the same page.

This is where an ordinary Christian most often fails to believe what he says he believes. Ask a man at eleven in the morning whether his sins are forgiven and he will say yes without hesitating. Ask him what happens at three in the morning, when a particular memory arrives — the thing he said, the person he damaged, the year he does not talk about — and a different answer comes out. He keeps his own copy. He has agreed that God wiped the record, and he goes on consulting one that he maintains privately, and he calls the maintenance of it humility.

It is not humility. It is a quiet insistence that the sponge did not work. What Peter told a crowd who had murdered the Son of God is that the record can come off the page altogether; and if that is true of them, then the private file a believer keeps on himself is evidence of nothing except that he has not yet believed the sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: "that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two promises come out of that turning, and both are worth slowing down over.

The first is times of refreshing... from the presence of the Lord. The word behind refreshing means a breathing space, a let-up, relief from pressure; in the Greek Old Testament it turns up in an unlikely place — when the plague of frogs stopped and Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart (Exodus 8:15). It is the word for getting your breath back. And notice where the relief comes from. Not from a change in the circumstances but from the presence of the Lord, which is the difference between a man whose troubles have lifted and a man who has stopped being alone inside them.

The second is about where Jesus is now, and it is one of the very few sentences in the New Testament that says. Whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things. The must is not a restraint laid on him; it is the word Scripture uses for divine necessity, the same sort of must that stood over the cross. Heaven is not detaining Christ. There is an appointed span and he is keeping it — which settles in passing what to make of every claim that he has quietly returned already, or is presently on earth in some concealed form. He is where this sentence says he is, and he stays there until a date that has been fixed.

That phrase, restoring all things, deserves a note, because it is the anchor text of those who teach that in the end everyone will be saved and hell will empty. The Greek behind it gave the doctrine its historic name, and it has been pressed into service from Origen's day to our own. The hope is understandable; more than one Christian has privately wished it were so.

But Peter defines his own term two verses later, and he leaves no room for it: every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people (v. 23). A man does not promise universal salvation and then, in the next breath, warn of being cut off. The restoration he means is the one the prophets promised — the renewal of a broken creation, the world put right, what Paul calls the liberation of creation itself from its bondage to decay. It is the healing of the world, not the reversal of the judgment; and this whole sermon is a plea to repent precisely because that judgment is real. Peter has just told them their only safety is to turn. He would hardly say that if turning made no difference in the end.

Which leaves a reader holding both halves at once, and Peter does not pretend the not-yet is easy. The restoration is certain, it is dated, and it is not here. The refreshing is available now, and it is not the same thing — it is a breathing space in the middle of a world that is still broken, coming from the presence of a Lord who is still in heaven. Anybody who has been told that the Christian life ought to feel like the new creation already has been sold something Peter did not offer. What he offers is enough air to keep going, a fixed point on the calendar, and the certainty that the one who fixed it is coming back for the rest of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses said, 'The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter now reaches for the only promise in the books of Moses that says another prophet is coming, and it is worth knowing the circumstances in which it was given, because they are heartbreaking.

At the foot of the mountain the people had heard God speak out of the fire, and they could not bear it. They came to Moses and begged him to make it stop: let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die. And God's answer is the astonishing part. He does not rebuke them. He says they are right in what they have spoken — and then makes the promise Peter is quoting: I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth (Deuteronomy 18:16–18).

So the promise of the coming prophet is God's answer to a people who could not survive hearing him directly. They asked for a voice they could live through. He said he would give them one — a man, from among themselves, with God's own words in his mouth. And what he finally sent was his Son, who could be listened to for three years by fishermen on a hillside without anybody dying of it.

A prophet like me. The likeness is specific. Moses spoke with God face to face as a man speaks with his friend; Moses mediated a covenant; Moses did signs; Moses brought a people out of slavery and led them toward a country they had never seen. Every one of those is true of Jesus and truer, which is exactly how the New Testament handles the comparison — a servant in the house, and a Son over it.

You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you. Not consider him, not weigh him against other authorities. Listen. Peter is pointing out to a temple crowd that the obligation to obey Jesus does not originate with Christians. It was laid on Israel by Moses, in the law they revere, centuries before anybody had heard of Nazareth.

One question a reader may well have met should be answered briefly, since it is pressed with some force. Islam claims this verse for Muhammad, on the ground that he came from among the brothers of Israel — that is, from Ishmael's line. The text will not carry it. In Deuteronomy the phrase from among your brothers is used repeatedly of a fellow Israelite and is set directly against the foreigner: Israel's king must be one from among your brothers... you may not put a foreigner over you (Deuteronomy 17:15). The prophet is promised from inside Israel, as the answer to Israel's own request at Israel's own mountain. And the New Testament shows the question being asked in precisely those terms in the first century — crowds asking whether Jesus is the Prophet, and priests sending men to ask John the Baptist the same thing. Peter is settling a question his hearers already had, not inventing one.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people. And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 23 is the hardest sentence in the chapter, and Peter puts it in deliberately.

It is also, strictly speaking, not a quotation of Deuteronomy 18. There God says of the man who will not listen, I myself will require it of him. Peter sharpens it by finishing the sentence with a phrase out of Leviticus — shall be destroyed from the people, which is the language used of anyone who refuses to humble himself on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 23:29). The two passages are welded together, and the effect is intended: to refuse the Prophet is not a difference of opinion. It is the same category of thing as standing outside on the one day in the year when the nation's sin was dealt with.

The verse also does something else, and it is the reason it should be read alongside the promise just before it. The restoring of all things in verse 21 has been made to carry the hope that in the end nobody is lost. Verse 23 stands two verses away, in the same breath of the same sermon, and rules it out. Peter does not restore all people. He restores all things — and then he warns.

It is worth being clear-eyed about why that is not cruelty. A warning is cruel if it is false, or if it arrives too late to act on, or if there is no way out of what it threatens. This one is true, it is early, and Peter has just spent four verses describing the way out. Nobody in that colonnade is being frightened without being handed a door in the same paragraph. The unkind thing would have been to leave the sentence out — which is generally what people are asking for when they ask for a gentler gospel.

Then verse 24, and a small detail with a long reach: from Samuel and those who came after him. Why Samuel? Because with Samuel the line of the prophets properly begins after Moses — and because Samuel is the man who anointed David, so that the prophetic succession and the royal line start on the same page of the same book. Peter is saying that the whole tradition, prophets and kings together, has been pointing down a corridor toward these days.

Which is a phrase to stop on. These days: the ones his hearers are standing in, in ordinary clothes, on an ordinary afternoon, having come up for the three o'clock prayers as they do every week. Every prophet from Samuel onward had been talking about this fortnight. It is worth a Christian remembering, on a Tuesday, in the middle of a life that feels entirely unremarkable, that he is living inside the period the prophets strained forward to see, and that the men who wrote the book he reads at breakfast would have given a great deal to stand where he is standing.

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, 'And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.' God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter ends the sermon by telling them who they are. You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant — not spectators at somebody else's story, not late arrivals to a religion, but heirs. Everything he has been quoting at them is family property.
