'Leader and Savior' (archēgon kai sōtēra) — the crucified one is now the Leader who blazed the trail through death to resurrection and the Savior who offers repentance and forgiveness. 'To give repentance to Israel' — repentance itself is God's gift, not human achievement; the same God who commands it supplies it through the exalted Jesus. Two witnesses testify to these things: the apostles (human eyewitnesses of the resurrection) and the Holy Spirit (divine confirmation given to those who obey). The council cannot refute either witness.

In what way is the Holy Spirit a 'witness'? Jesus had promised exactly this pairing: 'the Spirit of truth... will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness' (John 15:26–27) — two witnesses, as the Law required (Deut. 19:15). The Spirit testifies in several joined ways. First by his very outpouring, since the fact that God has poured out the Spirit is itself proof that the crucified Jesus is risen and enthroned, for only the exalted Christ could send him — 'having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves see and hear' (Acts 2:33). The Spirit's presence in the church is living evidence of the resurrection the apostles proclaim. He testifies, too, by empowering the witnesses themselves, emboldening them and speaking through them (Acts 1:8; 4:8, 31). He testifies outwardly, in the signs and wonders and the transformed, multiplying church — God bearing witness 'by gifts of the Holy Spirit' (Heb. 2:4). And he testifies inwardly, pressing the truth home on the conscience, convicting the world of sin and righteousness and judgment (John 16:8–11) and confirming the gospel within the believer (Rom. 8:16). So the council faces not merely the word of a few fishermen but the testimony of God himself: a witness they can imprison no more than they could keep the prison shut.

Two things in the first half of Peter's sentence should not be hurried past. Leader renders archegos, a word with no tidy English equivalent: it carries the sense of the one who goes first and opens the way — a pioneer who cuts the track others will walk, a founder in whom a whole people begins. Peter is saying that Jesus did not merely arrange a rescue from a safe distance. He went through death himself, first, and came out the other side, and the road exists because he made it. Nobody who follows him into that country will be going anywhere he has not already been.

And then, quietly, the phrase that ought to stop anybody who has ever tried and failed to repent: God exalted him to give repentance. Repentance is here a thing handed over, not a thing achieved. That cuts against the way most people instinctively hear the command — as though God stands at a distance requiring a change of heart that we must manufacture before he will look at us. Peter says the exalted Christ dispenses it. Anyone who has genuinely wanted to be sorry for something and found that he could only regret the consequences knows the difference between working up remorse and being given a new mind about a thing. The first cannot be done to order. The second is a gift, and the place to go for it is the one who was exalted to hand it out.

One clause here needs a guard, because it has been misused: the Spirit is given to those who obey him. Read carelessly that turns the Spirit into a wage. But the obedience Peter has in mind is not a record of performance; it is the same word he used of himself two verses earlier, when he said we must obey God rather than men — and what he meant there was believing God's word about his Son and acting on it. That is the obedience the New Testament calls the obedience of faith. The Spirit is not the prize for a life already put right. He is the one who puts it right, and he comes to people whose response to the message about Jesus has been surrender rather than management.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council's response to the apostolic declaration is rage — not refutation, not deliberation, but the visceral fury of those whose authority has been publicly and repeatedly defied. They 'wanted to kill them' — the same impulse that led to the crucifixion is now directed at his witnesses. But God's providential care for his messengers operates through an unlikely instrument: Gamaliel, the most respected Pharisee of his generation (Paul's own teacher, 22:3), whose caution and authority are sufficient to pause the council's murderous intent.

Beyond the New Testament, Jewish sources tell us a fair amount about Gamaliel — though it is best weighed as tradition rather than certified biography. He is remembered as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder (Gamaliel I), one of the most honoured sages of his age and, by Jewish tradition, a descendant (commonly, the grandson) of the famed Hillel and a leader of Hillel's school; he is traditionally reckoned the first to bear the exalted title 'Rabban' ('our master'), a rank above 'Rabbi.' The Mishnah pays him a striking tribute: 'When Rabban Gamaliel the Elder died, the glory of the Torah ceased, and purity and piety died' (Sotah 9:15). Tradition also credits him with several legal rulings (takkanot) made for the public good, including protections for women in the law of divorce (Mishnah Gittin 4). And, as Luke notes elsewhere, the young Saul of Tarsus — the future apostle Paul — was trained 'at the feet of Gamaliel' (Acts 22:3). (A much later Christian legend claimed Gamaliel secretly became a believer and that his remains were found in AD 415; but this has no historical foundation and should be set aside.)

Luke's word for the council's rage repays a moment. They were, literally, sawn through — cut in two by what they had heard. And that is worth setting beside the only other place in Acts where a crowd hears an apostolic sermon and is described as being cut. On the day of Pentecost the people were cut to the heart and said, brothers, what shall we do? (2:37). Here the same message, delivered by the same man, about the same risen Christ, cuts men in exactly the same place and produces a decision to kill him. Stephen will meet the identical reaction from this identical body a chapter later, and it will finish the way it wanted to finish here (7:54).

That is the sober truth about preaching Christ, and it is a comfort as well as a warning. The gospel is never neutral and it very rarely leaves people where it found them; it either breaks a man open or hardens him, and the wound feels much the same from the inside at first. Three thousand went one way in chapter 2. This council went the other. Nothing in the message had changed.

And into that room, at the moment murder is being openly proposed by the supreme court of Israel, God sends a Pharisee. Not an angel this time, not an earthquake, not a miracle of any kind. A respected old teacher stands up and asks for the room to be cleared, and eleven men live. Providence does not always arrive with the doors opening of their own accord; sometimes it arrives as the one person present whose opinion the others cannot afford to dismiss.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, followed him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gamaliel opens with a warning, and it is worth registering how serious it is. Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. He is addressing the supreme court of his nation, in session, which has just openly proposed killing eleven prisoners without a trial, and he tells them to be careful. He is the only man in the chamber who says anything of the kind.

His argument is drawn entirely from recent memory. Judea in living recollection had produced a run of men who gathered a following, claimed to be somebody, and came to nothing when they were killed. Gamaliel names one, and will name a second, and his reasoning is simple: movements of that kind collapse when their leader dies, so let time do the work and keep the council's hands clean. (The two names he cites carry a long-standing historical objection to Luke's accuracy; it is answered on vv. 37-38.)

As practical advice it is shrewd, and God used it, and eleven men went home alive because of it. As a way of settling what is true it is worthless, and it is worth being clear about why, because the same reasoning is offered constantly today in a religious voice. Durability is not a test of truth. Plenty of false things last for centuries; Gamaliel was making his case inside a temple that had stood a long time and was forty years from being rubble. Plenty of true things are crushed early and stay crushed for a generation. Applied consistently, his rule would have condemned nearly every prophet Israel ever had, all of whom were dismissed, imprisoned or killed and none of whom looked durable at the time.

The deeper problem is that Gamaliel's rule allows a man to avoid the only question in the room. The apostles had not asked the council to predict their movement's future. They had made a factual claim: God raised Jesus from the dead, and we saw him. That claim can be investigated. It has witnesses, a location, a date, and an empty tomb whose emptiness nobody in that chamber disputed. Gamaliel proposes instead that they wait and observe the outcome — which is a decision not to look.

That posture is extremely common and it is always presented as open-mindedness. If Christianity is real it will survive without my verdict; if it is not, my verdict will not have mattered. It sounds humble and it is in fact the one position that cannot be held. A man deciding whether Jesus rose from the dead is not an observer of the case; he is a party to it. Waiting to see how it turns out is itself an answer, and it is the answer given by everyone who has ever intended to look into it properly later. Gamaliel had the evidence, the intelligence, and the standing to settle it, and he chose the one course that required nothing of him. So far as Scripture records, he died having chosen it.

verseByVerse.quote: "After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas the Galilean's revolt at the time of Quirinius's census (AD 6) was better known and more politically charged than Theudas's movement — the mention of it would have resonated deeply with the council. Gamaliel's principle ('if it is of man, it will fail') is the kind of wisdom that sounds profound but avoids the actual question: is it of God? His counsel is a deferral, not a judgment. But it serves God's purpose: the apostles are not killed, the mission continues, and Gamaliel himself is perhaps set wondering whether this movement is different from the ones he named.

These two names carry a well-known objection, and since Luke's standing as a historian matters to this whole book it should be met. Josephus describes a Theudas who led a revolt under the procurator Fadus, and dates it to about AD 44 — a decade or more after Gamaliel is speaking here. Worse, Gamaliel places Judas the Galilean, whose rising came at the census of AD 6, after Theudas. On the face of it Luke has the order backwards and the date impossible, and this is regularly produced as proof that he invented the speech.

Two things need saying. The first is that Theudas was a common name in a country that was full of failed insurgents. Josephus himself says that after Herod the Great died in 4 BC there were countless disturbances in Judea, and he names several leaders who gathered a following and were cut down. Gamaliel's Theudas had about four hundred men; the one Josephus dates to the forties drew a great crowd to the Jordan. There is no difficulty in supposing two men of the same name, forty years apart, in a generation that produced rebels by the dozen.

The second is worth weighing before conceding anything. The objection assumes that where Luke and Josephus differ, Josephus is the standard and Luke the suspect. Josephus is a valuable historian and a demonstrably careless one in places, and that assumption has not aged well. Luke was long said to have blundered over the titles of local officials — the politarchs of Thessalonica, the proconsul of Cyprus, the first man of Malta — and inscription after inscription has since shown him exactly right, in details a forger would have had no way to know. A writer with that record has earned the benefit of the doubt about a rebel's name.

verseByVerse.quote: "but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!" So they took his advice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gamaliel's last sentence is the sharpest thing said in the chamber all day, and he almost certainly did not know how sharp it was. You might even be found opposing God. The word he uses (theomachoi, God-fighters) appears nowhere else in the New Testament, and it did not come out of the synagogue; it belonged to the world of Greek tragedy, where the man who sets himself against heaven is destroyed by the attempt, usually while believing he is defending something. Gamaliel raises it as a remote hazard, a possibility worth insuring against. It is the actual position of every man he is speaking to.

And that is the exquisite thing about the sentence. He describes the council's situation with perfect accuracy while presenting it as a hypothesis. They are not at risk of opposing God; they have arrested his messengers twice, ignored an empty prison reported by their own officers, and just now discussed murdering eleven men for saying that God raised Jesus. The wisest man in the room got nearer to the truth than anyone else present and still treated it as a remote contingency. It is possible to be right about God in the conditional and wrong about him in the indicative.

Then Luke writes five flat words: so they took his advice. And the next verse tells you exactly what taking it amounted to. They did not kill the apostles; they had them stripped and flogged and repeated the order to be silent. So this is what a court does when it has been warned that it may be fighting God: it reduces the sentence and carries on. Gamaliel's own argument, taken seriously for five minutes, demanded an investigation, because a body told there is a real possibility it is at war with the Almighty cannot rationally respond by doing nothing and waiting. Nobody proposes finding out. They amend the punishment and move to the next item.

There is a further quiet irony that Luke may well intend his reader to catch later. Three chapters from here a young man is standing at a stoning, holding the coats, approving; and he tells us himself that he was brought up in this city at the feet of this same Gamaliel (22:3). Saul of Tarsus had this exact warning from his own teacher, and went out and did the very thing it warned against, until a voice on a road asked him why he was persecuting me. Gamaliel's word turned out to be a prophecy about his best student.

But the sentence to carry away from this scene is not about Gamaliel at all. Eleven men who could not defend themselves, in the hands of a court that wanted them dead, were delivered by an argument they did not make, from a man who was not on their side, for reasons that were not the right ones. The church's survival that morning did not depend on its case being heard, its friends being influential, or its enemies being reasonable. It never has. What Gamaliel offered as a warning against a possibility, the apostles could have offered as a statement of fact: nothing that is of God will be overthrown, and the men holding the whip have never once been told what the outcome would be.

verseByVerse.quote: and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council cannot kill the apostles (Gamaliel's counsel has prevented it) but they can punish them — and they do: forty lashes less one (the standard Jewish punishment for contempt of authority). The charge is repeated: 'not to speak in the name of Jesus.' The beating is meant to break the boldness; the charge is meant to silence the proclamation. Neither will succeed. The apostles emerge from the flogging not broken but unbowed, not silent but more vocal. Suffering for the name does not diminish their willingness to speak it.

A brief word for the everyday reader on what 'speaking in the name of Jesus' means. In the Bible a 'name' stands for the whole person — his identity, his character, and above all his authority. To do or say something 'in someone's name' is to act on his behalf, as his representative, by his authority — the way an ambassador speaks not his own mind but his king's, or a constable says 'stop, in the name of the law.' So when the apostles 'spoke in the name of Jesus,' they were not merely mentioning him; they were publicly proclaiming who he is — the crucified and risen Lord — and calling people to trust and obey him, and doing it as his authorized messengers, backed by his authority and not their own (as when the lame man was healed 'in the name of Jesus Christ,' 3:6, and 'there is salvation in no one else,' 4:12). That is exactly what the council wanted to stop: not idle talk, but the authoritative announcement that Jesus is Lord. To forbid the name was to forbid Christ himself.

It is worth knowing what the sentence actually was, because English translations pass over it in three words. The synagogue flogging was forty strokes less one — the law permitted forty and the practice stopped at thirty-nine so that a miscount could not break it (Deuteronomy 25:1–3). The man was stripped to the waist and bent over, and the strokes were laid on with a leather scourge, a third of them on the chest and the rest across the back. Men were carried away from it. Paul, who received the same punishment five separate times, thought it worth listing among the things that nearly killed him (2 Corinthians 11:24). This is not a formality or a caution. Eleven men left that chamber unable to stand straight.

And notice the incoherence of what has just happened, because it is the most damning thing in the chapter. Minutes earlier the council was warned by its most honoured member that it might be found fighting against God. It accepted the advice. Then it had the men beaten and told them again to stop speaking. A body that genuinely thought it might be opposing the Almighty had one reasonable course and did not take it. They kept the verdict and lowered the sentence, which is what men do when they have decided the question already and are only negotiating the cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and proclaiming Jesus as the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eleven men walk out of the Sanhedrin with their backs opened, and Luke says they were rejoicing. Not resigned. Not composed. Not bearing it well. Rejoicing, on the way home, out loud enough that somebody remembered it.

And the reason he gives is a sentence that should not be able to exist: they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour. Two words that cannot stand together. To be counted worthy is to be honoured, singled out, judged fit for something valuable; dishonour is public shame, the thing every man in that culture organised his life to avoid. Luke welds them. Whatever had happened to these men, it had reversed the sign on the whole transaction. They walked into that room as defendants and came out feeling that they had been given something. Not long before, this same group had been arguing on a road about which of them was the greatest. The argument is over. The prize turned out to be a flogging.

Then the phrase that ought to stop a reader: for the Name. That is all Luke writes. No qualifier, no possessive, nothing to say whose name is meant. Every Jew reading it would feel the weight of that construction, because in Jewish speech the Name was how you referred to the God of Israel when you would not pronounce the divine name itself. And here is Luke, writing about a carpenter executed six weeks earlier outside the city wall, and he uses the phrase absolutely, as though there could be no confusion about which name is meant. Among these people there was not. The council in this very chapter refused to say the name at all, calling him this man (v. 28); the apostles have stopped needing to say it, for the opposite reason.

Now a guard is needed here, because this verse has been laid on suffering people as a demand, and it is not one. Three things keep it honest. First, they are not rejoicing in the pain; they are rejoicing in what the pain meant — that the Lord they had abandoned in a garden had now counted them fit to be shamed on his account. Nobody is asked to enjoy a scourge. Second, this is a specific kind of suffering: dishonour incurred for Christ, in the course of obeying him. A diagnosis is not dishonour for the Name. Neither is a bereavement, a betrayal, or a depression that will not lift. Those are real and Scripture speaks to them elsewhere and at length; this verse is not the text to beat a grieving person with. Third, this joy is a thing given, not manufactured. It arrived in them on the way out of that building. It is not a mood that a Christian owes in advance and is failing to produce.

And to anyone who reads this and quietly concludes he could never do it — that if it cost him his job, his family's standing, or a beating, he would fold — look at who is walking out of that chamber. The man in front is Peter. Seven weeks ago, with nothing at stake but a servant girl's opinion beside a fire, he swore he had never met Jesus, and then went out and wept. Nobody in history has a worse record under pressure than the man leading this procession. What changed was not his temperament. Something was given to him that had not been there in the courtyard, and it is given to people when it is needed and not before. The measure of what you could bear today is not the measure of what you would be carried through tomorrow.

Luke ends the chapter with the council's order and its answer set side by side. They were charged not to speak in the name of Jesus. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus. Every day — not resumed after a decent interval, but daily, from that day. In the temple, which is the most public and most dangerous place in the city, and belongs to the men who ordered the flogging; and house to house, at kitchen tables, where the church has always done most of its real work. Both together, and neither instead of the other.

They did not cease. It is a strange note to end on, and it is the right one. The whole apparatus of the most powerful religious body in the world had been brought to bear on eleven provincials over two days — arrest, imprisonment, formal trial, corporal punishment, legal injunction — and by the following morning the only measurable result was that the message was being preached in more houses than before. He is worth this, was the verdict of the men with the wounds. Two thousand years later the name they would not stop saying is spoken every hour in every language on earth, and nobody can tell you the name of a single man who sat on the council that day.

5.theology: The Holiness of God in the New Covenant Community. The deaths of Ananias and Sapphira are not anomalies — they have a precise parallel in Leviticus 10, where Nadab and Abihu are struck dead at the founding of the tabernacle worship. At every founding moment of a new covenant expression, God makes his holiness unmistakable. He did it at Sinai. He did it in the wilderness. He does it here, at the birth of the church. The message is the same: I am holy. You are dwelling in the presence of the Holy One. This is not a place for pretence. It is not that God is more severe in the new covenant than the old; it is that the new covenant community lives in an even closer proximity to the Holy Spirit than any previous generation, and proximity to holiness demands purity.
5.examples:
Then: A Jerusalem church five weeks old, discovering that the Spirit who fills them also searches them — and that the God of grace is also the God of holiness. The fear that fell on the church was not paralyzing; the next verse tells us that believers were added to the Lord in multitudes. Healthy fear of God does not drive people away from him; it drives away the casual, and draws in the sincere.

Now: The contemporary church has largely lost the category of the fear of God. We speak of grace, love, and welcome — and rightly so. But a church that never trembles before the holiness of God has not understood grace; it has domesticated it. Ananias and Sapphira remind every generation that the Spirit cannot be fooled, that the church is not a social club, and that God’s presence is still a consuming fire.

6.title: The Choosing of the Seven
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. <sup>2</sup>And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, “It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. <sup>3</sup>Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. <sup>4</sup>But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” <sup>5</sup>And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. <sup>6</sup>These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them. <sup>7</sup>And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. <sup>8</sup>And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people. <sup>9</sup>Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen. <sup>10</sup>But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking. <sup>11</sup>Then they secretly instigated men who said, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” <sup>12</sup>And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council, <sup>13</sup>and they set up false witnesses who said, “This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, <sup>14</sup>for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us.” <sup>15</sup>And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
6.overview:
The church is growing — and growth creates problems. The Hellenist widows are being neglected in the daily distribution. This is not a scandal; it is what happens when an organism grows faster than its structures can accommodate. The twelve could try to do everything. Instead they do something remarkable: they name the problem plainly, they define their own calling with precision (“we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the Word”), and they delegate to men of character and Spirit.

The result is instructive: “the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem.” When the church’s structures serve the Word rather than compete with it, the Word runs. Ministry organisation is not bureaucracy — it is stewardship of the mission.

But Luke also introduces Stephen, and with Stephen the chapter darkens. He is full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, full of grace and power. He does wonders no one can deny. He speaks with a wisdom the opposition cannot withstand. So they do what those who cannot win an argument always do: they lie. And Stephen, standing before the council with false witnesses arrayed against him, has a face like the face of an angel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Appointment of the Seven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The first quarrel in the history of the church is not about doctrine. It is about a food queue.

Both parties are Jews and both are Christians; the fault line runs between Greek-speaking believers from the Diaspora and Aramaic-speaking believers native to Judea, and it runs through language, culture and accent rather than through belief. The Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution — and Luke's word means exactly that, looked past rather than turned away. Nobody had decided to starve them. They were simply not seen, in a community that three chapters earlier had been described as being of one heart and soul.

What the apostles do about it is the point of the passage. They do not settle it privately, and they do not deny it. They call the whole congregation together, state the one thing they cannot afford to be dragged off — prayer and the ministry of the word — and then ask the church to choose seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, to run the distribution. Every name the congregation returns is Greek, and the last man on the list was not born a Jew at all. The group that raised the complaint is handed the entire operation, and nobody is recorded as objecting.

Then verse 7, which is one of Luke's hinge sentences: the word of God kept increasing, the disciples multiplied, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. Men whose livelihood, tribe and standing were bound up with the altar began confessing that the sacrifice had been made. Luke sets that immediately after an argument about widows and bread, and the placing is not accidental.
verseByVerse.theology:
Word and Service in the Church

The apostles' refusal to give up preaching the word of God to serve tables (v. 2) is about vocation, not about dignity, and the passage guards against the misreading in the very next sentence: the men appointed to the tables must be full of the Spirit and of wisdom, which is not a lower bar. The whole argument turns on a single Greek root that appears on both sides of it — the apostles will not abandon the service of the word in order to serve tables. Waiting on widows and preaching to thousands are not two categories, one menial and one spiritual. They are two forms of one thing, and the only question is which form a particular man is called to. Nor are the Seven junior figures: Stephen is preaching within a paragraph and dead within a chapter, and Philip is still being called an evangelist twenty years later. What the passage protects is not the apostles' status but the church's food supply — a congregation whose teachers are buried in administration will in time be starved of the word, and a congregation whose widows are overlooked has already stopped believing what it preaches.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The overlooked widows were almost certainly the very women Luke described in chapter 2 — Diaspora Jews who had come home to Jerusalem to die near the temple. Their husbands died, and the widows were left in a city where they had no land, no clan and no relatives, and could not follow the conversation at the distribution. Now: The question every congregation has to keep asking is not whether it would refuse anyone. It is who is currently being looked past — the people whose absence nobody notices, because they were never in the middle of the room to begin with.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke dates the trouble precisely: in these days when the disciples were increasing in number. The problem is a symptom of the growth. Nothing had gone wrong with the church except that there was more of it than the existing arrangements could see.

Both groups in this quarrel are Jews and both are Christians. The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews, mostly born in the Diaspora or returned from it, who read their Scriptures in Greek and thought in a Greek idiom. The Hebrews were Aramaic-speaking Jews native to the land, who read the Hebrew text. The line between them is language, culture and accent, not theology — which is worth registering, because it is the line along which the first Christian conflict actually fell.

And the widows on the wrong side of it are almost certainly women this book has already told us about. Chapter 2 described Jews from every nation under heaven who were dwelling in Jerusalem, settled residents rather than pilgrims, many of whom had crossed an empire in old age in order to be buried near the temple. Those men died, as they had come to do. And their widows were left behind in a city where they owned no land, had no clan to fall back on, no sons in the district, and could not always follow what was being said around them. They were the most exposed people in the congregation, and they were the ones who got missed.

Luke's word for it is exact and it is the mercy of the sentence. It means to overlook — to look past. It occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Nobody had decided that these women should go without. There was no policy, no vote, no meeting at which the Hellenists were discussed and set aside. In the press of a distribution serving thousands of people, run by men who spoke a different language at home, the ones without a voice were simply not seen. That is how this kind of injustice nearly always happens, and it is why the people responsible are usually genuinely surprised to hear of it.

The word Luke uses for the complaint has a harder history — it is the word the Greek Old Testament uses over and over for Israel grumbling in the wilderness, and it never once means anything good there. But notice what he does not do with it. He does not rebuke the complainers, and neither do the apostles. The grievance was true, it was raised, and it was acted on inside a single meeting. There is a lesson in that for anybody inclined to treat every complaint in a church as a spiritual failure in the person making it. Sometimes the murmuring is right.

And the Twelve do not deal with it quietly. The twelve summoned the full number of the disciples — a congregation now numbering many thousands is called together and told there is a problem. They could have adjusted the rota and said nothing. Instead the failure is put in public, in front of the very people who had been neglected.

Their opening sentence has been misread for centuries, so it needs handling with care. It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables is not a clergyman declining a menial job. The proof is in the next verse, where the men who are to do that job must be full of the Spirit and of wisdom — which is not a lower standard, and in the event these are the men who go on to preach in synagogues and evangelise Samaria. What the apostles are protecting is not their own dignity. It is the church's food supply of a different kind: a congregation whose teachers disappear into administration will be starved within a generation, and the widows will still not be fed.

Which leaves a question a reader can put to his own church, and it is sharper than the one usually asked. Not: would we turn anybody away? Almost nobody would. But who is currently being looked past — who is in the building and not in anybody's line of sight, because they never were in the middle of the room, and because asking would require somebody to find out?

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at what the apostles ask for in a man who is going to hand out food. Of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom. Three qualifications, and not one of them is administrative. Nothing about numeracy, or organisation, or a head for logistics — which is what the work actually called for. The church's first job description asks for reputation, the Spirit and wisdom, and then sets the men to work on a food queue.

Notice also who does the choosing. Pick out from among you — the apostles set the standard and the congregation makes the selection. No slate is presented. The people who had raised the complaint are handed the pen.

Then the Twelve state their own limit, and the wording repays attention: we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word. The verb for devote is the one Luke used of the whole church at 2:42 — to stick at a thing and refuse to be prised off it. And prayer is named first. It is worth sitting with the fact that when the apostles listed the two things they could not afford to be dragged away from, one of them was the thing nobody in the congregation would have noticed them dropping. (cf. 1 Tim. 4:13; 2 Tim. 4:2)

Anyone who belongs to a church that elects deacons will want to know whether this is where they come from. The answer is yes and no, and the distinction is worth having. Luke never calls these men deacons. The noun is not used of them here or anywhere else; later he simply calls Philip one of the seven (21:8). What is used, twice and pointedly, is the word underneath it: the apostles will not give up the service of the word in order to serve tables. Both halves of that sentence are the same root, and that is the whole argument. Waiting on widows and preaching to thousands are not two categories, a menial one and a spiritual one. They are two forms of the one thing, and the only question is which one a particular man is called to.

So the church has always been right to see the seed of the office here, and Paul's later requirements for deacons — men of dignity, tested, holding the faith with a clear conscience (1 Tim. 3:8-13) — plainly grow from the same soil as the qualifications set out in this verse. But do not reduce these seven to an administrative committee. Watch what they actually do next. Stephen is arguing in synagogues within a paragraph and is dead within a chapter. Philip takes the gospel to Samaria, baptises an Ethiopian official on a desert road, and is still being called an evangelist twenty years later. Neither of them stayed at the tables. Whatever the church later made of the office, it began with men so full of the Spirit that the job could not hold them.

And notice what the first appointment in the history of the church was actually for. Not a building programme, not a doctrinal commission, not a mission board. Some widows who spoke the wrong language were being missed at the food distribution, and the apostles treated that as serious enough to reorganise the leadership of the church over it. That is worth sitting with. The complaint came from the minority group, and the solution handed the entire operation to seven men with Greek names. They did not manage the grievance; they gave the aggrieved the keys.

verseByVerse.quote: And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the list of names and something jumps out that would have been unmissable to Luke's first readers. Every one of the seven is Greek. Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, Nicolaus — there is not a Hebrew name among them. And the last man is identified as a proselyte of Antioch, which is to say he was not born a Jew at all. He had converted in a Syrian city, and he is now on the body running the welfare of the Jerusalem church.

Consider what the congregation has just done. A minority group complained that its widows were being overlooked. The majority could have appointed four Hebrews and three Hellenists, which would have been fair, and defensible, and would have left the Hebrews in control of the money. Instead they handed the whole operation to the people who had raised the complaint.

What they said pleased the whole gathering. It is worth marking the moment, because it does not come again: a church with money, a grievance and an ethnic fault line running through it settles the matter in one meeting, by giving the power away.

'Full of faith and of the Holy Spirit' — but how could anyone tell? The apostles told the church to pick out such men (v. 3), so the fullness was no hidden claim but something the congregation could recognise. It shows itself, and over time unmistakably. In character — the fruit the Spirit grows: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, gentleness, self-control (Gal. 5:22–23), steady enough to earn 'good repute.' In wisdom — how a man speaks and handles matters (Stephen's, which his opponents 'could not withstand,' v. 10). In faith, a settled trust and boldness; and soon, in Stephen, in grace and power, 'great wonders and signs' (v. 8), even a face shining 'like the face of an angel' (v. 15). The church needed no special revelation; they saw the Spirit in how he lived, spoke, and served — Jesus' own rule, 'you will recognise them by their fruits' (Matt. 7:16, 20). And note the lovely ordinariness: these Spirit-filled men were chosen to wait tables and settle a food dispute; fullness of the Spirit is proved first in humble, everyday service, not only the spectacular.

'They prayed and laid their hands on them.' The Bible uses this gesture several ways, best read against its Old Testament roots: for blessing (Jacob over Ephraim and Manasseh, Gen. 48:14; Jesus over the children, Mark 10:16); for identifying with a sacrifice (the worshipper's hand on the animal, Lev. 1:4; the high priest's on the scapegoat, Lev. 16:21); and, closest here, for commissioning to an office. The pattern is Moses and Joshua: 'Take Joshua... a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him... and commission him' (Num. 27:18–20), so that afterward 'Joshua... was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him' (Deut. 34:9). Just so here: the seven are publicly set apart, with prayer that God would equip them by his Spirit. The New Testament keeps the practice for appointing to ministry — Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:3), Timothy's gift given 'when the council of elders laid their hands on you' (1 Tim. 4:14; 2 Tim. 1:6). Two things to hold: it is never magic — always joined to prayer, and it is the prayer that asks God to act; and it is a public act, the church openly recognising those God has called. (Scripture even warns against doing it lightly: 'do not be hasty in the laying on of hands,' 1 Tim. 5:22.)

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This sentence is doing more work than it looks. Luke uses a formula of this shape half a dozen times in Acts — the word increased, the disciples multiplied — and every time it marks the close of a section and the opening of the next. He is putting a full stop at the end of the church's Jerusalem years. What follows is Stephen, and then a persecution, and then Samaria, and then the world.

Notice the odd subject of the first clause. Not the church increased: the word of God increased. Luke habitually talks about the message as though it were the living thing and the congregation merely the visible result — a seed with its own vitality, growing in ground that did not manufacture it. It is a small habit of speech with a large theology inside it.

But the sentence exists for its last clause, and it is startling: a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.

It is easy to misread who these men were. This is not the Sanhedrin changing its mind, and it is not the high-priestly dynasty. Those men appear in this book only as opponents. The ordinary priesthood was an enormous body — Josephus reckons the priests and Levites in the tens of thousands — divided into courses that served at the temple for two weeks in the year, and spent the other fifty weeks at home in the villages of Judea working an ordinary trade. Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, was one of them, and Luke's own Gospel opens with him burning incense on the one occasion in his life that the lot fell to him. These are the rank and file of the temple workforce, and they were not rich.

Which makes the cost of what they did very sharp indeed. A priest who confessed Jesus was saying that the sacrifice he assisted at every morning had been superseded — that the machinery he had been trained for, the altar his tribe existed to serve, the whole apparatus that gave his family its identity and its livelihood, had done its work and was finished. He was not changing his opinion about a religious question. He was declaring his own profession obsolete, having watched, perhaps, a man die outside the wall on the afternoon the lambs were being killed. Some of them had very likely been on duty that day.

Luke's phrase for what they did is worth keeping too: they became obedient to the faith. Not persuaded of it, not interested in it. The faith is something a man obeys, which is exactly how Paul frames the whole business at both ends of his letter to Rome. Believing, in the New Testament, is a thing you do with your feet as well as your mind.

And then there is the placing, which is the quiet argument of the chapter. Luke reports a row about widows and bread, a congregational meeting, and the appointment of seven men to a distribution list — and then, in the very next sentence, tells us the word spread and the priests started coming. He does not say the one caused the other, and it would be crude to pretend that sorting out administration produces revival; God is not a mechanism. But he has put the two side by side, and the implication is hard to miss. A church whose Greek-speaking widows go hungry while it preaches that the risen Christ has made one people out of many is making an argument against itself, and everybody watching can hear it. Remove the contradiction and the message can be heard for what it is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Stephen: The Man Who Couldn't Be Stopped
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Stephen was appointed to a food distribution and is preaching within a paragraph. Luke credits him with great wonders and signs — language he has so far used in this book only of the apostles — and then puts him into a synagogue argument that he wins so completely that his opponents change their method rather than their minds.

Who those opponents were is worth knowing, because Luke names them with care: the synagogue of the Freedmen, together with men of Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia. These are freed slaves and their descendants, and Greek-speaking Jews of the Diaspora — which is to say Stephen's own people. The church's first great confrontation is Hellenist against Hellenist, an argument inside a community rather than across a border. And one homeland on that list is Cilicia, the province of Tarsus, which is where the young Pharisee standing at the edge of the next chapter had come from.

They could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking — and Luke is reporting the fulfilment of a promise he had himself recorded in his first volume, in almost the same words. What follows is what men do when they have lost an argument and kept the power. They suborned witnesses, stirred up the crowd that had until now been the church's protection, and brought Stephen before the council on a charge of blasphemy against Moses and God.

The charge is a distortion rather than an invention, which is exactly what makes it work: Stephen had been saying something genuinely explosive about the temple and the customs, and the witnesses kept the topic and removed the reason. Then the chapter ends on a detail Luke leaves entirely unexplained. The court trying a man for speaking against Moses looks up and sees a face like the one Moses brought down the mountain. They see it, and they proceed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cost of Prophetic Witness

Stephen's arrest follows the shape of his master's with a precision Luke's first readers cannot have missed: suborned witnesses, a charge concerning the temple and the law, a council, a verdict of blasphemy. The accusation that Matthew and Mark record against Jesus is in fact the accusation Luke records against Stephen — the servant is handed the master's charge sheet. Reformed theology has read this as more than a coincidence of circumstance. Where the gospel genuinely threatens entrenched religious power it meets the same resistance in the same order, because the objection is never finally to the argument — the argument had already been lost at verse 10 — but to what conceding it would cost. What Stephen's case adds to the pattern is the sober detail that winning the argument and losing your life are entirely compatible, and that Luke plainly did not consider the second to be a reversal of the first.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's opponents could not withstand his wisdom, and rather than yield to it they changed the subject to blasphemy and found men who would swear to it. The gospel does not always win in the short term; sometimes the first thing it wins is a grave. Now: The promise attached to moments of that kind is more modest, and more useful, than it is usually made out to be. A believer put on the spot is promised a mouth, not a result — that he will not be left standing there with nothing to say. Whether he is believed, and what it costs him, are God's business.

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses ago this man's job was to see that the widows got their share of the bread. Luke now has him working great wonders and signs among the people.

And there is a quiet fact underneath what follows, worth registering before the words are examined. Stephen enters Scripture about four verses ago and is dead by the end of the next chapter. In that short space Luke gives him more superlatives than he gives most of the Twelve — and tells us nothing else about him whatever: no home town, no trade, no family, no age, no account of how he came to believe. He has two chapters, one sermon, and a shining face.

What does 'full of grace and power' mean? It is the third time Luke describes Stephen with 'full of...' (full of faith and the Spirit, v. 5; of the Spirit and wisdom, v. 3; now of grace and power) — he is a man saturated by God. Grace (charis) carries two notes that belong together: the favour of God resting richly upon him — his life freely enabled and blessed by God, nothing of it earned — and the graciousness that such favour produces, the winsome, Christlike attractiveness of a man shaped by grace (the same word lies behind Jesus' 'gracious words,' Luke 4:22, and 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14). Power (dynamis) is the Spirit's enabling might — the very power Jesus promised, 'you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you' (Acts 1:8) — here overflowing in 'great wonders and signs.'

Note the order: grace first, then power. The favour and gracious character come first, and the power flows out of a life already full of grace; power without grace is a dangerous thing, but Stephen had both. And mark who this is: not an apostle, but one of the seven chosen to wait on tables (vv. 3–5) — yet full of grace and power and working wonders that Luke had until now reported of the apostles alone (2:43; 5:12). The grace and power of God were never the private property of the Twelve; they filled a humble table-servant who was wholly yielded to the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the first mention of a synagogue in Acts, so a word on what it was. The synagogue (Greek synagōgē, simply 'a gathering') was the local Jewish assembly and meeting-house — not the temple (there was only one temple, in Jerusalem), but a community centre found in every town and city where Jews lived, for the reading and study of Scripture, prayer, and teaching. It arose after the Babylonian exile, when the temple lay in ruins and the people were scattered, and by Jesus' and Paul's day it was the heartbeat of Jewish life everywhere. (For its origins, how a synagogue service ran, and whether Jews still gather so today, see the fuller note at 13:15.) A great city like Jerusalem held many synagogues, often grouped by homeland or language — which brings us to this one.

'The synagogue of the Freedmen' — who were these opponents? 'Freedmen' (Libertinoi, a Latin word, libertini) means freed slaves and their descendants. The likeliest background is that these were Jews, or the children of Jews, who had been taken captive — many when the Roman general Pompey conquered Jerusalem in 63 BC — carried off to Rome as slaves, later set free, and whose families formed a distinct community; some settled again in Jerusalem with their own synagogue. Jerusalem held many such synagogues for Greek-speaking Jews of the diaspora, and Luke names several homelands here: Cyrene (North Africa), Alexandria (Egypt), and Cilicia and Asia (regions of Asia Minor). (Whether this means one synagogue or two or more is grammatically uncertain; the number is not the point.) Notice that these were all Hellenistic (Greek-speaking) Jews — the very group Stephen himself belonged to (6:1). So this first great clash is a debate among fellow Greek-speaking Jews, Hellenist against Hellenist.

And one homeland on the list should make the reader sit up: Cilicia — the province of Tarsus, and so the home region of Saul (Paul), who appears just a few verses later, standing by and approving Stephen's death (7:58; 8:1). Scripture does not say outright that Saul was among these particular disputants, but he was a zealous Cilician Pharisee, present at the scene; many think it likely he was in the thick of it. They 'rose up and disputed with Stephen' — and finding (v. 10) that they could not withstand his Spirit-given wisdom, they would soon abandon argument for false witness and violence. The synagogue debate is the arena of the church's first great apologetic confrontation — and, quite possibly, the place where the future apostle Paul first set himself against the name of Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sentence, and it is a promise being kept word for word.

Years earlier, on the road to Jerusalem, Jesus had told his disciples what would happen when they were dragged in front of synagogues and rulers and authorities: I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict (Luke 21:15). Luke wrote that sentence in his first volume. He now writes, in his second, that they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking. The same verb for withstanding, the same word for wisdom, the same author. He is showing his reader the promise and then the receipt.

The verb is a strong one — to stand against, to hold a line. It is the word used for resisting the devil, and for Paul opposing Peter to his face at Antioch. These men were not politely unconvinced. They set themselves against him and could not hold the position.

And consider whom they failed to withstand. Stephen is not an apostle. He has no training that Luke mentions, no commission to teach, and a job that consists of seeing that widows are fed. He had been in office a matter of weeks. The men across the room were Diaspora Jews of the synagogue of the Freedmen — literate, argumentative, thoroughly at home in Greek, the sort of men who had spent their lives in exactly this kind of dispute. They lost.

Now the guard, and it is essential, because this verse is regularly made to promise something Scripture does not promise. It does not say Stephen's opponents were persuaded. It says they could not withstand him — and the very next verse tells you what they did instead. He won the argument comprehensively and was dead within a chapter. That is the actual sequence, and any use of this promise which implies that a believer who trusts God will come out of such conversations with the other man conceding is not describing what happened here.

What is promised is both better than a debating record and more limited than one. It is that when a Christian is put on the spot for Christ, he will not be left with nothing to say. Not that he will be believed. Not that he will be safe. That he will not be silenced.

Which is worth knowing in advance by anyone who dreads that kind of moment — the family lunch where the subject suddenly arrives, the colleague who wants to know how an intelligent person can believe any of it. Most people's fear in those moments is not of being argued into a corner. It is of standing there empty. This verse speaks to that fear exactly, and declines to speak to the other one. The mouth is promised; the outcome is not.

And one further thing should be said plainly, because it explains the rest of the chapter. It is entirely possible to be comprehensively out-argued and completely unmoved. Everyone has done it — the moment when the point lands and, instead of yielding, you change the subject, or turn on the man, or observe that everybody is entitled to their opinion. Verse 11 is that same manoeuvre carried out by professionals, with money and perjured witnesses, and it ends in a killing. The distance between the small version and the large one is shorter than most of us would care to measure.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they secretly instigated men who said, "We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God." And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word Luke uses for what they did is a technical one and it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It means to suborn — literally, to put a man in underneath, to plant him. They did not find witnesses. They installed them.

Think about what that involves. Somebody had to identify men willing to swear a false oath in a capital case. Somebody had to brief them on what to say. Somebody had to be confident enough of their nerve to stand them up in front of the Sanhedrin. This is not a crowd losing its temper. It is a considered operation, with a plan and a budget, undertaken by religious men against someone they had failed to answer in open debate the week before.

Then the charge itself: blasphemous words against Moses and God. Note the order — Moses first. In an accusation drafted to secure a conviction, the name placed first is the one expected to do the work, and here it is not God's. What they had actually heard Stephen discuss concerned the law and the temple, and they knew perfectly well which half of that would move a room.

Then they stirred up the people, and this is the hinge of the whole narrative, and it is easily read straight past.

Go back over the previous three chapters. When Peter and John were arrested, the council could find no way to punish them because of the people (4:21). When the apostles were seized the second time, the captain of the temple brought them in without force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people (5:26). Twice now the crowd has been the church's protection and the authorities' constraint. Here, for the first time, the crowd is turned — and the moment it turns, the church has its first martyr. Peter walked out of that chamber alive. Stephen will not. The variable Luke has been quietly tracking through four chapters has just moved.

The mechanism deserves naming, because it is the oldest one there is and nobody has improved on it. When a man cannot be answered, he is re-described. Nobody in that synagogue set out to prove Stephen wrong a second time; they set out to change what he was accused of, so that the argument would never have to be had again. It works because a crowd cannot check, and because a summary always travels faster than the thing it is a summary of.

Two things should be said before a Christian reader settles too comfortably into this passage. The first is that it describes what was done to a man who was genuinely innocent, and it is not a licence to file every criticism under persecution. Some criticism of Christians is accurate, and the reflex that reaches for Acts 6 is a very efficient way of never having to look at it. The second is harder. The church has, over the centuries, run this exact operation on other people — the misquoted opponent, the summarised heretic, the man whose actual words nobody troubled to read. Luke is describing a human technique, not a specifically anti-Christian one, and the people using it here were the religious ones.

verseByVerse.quote: and they set up false witnesses who said, "This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke gives the verdict before the evidence — they set up false witnesses — and then reports what they said. The interesting thing about it is how much of it was true.

Take the accusation apart. Jesus had spoken about this temple being thrown down, not one stone left on another; he had also said something about destroying a temple and raising it in three days, which his hearers misunderstood at the time and which John tells us was about his body. The customs delivered by Moses were indeed going to change — the whole New Testament argues that they did, and one letter spends thirteen chapters on nothing else. And Stephen had certainly been talking about both, at length, in a synagogue, to men who could not answer him.

So this is not the case of a blameless man slandered with an invented story. The subject matter is genuinely his. What the witnesses did was subtler and far more effective than invention: they kept the topic and removed the reason. Destroy in place of fulfil. Change in place of complete. Nothing about a new covenant; nothing about a temple that had finished the work it was built for; nothing about the one in whom God had come to live among his people. Strip out the framework, keep the residue, and then report the residue accurately.

It is the technique of describing a surgeon as a man who cuts people open with a knife. Every word is true. The account is a lie.

They add two touches of their own to finish the job. Never ceases — the suggestion of an obsessive who cannot leave the subject alone, which is a characterisation dressed as a fact. And this holy place, said inside the building, to the men who ran it, so that the offence stops being theological and becomes personal. They are not inviting the council to judge a doctrine. They are telling seventy-one men that their life's work has been attacked.

Now the application, and it cuts in a direction readers may not expect. Christians who are misrepresented — and they are, and it is genuinely painful — reach for this passage very naturally. Before doing so it is worth asking a hard question: is the thing being distorted actually something I said? Stephen's answer was yes. He had said it, and he says it again at far greater length in the next chapter, ending by telling the council to their faces that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. He was not misquoted about his views. He was misrepresented about his reasons.

That is a considerably better position to be in than the alternative, and it is worth aiming at. If a man is going to be misrepresented, let it be because he said something worth distorting.

verseByVerse.quote: And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke closes the chapter on a sentence he never explains, and the reader is meant to carry it into everything Stephen says next.

First the staring. The verb is the fixed, deliberate gaze Luke is fond of — the same word used of Peter locking eyes with the beggar at the temple gate. And it is all who sat in the council: seventy-one men in a semicircle, every one of them looking at the same face, and looking long enough that it was still being described years later to the man writing this account. There was a young Pharisee from Cilicia at this trial who would afterwards spend a great deal of time in Luke's company.

And what they see is the face of an angel. Luke offers no gloss, and the temptation is to take it as a general remark about serenity. It is far more precise than that, and the precision is devastating.

Stephen is on trial for speaking blasphemous words against Moses. There is exactly one man in the Old Testament whose face is described as having been altered by nearness to God, and it is Moses. He came down from the mountain carrying the two tablets, and the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God, and the people were afraid to come near him, and he put a veil over it (Exodus 34:29–35). The court assembled to try a man for defaming Moses looks up and sees the one face in Jerusalem that looks like Moses' did. They have the charge sheet in front of them and the answer to it in front of them at the same moment, and they proceed with the trial.

There is a second echo, and it comes from this same book. Two chapters ago another council looked at two unqualified men and recognised that they had been with Jesus. A shining face was, in Israel's own Scriptures, the recognised mark of a man who had been with God. These were not ignorant men. They knew what they were looking at.

Now the pastoral care this verse needs, because it turns into a burden very quickly. It does not establish that a faithful Christian will look radiant under pressure. A great many faithful people have gone to prison, to a diagnosis, or to their deaths looking precisely as frightened as they were, and Scripture nowhere treats that as a failure of faith — the Lord himself sweated in a garden and asked for the cup to be taken away. This is not a standard anyone is being asked to meet. It is a gift, given once, to one man, and Luke is careful to report it as something the observers saw rather than as something Stephen felt.

And it is worth asking what kind of God does this. He does not deliver Stephen. There is no earthquake, no angel opening a prison door as there had been for Peter, no crowd too dangerous to defy. Within the hour this man will be dragged outside the wall and killed with stones by people who have just heard him preach. What God gives him instead is a face. He is not spared and he is not left alone: the same glory that met Moses on the mountain comes to rest on a man about to be executed for allegedly slandering him, in the last hour of his life, where every one of his judges can see it. Whatever else this is, it is not the conduct of a God who has lost control of the proceedings.

Then Luke lets the sentence hang. And the next thing that happens is that the high priest turns to the shining man and asks him whether the charges are true.

6.theology: Word and Deed, Order and Spirit. Acts 6 is the New Testament’s foundational text on church structure. It establishes that the body has different members with different callings; that no one person can or should do everything; that the criterion for all ministry, however practical, is character shaped by the Spirit; and that when ministry is rightly ordered, the Word — not the institution, not the ministers — is what grows. This is not a management manual; it is a theology of the church as the body of Christ, each member functioning according to its calling, all of it in service of the one mission: that the Word of God would run and be glorified.
6.examples:
Then: A rapidly growing Jerusalem church discovering that love without structure produces injustice — the widows being neglected are real women with real needs — and that structure without love produces dead religion. The seven are the church’s solution: Spirit-filled servants who bring both.

Now: Every growing church faces the tension of Acts 6: how do we care well for people without the leaders becoming so consumed with management that the Word is starved? The answer is not to choose between pastoral care and proclamation; it is to raise up men and women of Spirit and wisdom to share the load — and then to watch what God does with a church that is both devoted to the Word and devoted to its neighbours.

7.title: The Speech of Stephen
7.text: <sup>1</sup>And the high priest said, “Are these things so?” <sup>2</sup>And Stephen said: “Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, <sup>3</sup>and said to him, ‘Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.’ <sup>4</sup>Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. <sup>5</sup>Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child. <sup>6</sup>And God spoke to this effect—that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. <sup>7</sup>But I will judge the nation that they serve, said God, and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.’ <sup>8</sup>And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs. <sup>9</sup>“And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him <sup>10</sup>and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household. <sup>11</sup>Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. <sup>12</sup>But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit. <sup>13</sup>And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh. <sup>14</sup>And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all. <sup>15</sup>And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, <sup>16</sup>and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem. <sup>17</sup>“But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt <sup>18</sup>until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph. <sup>19</sup>He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. <sup>20</sup>At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father’s house, <sup>21</sup>and when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. <sup>22</sup>And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds. <sup>23</sup>“When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. <sup>24</sup>And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian. <sup>25</sup>He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. <sup>26</sup>And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?’ <sup>27</sup>But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? <sup>28</sup>Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ <sup>29</sup>At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons. <sup>30</sup>“Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. <sup>31</sup>When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.’ And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. <sup>33</sup>Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. <sup>34</sup>I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.’ <sup>35</sup>“This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. <sup>36</sup>This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. <sup>37</sup>This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.’ <sup>38</sup>This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us. <sup>39</sup>Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, <sup>40</sup>saying to Aaron, ‘Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.’ <sup>41</sup>And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. <sup>42</sup>But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring to me slaughtered beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? <sup>43</sup>You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’ <sup>44</sup>“Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. <sup>45</sup>Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David, <sup>46</sup>who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. <sup>47</sup>But it was Solomon who built him a house. <sup>48</sup>Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, <sup>49</sup>‘Heaven is my throne, and earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? <sup>50</sup>Did not my hand make all these things?’ <sup>51</sup>“You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you. <sup>52</sup>Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, <sup>53</sup>you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it.” <sup>54</sup>Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. <sup>55</sup>But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. <sup>56</sup>And he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” <sup>57</sup>But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and ran together at him. <sup>58</sup>Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. <sup>59</sup>And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” <sup>60</sup>And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
7.overview:
Stephen’s speech is the longest in Acts and one of the most daring pieces of rhetoric in the New Testament. He does not defend himself. He puts Israel on trial. From Abraham to Solomon to the council before him, he traces a single thread through the whole of salvation history: God always moves forward, and Israel always resists. The patriarchs sold Joseph into Egypt — but God was with him. Israel rejected Moses — twice — but God used him to redeem them. Israel turned to idols in the wilderness. Israel refused to keep the law they received. And now the same pattern reaches its fullest expression: they have betrayed and murdered the Righteous One himself.

The speech dismantles the two pillars of Jewish security: the temple and the law. The Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands — he never did. And the law you received from angels, you never kept. Strip away the temple and the law as sources of security, and what remains? Only the God who appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, before there was any temple, before there was any law — the God who has been moving toward his people and through his people and despite his people, from the beginning.

Then Stephen looks up and sees what the council cannot see: the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. Standing — not seated.
