That is the missionary logic of the whole book in one household. God is not indifferent to the man reaching after him in the dark. He is so far from indifferent that he will rearrange the church to reach him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.' So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last sentence of Cornelius's speech is the one to keep, and it is worth learning by heart.

Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.

Take it in pieces, because each phrase is doing work. We are all here — nobody is missing, the room is full, the invitations were accepted. In the presence of God — they are not primarily aware of Peter; they know whose house this has become. To hear all — not the parts that suit them, not a summary, all of it. That you have been commanded by the Lord — they are not expecting Peter's opinions. They have assumed from the start that he is under orders and that they are about to hear what the orders were.

No preacher in the history of the world has walked into a better room than that. There is no resistance to overcome, no attention to win, no suspicion to disarm; the congregation has assembled itself, prepared itself, and stated in advance that it intends to obey. Peter's whole introduction has been taken out of his hands.

And it did not happen by accident. Behind that sentence lie four days of a man going round a garrison town telling people what had happened to him while he prayed, and behind that lie the years of praying and giving that Luke set out in verse 2. This room is what the preparation of a heart looks like when it has spread to a household.

It is worth turning the sentence round and letting it look at us. Most Christians hear preaching on the assumption that some of it will be interesting and some will not, and that the appropriate response is assessment. Cornelius's household came expecting to be commanded by God through a man, and said so out loud before he opened his mouth — and the Holy Spirit fell on them before he had finished. It is not certain that those two facts are unrelated.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter opened his mouth and said: "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly I understand. That is how the sermon opens, and it is an admission. Not as I have always taught, but I am now getting it — the first words of the first sermon ever preached to Gentiles are a man saying out loud, in front of the congregation, that he has just changed his mind.

Then the sentence itself: God shows no partiality. The Greek word is a vivid compound meaning to receive the face — to make a judgement on the strength of who somebody visibly is. It is courtroom language, the term for a judge who decides by looking at the parties, and the Old Testament uses it to describe exactly the sort of magistrate God is not. He does not take the face.

And Peter says it while looking at a room of faces he had been raised to sort. That is the force of truly I understand: he is not quoting a principle he learned in the synagogue — he had known the principle for fifty years — he is saying that he has finally seen where it goes. In every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. (cf. Rom. 2:11; Gal. 3:28)

One clarification, since 'anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable' is sometimes taken to mean that sincere people of any religion are saved without Christ. The passage itself rules that out. The point is that God plays no favourites by nation — he welcomes seekers from every people, not Jews only. But 'acceptable' does not mean 'already saved apart from the gospel': devout, praying Cornelius still needed to hear and believe, for the angel said Peter 'will declare to you a message by which you will be saved' (11:14; 10:43, 'everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness'). God 'accepted' Cornelius's God-fearing search by sending him the gospel, not by counting him saved without it. The precious missionary truth here is that the honest seeker in any nation, God will see to it that the gospel reaches him — yet salvation remains through Christ alone, received by faith. (Inclusivists read 'acceptable' more broadly; Cornelius's own story — a seeker who still had to hear and believe — tells against it.)

verseByVerse.quote: "As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter begins the story where it began — the word that he sent to Israel — and he does not apologise for it. The gospel came to the Jews first; that is simply the history, and Peter states it in a Gentile drawing room without embarrassment. This message has an address it started from.

And what it is, is good news of peace. That phrase is out of Isaiah, where a runner comes over the hills with news that the war is over and God has come back to his people — how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace. Peter is standing in front of a professional soldier and using the vocabulary of a herald announcing the end of hostilities. Cornelius would have understood the picture better than most people in the room.

Then, dropped into the middle of the sentence in brackets, the largest claim in the chapter.

He is Lord of all.

Three words. Not Lord of Israel, not Lord of the church, not Lord of those who acknowledge him. Of all — and the phrase in Greek puts all first for emphasis, so it lands as of all he is Lord. Peter is talking to an officer of the empire whose formal creed was that Caesar is lord, in a city named after Caesar, with a temple to Caesar on the seafront, and he says it in an aside.

But it is not primarily a political sentence, and it is doing something specific in this sermon. Peter has just said that God shows no partiality, and a hearer might reasonably ask on what grounds. Here is the ground. The reason the gospel cannot be kept inside one nation is not that God has become broad-minded; it is that the man at the centre of it owns everything. A local Lord may have a local people. A Lord of all has no outsiders — only subjects who have not yet been told.

And it is the sentence that makes sense of what has been happening for two chapters. Peter has been dragged up a coast road against his instincts to a house he would never have entered, and the explanation is in the parenthesis: the one who sent him already owned the address.

verseByVerse.quote: "you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves know what happened. Peter is not introducing a stranger, and the assumption is worth noticing: he takes it for granted that a Roman household in Caesarea has followed the story of a Galilean preacher. They had. It had been in every town in the province for three years and had ended in a public execution outside Jerusalem sixty miles away, and news of that kind reaches a garrison.

So he starts where the public record starts — beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed — and gives them the ministry in one sentence. This is the shape of the earliest Christian preaching everywhere in Acts: not a philosophy, but an account of what a particular man did in a particular province within living memory, offered to people who could check it.

God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. The word anointed is the verb behind Christ, so Peter is explaining the title rather than just using it — a courtesy to a room that has not grown up with the vocabulary. Kings and priests were anointed with oil; this one was anointed with the Spirit.

And then the summary of a whole life, which is as good a sentence as exists in the New Testament: he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.

'All who were oppressed by the devil' — the word for oppressed (katadynasteuō) means to be tyrannized, held down under a cruel power. Peter is summing up Jesus' whole ministry of healing and deliverance as a rescue operation: he was prising people loose from the devil's grip. The phrase reaches wider than the cases of open demon-possession (on the nature of those 'unclean spirits,' and the caution that not every illness is a direct demonic act, see on 5:15–16). It gathers up all whom the devil's dark dominion held — for behind the whole reign of sickness, bondage, and death in a fallen world stands, ultimately, 'the works of the devil,' and 'the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy' them (1 John 3:8). Jesus himself could call a crippled woman one 'whom Satan bound for eighteen years' (Luke 13:16).

So every healing was a liberation, and a preview of total victory. Jesus came as the stronger man who binds the strong man and plunders his house (Mark 3:27), invading the devil's territory to set the captives free — 'if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you' (Matt. 12:28). And he pressed it to the very end: at the cross he 'disarmed the rulers and authorities' (Col. 2:15) and through death destroyed 'the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil' (Heb. 2:14). The comfort here is plain — whatever cruel power has held a person down, Jesus is the great Liberator, mightier than the devil, who rescues us 'from the domain of darkness' into his own kingdom (Col. 1:13; Acts 26:18). 'He went about doing good' — and the good he did was to break the oppressor's chains.

verseByVerse.quote: "And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we are witnesses of all that he did. Peter says it before he says anything about the cross, and he will say it again in the next verse. Everything in this sermon rests on the claim that the men saying it were there.

Then the death, and the way he puts it would have made a Jewish hearer flinch. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree.

He does not say crucified, which is the ordinary word and the one Cornelius would have expected from a Roman perspective. He reaches instead for a phrase out of Deuteronomy — a hanged man is cursed by God — the law about a body left on a tree, which every Jew knew and which was the standing objection to the whole Christian claim. A crucified Messiah was a cursed Messiah, and that was the end of the argument.

Peter uses the objection as his description. He does not avoid the scandalous word; he puts it in the sermon. Paul later takes the same verse and shows what it is for — Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — but Peter, years earlier, is already speaking of the cross in the vocabulary of the curse, which means the church had understood from very early on that the worst thing about the crucifixion was the point of it.

But God raised him on the third day. One conjunction carries the whole gospel. They put him to death; God raised him. Two subjects, two verbs, and the second reverses the first.

And note that the resurrection is consistently something done to Jesus by God in these early sermons. Not that he rose, though that is true elsewhere and the New Testament says it — but that God raised him, which is the language of a verdict. A court had ruled; a higher court has set the ruling aside. What men called a curse, God called his Son, and said so by emptying the grave.

And made him to appear — which leads directly into the strangest sentence in the sermon, and it is the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: "not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses.

It is an odd thing to volunteer, and it is the last thing an inventor of a story would include. If a man is fabricating a resurrection, he does not pause in the middle of the account to concede that the risen figure was not shown to the general public. Peter raises the difficulty himself, unprompted, in front of an audience that had not asked.

Why not to everybody? Scripture does not fully explain it, and it is honest to say so. But the logic is not hard to see. A public appearance in the temple courts would have compelled belief of a kind — the kind a man cannot get out of — and God's consistent way is to give sufficient evidence to those who will testify rather than overwhelming evidence to those who will not. And there was to be a definite, nameable, countable body of witnesses, so that the church's claim would rest on people who could be found and cross-examined rather than on a rumour that everybody had heard from somebody.

Then the detail Peter chooses as his proof, which is not the one anybody would predict. Who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.

Not: we saw him, we touched him, we heard him teach. We had meals with him. It is the most ordinary evidence available and by some distance the most difficult to explain away. A vision does not ask for something to eat. A hallucination shared by a dozen men does not take bread and hand it round. Luke's own Gospel records the risen Christ asking whether they had anything there, and being given a piece of broiled fish, and eating it in front of them — and John records breakfast on a beach.

The resurrection Peter is preaching is not a survival of the spirit or a continuing influence or a sense that he is somehow still with us. It is a man who was dead, sitting down to supper. That is what the apostles said they had seen, and it is why they could not be talked out of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two sentences, and between them they contain the whole of what the church has to say.

The first is the harder. He is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. Peter has told them who Jesus was, what he did, how he died and that God raised him — and the conclusion he draws from all of it is that this man will judge the human race. The living and the dead is a phrase that closes every exit: nobody is too long buried to be included and nobody is too much alive to be exempt.

It is worth noticing that this is presented as part of the good news rather than as a threat attached to it. And it is good news, when you consider the alternatives — a universe in which nothing is ever finally called what it is, where the man who arranged the killing and the woman who was killed go into the same silence and nobody ever says which was which. A judgement is the guarantee that the accounts will be settled. What makes it terrifying is not that there is a judge; it is that we are in the dock.

Which is why the second sentence has to come immediately, and does. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.

The judge and the Saviour are the same person. That is the whole architecture of the gospel in one movement, and it is the only arrangement under which anybody could survive the first sentence. The one appointed to assess the living and the dead is the one on whose name a man may call and be forgiven — and he is offering it now, in a front room in Caesarea, before the bench is ever taken.

Then look at the width of the last sentence, because Peter has chosen every word of it for the people in front of him. All the prophets — so this is not a novelty, it is what Israel's Scriptures were for. Everyone who believes — not every Jew, not every circumcised person, everyone. Believes — not achieves, not qualifies, not is born into. And through his name, which is to say on his account and not on ours.

Peter never gets to say anything else. That word everyone is very nearly the last thing out of his mouth before the Holy Spirit interrupts him, and the interruption is God's way of saying that the word meant what it said.

verseByVerse.quote: While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Peter was still saying these things. He is interrupted. The most important sermon of his life is cut off in the middle by the Holy Spirit, and Luke evidently thought the timing worth recording precisely.

It matters because of everything that is not in this account. There is no appeal, no call to respond, no moment of decision, no prayer to repeat. Nobody is baptised first — the water does not appear until verse 47, and Peter has to ask for it. Nobody is circumcised, nobody has agreed to keep the law, nobody has been examined by anyone. God simply does not wait. He falls on a room of uncircumcised Gentiles at the point in the sermon where the word everyone has just been spoken, and the effect is to put his own signature under it before the sentence has cooled.

Then Luke turns the camera on the men Peter had brought with him. The believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed.

These are the six from Joppa — Jewish Christians, brought along as witnesses, who had walked thirty miles for exactly this purpose. And what they feel is not delight. It is astonishment: the word means they were standing outside themselves, knocked out of their own minds. They had believed for some time that Jesus was the Messiah. They had not remotely believed this.

It is one of the more honest sentences in the New Testament, and it is a mercy that Luke left it in. The first Christians did not arrive at the inclusion of the Gentiles by reflection, and they did not welcome it warmly when it came. They were shocked. Their own Scriptures had said it would happen, their Lord had told them to go to the ends of the earth, and when God did it in front of them they stood there with their mouths open.

Which should be a comfort to anybody who has watched God do something they had no framework for, and found their first reaction was not faith but bewilderment. That was the reaction of the six men who had been brought specifically as witnesses. And it did not stop God, and it did not disqualify them; they went back to Jerusalem and told the church what they had seen.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
How did anybody know the Spirit had fallen? Luke answers the question directly, because the whole argument of the next five chapters depends on the answer being checkable. They were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God.

The sign is the same sign as the first morning in Jerusalem, and that is the entire point of it. Not a similar experience, not a comparable enthusiasm — the same thing, recognisable instantly by men who had been in the upper room and had spent eight years telling people about it. When Peter reports this to the Jerusalem church he puts it exactly so: the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning, and when the council meets in chapter 15 he says God gave them the Spirit just as he did to us, and made no distinction.

Consider why God chose to do it this way. He could have converted that household quietly, and nobody in the room would have doubted it — the sermon was believed, the response was genuine, and Peter could have baptised them and gone home. Instead he gave a sign that could not be described in any language except the one already used of Pentecost, in front of six Jewish witnesses who would be required to give evidence. The demonstration was not for Cornelius. It was for Jerusalem.

And it settled the question before the argument could begin. Once the Spirit had been given on exactly the same terms as at Pentecost, there was no case left to make for a two-tier church — no possibility of Gentile believers as associate members, admitted on probation, conditional on circumcision, seated at a separate table. God had already decided, publicly, and the church spent the following years catching up with a decision it had not been consulted about.

The other thing worth hearing in the verse is what these people were actually doing with the gift. Extolling God. Not analysing it, not asking what it meant, not wondering whether it would last. A Roman officer's household, five minutes into the Christian faith, was in the middle of its front room magnifying the God of Israel out loud in languages nobody had taught them — and the sermon that produced it had not even finished.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can anyone withhold water?

Peter puts it as a question, and the question is not really addressed to the room. It is addressed to the six men standing behind him, and through them to the church in Jerusalem, and it is unanswerable. The argument runs backwards from a fact nobody present can dispute: these people have received the Holy Spirit just as we have. Everything else is now a formality. If God has given the greater thing, on what possible ground does a man withhold the lesser?

It is worth noticing what Peter does not do. He does not send to Jerusalem for a ruling, though the question is momentous and he will certainly be answering for it later. He does not impose conditions or a probationary period. He does not require circumcision, which is what the whole church will be arguing about for the next several years. He watches what God has plainly done and refuses to be more cautious than God.

And then, having asked whether anyone can withhold it, he commanded them to be baptised. Not invited, not offered. It is the same word used of a military order, which the head of that household would have recognised. The question was for the Jewish witnesses; the command was for the Gentile believers.

The last clause is easy to skim and is the quiet triumph of the chapter. Then they asked him to remain for some days. A Jewish apostle who that morning had never entered a Gentile house stays on as a guest in one — eating at that table, sleeping under that roof, for days — and the man who wrote by no means, Lord across a sheet full of animals had stopped arguing entirely.

'Baptized in the name of Jesus Christ' — the apparent tension with Jesus' own command to baptize 'in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matt. 28:19) is treated more fully at 2:38 (including why the 'Jesus Only' / Oneness reading goes wrong). In brief: Luke is not recording the exact words spoken over the candidate; he is describing the baptism's character — it was Christian baptism, baptism that belongs to Jesus and marks a person out as now his, as distinct from John's baptism or any other washing. To be baptized 'into the name of Jesus' is to be baptized into the whole triune God, for you cannot have the Son without the Father who sent him and the Spirit he gives — and this very scene proves it, with the Father anointing (10:38), the Son saving, and the Spirit falling on the household (10:44).

So, as to 'the way we should do it': we follow Jesus' own explicit instruction and baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19) — the words the Lord himself gave, and the church's practice from the earliest days (the Didache, around AD 100, already prescribes them). The Acts phrase 'in the name of Jesus' does not compete with that formula; it simply names whose baptism it is. The two say one thing from two angles: those baptized belong to Jesus, and to belong to Jesus is to belong to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

10.theology: Election and the Nations. Acts 10 is the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham: “in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). The blessing always intended to reach the Gentiles; what Acts 10 shows is the mechanism — the proclamation of Jesus Christ, Lord of all, and the sovereign gift of the Holy Spirit to all who believe. The Gentile mission is not an emergency plan devised when Israel rejected the Messiah. It is the ancient plan of the God who chose Abraham in order to bless the world through him. Peter’s visit to Cornelius is, in the deepest sense, the arrival of what Genesis 12 promised. The God who shows no partiality has always intended a people from every nation. Acts 10 is that intention breaking into history.
10.examples:
Then: A Roman soldier who prayed toward Jerusalem and a Jewish fisherman who would never have entered a Gentile home — brought together by two visions, thirty miles apart, orchestrated by the God who wastes nothing and plans everything. The Spirit fell. The barriers fell. The church was never the same.

Now: The church in every generation must resist the temptation to build walls that God has torn down. The divisions that seem most natural — racial, cultural, economic, denominational — are the ones most likely to be the new versions of the Jewish-Gentile divide. What God has made clean, do not call common. The community of the Spirit is wider than our instincts, and deeper than our categories.

11.title: The Church at Antioch
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. <sup>2</sup>So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him, saying, <sup>3</sup>“You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.” <sup>4</sup>But Peter began and explained it to them in order: <sup>5</sup>“I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me. <sup>6</sup>Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>7</sup>And I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’ <sup>8</sup>But I said, ‘By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ <sup>9</sup>But the voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, do not call common.’ <sup>10</sup>This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven. <sup>11</sup>And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. <sup>12</sup>And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man’s house. <sup>13</sup>And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, ‘Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; <sup>14</sup>he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’ <sup>15</sup>As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. <sup>16</sup>And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ <sup>17</sup>If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God’s way?” <sup>18</sup>When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, “Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.” <sup>19</sup>Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews. <sup>20</sup>But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. <sup>21</sup>And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord. <sup>22</sup>The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose, <sup>24</sup>for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord. <sup>25</sup>So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, <sup>26</sup>and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians. <sup>27</sup>Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. <sup>28</sup>And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius). <sup>29</sup>So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. <sup>30</sup>And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
11.overview:
The Jerusalem church is disturbed. Peter has eaten with Gentiles. In the world of first-century Judaism this was not a minor breach of etiquette; it was a fundamental transgression of the boundaries that defined the covenant people. And so Peter explains — not defending himself, but laying out the sequence of God’s action: vision, voice, Spirit, Gentiles praising God. And the argument that silences the critics is the simplest and most devastating: “who was I that I could stand in God’s way?” When God moves, the only question is whether you will move with him.

Meanwhile, two hundred miles to the north, the scattered believers who fled Stephen’s death are doing something unprecedented. Some of them — unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene — begin speaking to Gentiles in Antioch about the Lord Jesus. Not Peter. Not the twelve. Unknown disciples, obeying the impulse of the Spirit, doing what had never been done before. “And the hand of the Lord was with them.” A great many believed and turned to the Lord.

Antioch becomes the first truly multi-ethnic church, the first church not rooted in a synagogue, the birthplace of the word “Christian” — and the sending base from which the whole Gentile mission will be launched. The church that began in a frightened upper room in Jerusalem is now planting itself in the third largest city of the empire. God is moving with speed and surprise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The most important thing that had ever happened to the church happened in Caesarea, and the church's first reaction was a complaint.

News reaches Jerusalem before Peter does, and when he arrives there is a delegation waiting. Luke names them — the circumcision party, the first named faction in Christian history — and he uses a pointed verb for what they did: they took issue with him, which is the same word the Spirit had used when telling Peter to go with the men making no distinction. The men objecting to Peter are doing the precise thing Peter was forbidden to do.

And notice what the charge actually is. Not that he preached to Gentiles, and not that he baptised them. You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them. The complaint is about a meal. Which is not as trivial as it sounds — a shared table was the ancient world's plainest declaration that two people belonged to the same company — and it is exactly the point on which Peter himself will lose his nerve years later at Antioch, when men from this same party come down and he withdraws from the Gentile table and Paul has to face him down in public.

Peter's defence is not an argument. It is a story, told in order, from the roof in Joppa to the Spirit falling in Caesarea, with his own refusal left in and the offensive details sharpened rather than softened, and six eyewitnesses standing in the room. He never claims he was right. His closing sentence claims only that he was not in a position to stop it: who was I that I could stand in God's way?

And the room falls silent, and then praises God. It is worth marking that the argument died before the worship started, and worth marking too how long the practice took to catch up with the principle — because the very next verse goes back several years and reports believers scattered across three provinces speaking the word to nobody but Jews.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel's Reach and the Church's Lag

What this passage shows is not a wicked church being corrected but a devout one being overtaken. The men who met Peter at the door were not bigots inventing a rule; they were holding to a boundary God himself had drawn, for reasons he himself had given, which had been kept at enormous cost for centuries. Their difficulty was that the boundary had done its work and been retired, and nobody had told them. Reformed theology has taken the episode as the clearest case in Scripture of the Spirit going ahead of the church's understanding — and of how he settles such questions. Not by a decree, not by a text, and not by an apostolic ruling: by doing the thing in public, in front of witnesses who could be cross-examined, and letting the church draw the conclusion. It is also a warning about the gap between conviction and conduct. The Jerusalem church conceded the principle in verse 18 and was still arguing about the practice at a council several years later, and Peter, who won this argument, later behaved as though he had lost it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter's answer to a hostile hearing was to narrate what had happened, including the parts against himself, with six men present who had seen it. He produced no proof text and pulled no rank. Now: That is still the strongest thing available in a disputed matter, and the rarest. A man who tells the story straight, admits where he resisted, and brings witnesses is very hard to answer — and a man who says only that God told him, with nothing checkable attached, has said nothing anybody can test.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two sentences, and a great deal is happening in them.

The first is that the news travelled faster than the man. The apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard — not just Jerusalem, but the whole province. Something like this does not stay in Caesarea; six men had walked home from it with a story, and by the time Peter came up to the city everybody had heard a version.

The second is that Luke names a faction. The circumcision party — literally those of the circumcision — and it is the first time in this book that a group inside the church is identified as a party with a position. They are not outsiders. They are believers, in Jerusalem, who hold that a man who wants in must come in the way God has always specified. Paul uses exactly the same phrase years later, in a letter, describing the men whose arrival at Antioch made Peter get up from a Gentile table — so this is not a passing mood. It is a standing party with a policy, and it will run through the next four chapters and out into the epistles.

And then the verb Luke chooses for what they did, which is the sharpest thing in the sentence and is invisible in English. They criticised him — and the word is the same one the Spirit had used on the stairs at Joppa, when Peter was told to go with the three men making no distinction. It is the verb for separating, sorting, discriminating between one thing and another.

So the sentence reads, to anyone with the Greek: the Spirit told Peter not to discriminate, and here are the brothers, discriminating. Luke does not comment. He simply uses the word twice, ten verses apart, and lets the reader find it.

It is worth being fair to them before the passage moves on. These men were not inventing a prejudice. They were defending a boundary God had drawn himself, in writing, for reasons he had given, which faithful Israelites had died rather than cross. From where they stood, Peter had done something indefensible, and the fact that it had gone well was not obviously an argument — plenty of wrong things go well. Their instinct to ask him about it was not the instinct of small men. It was the instinct of serious ones who had not yet been told what God had decided.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the charge, and the first thing to notice is what it is not.

They do not say you preached to Gentiles. They do not say you baptised uncircumcised men, which is the far larger question and the one that will dominate the council in chapter 15. They say: you went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.

The complaint is about a meal.

That looks trivial to a modern reader and it was nothing of the sort. In the ancient world a shared table was the plainest public statement two people could make about each other. You ate with your own; hospitality created obligation, and eating in a man's house said, in front of everybody, that you and he belonged to one company. A Jew could trade with a Gentile, employ one, serve under one and argue with one. Sitting down to supper was different, and everybody on both sides understood exactly what it meant.

So the circumcision party have gone straight to the real issue, and they have better instincts than they are usually given credit for. Preaching to Gentiles could be a mission. Eating with them is a verdict. If Peter can sit at Cornelius's table, then the wall is down, and everything else follows.

And now the thing that must be said about this verse, because it makes the whole passage honest rather than triumphant. Peter wins this argument. He wins it completely; the room falls silent and praises God. And some years afterwards, at Antioch, Peter is eating with Gentile believers as a matter of course when men arrive from this same circumcision party — and he gets up from the table. He withdraws, and the other Jewish believers follow him, and even Barnabas is carried along, until Paul confronts him in front of everybody for not walking straight with the truth of the gospel.

The same man. The same issue. The same party. Having stood in Jerusalem and told them all why the wall was down, he later got up from a table because he was afraid of them.

There is no comfort in that and there is a great deal of use. A conviction can be argued to a conclusion, defended in public, praised by the church, and still not have reached the part of a man that decides where he sits at dinner. Peter's theology was right in chapter 11 and his feet were wrong in Galatians, and the gap between the two is where most Christian failure actually lives.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter began and explained it to them in order: "I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter began and explained it to them in order.

The word for in order is the one Luke used in the preface to his Gospel when he told Theophilus he had decided to write an orderly account. It means sequentially, one thing after another, with nothing left out and nothing rearranged. Peter is not making a case. He is giving evidence.

And that is the most striking feature of this whole defence, once you look for what is absent from it. He does not quote Scripture, though he could have; Isaiah has a great deal to say about the nations, and Peter had used the prophets freely enough at Pentecost. He does not appeal to his office, though he is the leading apostle and had been given the keys. He does not invoke the commission to go to the ends of the earth, which every man in that room had heard from the Lord's own mouth. He tells them what happened, in the order it happened.

There is a reason that works better than an argument would have. An argument can be met with a counter-argument, and both sides go home unmoved; every man in that room was capable of debating the law with Peter and some of them would have enjoyed it. But an account of events, given in order, with witnesses present, has to be either accepted or called a lie. Peter narrows the options to two, and one of them is not available, because six men from Joppa are standing there.

Then he starts where the story starts: I was in the city of Joppa praying. Not I had been thinking about the Gentile question. He was on a roof at midday doing what he did most days, and the whole thing came down on him from outside. That matters to his case. If this had begun with an idea of Peter's, the circumcision party would be entitled to their objection. It began with a sheet.

And he says so with the same phrase Luke used in chapter 10 — something like a great sheet. Even under pressure, defending himself in front of a hostile room, Peter will not describe the thing more definitely than he saw it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. And I heard a voice saying to me, 'Rise, Peter; kill and eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Compare this retelling with Luke's own account in the previous chapter, and something worth noticing emerges: Peter's version is harder than the original.

Chapter 10 says the sheet held all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. Peter, reporting to a room full of Torah-observant Jews who are already angry with him, adds a category: animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. Beasts of prey — wild carnivores, the class of creature furthest from anything a Jew would put on a plate. He has volunteered the most repellent item on the list.

And he adds something else that is not in chapter 10: looking at it closely, I observed. He did not glance at the sheet and recoil. He examined it. He looked at what was in there, item by item, and knew exactly what he was being asked to do before he refused.

This is a man under examination making his own case worse on purpose, and it is the reason the defence works. Every instinct in that situation is to shade the account — to leave out the beasts of prey, to imply he had been unclear about what was in the sheet, to present the whole thing as more ambiguous and therefore more excusable. Peter does the opposite. He tells them precisely how offensive the command was, because the strength of his case rests entirely on the command having come from God, and a command that has been softened is no longer the command that came.

There is a general principle in that, and it applies well beyond first-century food laws. A man defending something God has done does not need to make it more palatable, and every attempt to do so weakens the only thing he has. The offensiveness of the instruction is part of the evidence that it was not his idea.

Rise, Peter; kill and eat. He quotes the words unaltered, including his own name in them. Whatever else the men in that room concluded, they could not conclude that Peter had drifted into this.

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said, 'By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.' But the voice answered a second time from heaven, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the shrewdest thing in the speech, and it is not a manoeuvre — it is simply honesty that happens to be devastating.

Peter tells them that he refused.

By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth. He puts his own objection into the record, in full, in the exact words he used — and they are the words every man in that room would have used. He is telling the circumcision party that when God gave him this command, his first reaction was theirs.

Consider what that does to the argument. They came to the meeting believing that Peter had gone soft on the law, and here he is testifying that he defended it to God's face. There is now no version of the story in which Peter is a man with loose views who was looking for an excuse. He was the man who said no. Whatever changed his mind was not in him.

It is worth learning as a habit, because it is one of the few things that actually moves people who disagree. Most persuasion begins by explaining why the other man's position is inadequate, and most persuasion therefore fails, because a man defending a position hears only that he is being attacked. Peter begins by demonstrating that he held their position, understood the reasons for it, and stated it more strongly than they had. Only then does he say what happened next.

And what happened next is the sentence that ends the matter: what God has made clean, do not call common.

Note that Peter does not paraphrase or apply it. He simply reports it, and lets it sit in the room. It had been said to him and it is now being said to them, in the same words, by the same voice, and it is exactly as unanswerable the second time. The only reply available to the circumcision party is the one Peter had already tried, and they have just heard how well it went for him.

verseByVerse.quote: "This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This happened three times.

Peter is producing it as evidence, and in that room it was strong evidence. A single extraordinary experience can be doubted by the man who had it, and much more easily by everybody else — a dream, a state of mind, something misremembered afterwards. A thing repeated three times, with the same voice, the same command and the same correction, has moved out of the category of impressions. Peter is telling the church that God said this to him until it could not be mistaken.

Three is his number and he must have known it. Three denials by a fire. Three questions on a beach. And now three refusals on a roof, each one answered. It is difficult to believe the man who lived through all three did not notice a pattern in how God dealt with him — and there is something almost tender in it. God did not correct Peter once and expect it to take. He said it again. And then he said it a third time.

And all was drawn up again into heaven. Then it stopped. No interpretation was offered, no application supplied, no instruction about what to do with it. The vision was withdrawn and Peter was left on a roof with a command he had refused and a sentence he could not argue with.

That is worth registering by anybody who has been given something from God that came without instructions — a conviction with no clear next step, a text that will not let go, an unshakable sense about something with nothing attached telling you what to do about it. Peter's vision did not come with a application, and it did not need one, because the application was already walking up the road and would be at the gate within the hour.

He did not have to work it out. He had to answer the door.

And there is a kindness in the arithmetic that should not be hurried past. God did not say it once and hold Peter responsible for having heard. He did not say it twice and let the silence do the rest. He said it three times, to a man who had already been forgiven three denials, and then took the sheet away.

Anyone who has needed a thing said to them repeatedly before it went in — and has assumed that the repetition was a measure of God's patience running out — should read the verse the other way round. The repetition is the patience. It is not that God grew exasperated and raised his voice. It is that he knew exactly how many times this particular man would need to hear it, and said it that many times.

verseByVerse.quote: "And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man's house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, at that very moment three men arrived.

Peter's whole case rests on timing, and here it is. The sheet has just gone back up. He is standing on a roof with no idea what any of it meant — and at that instant, not an hour later, three strangers are at the door asking for him by name, sent from a city thirty miles away by a man he has never met. Nobody arranged that. Cornelius's messengers had left Caesarea the day before the vision was given.

Then: the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction.

That phrase is the hinge of the defence, and it is the same word Luke used in verse 2 of the men now questioning him. They took issue with Peter; the Spirit told Peter to make no distinction. It is one verb, used twice, and Peter is quoting the Spirit's instruction back to a room full of people doing the opposite. He does not point it out. He does not have to; anyone listening in Greek heard it.

And then the sentence that wins the argument before it is finished: These six brothers also accompanied me.

These. They are in the room. Peter did not merely take witnesses to Caesarea — he brought them back to Jerusalem and up to this meeting, and at the critical moment he can turn and indicate six men who saw the whole thing. The law of Moses required two or three witnesses to establish a matter. He has brought double.

It is worth pausing on the foresight. On the morning Peter set out from Joppa he had a vision he did not understand and an instruction he had not been given a reason for — and he still had the presence of mind to think: whatever happens at the other end of this road, I will have to account for it, and my word alone will not be enough. So he took six men.

That is not timidity and it is not politics. It is a leader who knows that the church will have to be persuaded, that being right is not the same as being believed, and that the honest way to handle a claim nobody wants to hear is to make it checkable in advance. Anybody who has ever had to report something difficult to a body that would rather not hear it could do worse than copy him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, 'Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here Peter supplies the piece of information Luke has twice withheld — and the withholding was deliberate.

Chapter 10 gave the angel's message to Cornelius at verse 4, and gave it again in Cornelius's own words at verse 30. Both times it ran the same way: your prayers and alms have been remembered, send to Joppa for Simon called Peter. Both times it stopped there. Now, reporting to Jerusalem, Peter finishes the sentence: he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.

That clause is the whole reason Peter can stand in that room. Think about what he is demonstrating with it. Before he ever left Joppa — before the vision on the roof, before the knock at the gate — God had already told a Gentile that a message was coming by which he would be saved. The word was on record with the angel. Peter did not go to Caesarea and then decide that Gentiles could be saved. He was sent as the delivery of a promise that had already been made without him.

And it settles the question the story otherwise leaves open, which is why the clause matters far beyond this argument. Cornelius was devout, generous and prayerful, and God had noticed all of it. He was also, on the day the angel came, not saved — because the angel told him a message was coming by which he would be. There is no reading of that sentence which allows his piety to have been sufficient in itself, and there is no reading of it which allows the gospel to have been an optional enrichment for a man already safe.

The hard half and the kind half stand together here as they always do. The hard half: sincerity does not save, and God does not pretend it does. The kind half: God's response to a sincere man was not to leave him with his sincerity, but to dispatch an angel, arrange a vision, override an apostle's lifelong conviction and move him thirty miles up a coast road, in order to get him the message.

And note the last four words: you and all your household. The promise arrives with a family attached to it — the servants, the soldiers, the relatives Cornelius had gathered — which is how God had been speaking to households since Abraham, and which Peter had already announced at Pentecost when he said the promise was for them and for their children.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, 'John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I began to speak.

Peter is being precise, and the precision is his argument. Luke's account in chapter 10 says the Spirit fell while Peter was still speaking; Peter's own account says it happened as he began. He wants the room to understand how little of the work was his. He had not finished. He had not called for a response. He had barely got started, and God did not wait for the rest of it.

Then the comparison that ends the debate: the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning.

Not something similar. Not a lesser gift, or a partial one, or an unusual religious experience which might be interpreted in various ways. The same thing, and every man in that room had been there for the first one and could judge for himself. Peter calls Pentecost the beginning, which is how the church had come to date itself, and he is saying that what happened in a Roman officer's front room was the beginning happening again to different people.

And then the loveliest detail in the speech: I remembered the word of the Lord.

The theology arrived as a memory. Standing in Cornelius's house watching Gentiles speak in tongues, Peter did not reason his way to a conclusion; a sentence came back to him — John baptised with water, but you will be baptised with the Holy Spirit — spoken by Jesus on the Mount of Olives, some eight years earlier, in the last conversation before the ascension. Luke had recorded it in the fifth verse of this book. Peter had heard it, and it had sat in him for eight years doing nothing, and then it came up at the exact moment it was needed and explained everything he was looking at.

That is worth taking personally by anybody who wonders whether the slow business of getting Scripture into the memory is worth the trouble. Peter could not have looked it up; there was nothing to look up. What he had was what he had heard and kept. The moment came without warning and the sentence was there.

verseByVerse.quote: "If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God's way?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who was I that I could stand in God's way?

It is the last sentence of the defence and it is worth noticing what kind of sentence it is not. Peter does not say he was right. He does not say he had authority, or that he had weighed the matter and reached a considered view, or even that he had obeyed. He pleads incapacity. The leading apostle of the church, answering the church, says in effect: what was I supposed to do — stop him?

The logic is airtight because it has no moving parts. God gave the same gift to them as to us. He gave it when we believed; he gave it when they believed. The only variable that has been removed is the one the circumcision party was standing on. If God has done the identical thing on the identical terms, then the question is no longer whether Gentiles may be admitted. It is whether anybody proposes to overrule God on a matter he has already settled in public.

Nobody does. That is why the next verse records silence.

But a guard is needed here, because this verse is quoted in church disputes far more often than it is examined, and in the wrong hands it becomes a way of ending discussion rather than resolving it. Who was I to stand in God's way is not a formula for winning arguments by asserting divine backing. It works in this passage because of everything attached to it: a vision that was repeated three times, an independent vision given to a man thirty miles away, three messengers who arrived at the precise moment, an explicit word from the Spirit, six witnesses who can be questioned, and a public sign identical to one the whole room had personally seen eight years before. Peter is not saying God told me. He has just spent thirteen verses laying out the evidence, and only then does he draw the conclusion.

A man who says God told him and produces none of that has said something quite different, and the church has been damaged by people who learned Peter's last sentence without noticing that it came at the end.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, "Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life." Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard these things they fell silent.

Silence first, and the order matters. Before there is any praise there is a roomful of men with nothing to say — the objection simply runs out. Luke does not record anyone conceding, or apologising, or explaining how they had come to see it differently. The argument stops because there is no longer anything on the other side of it.

Then the praise, and the sentence they produce is remarkably well judged for men who have just lost a debate: Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life. Note the verb. Not the Gentiles have repented, which would be a report, but God has granted — they identify the giver in the same breath in which they concede the point, and what they praise him for is not that a barrier fell but that people were given life.

And then verse 19, and Luke does something abrupt. He drops the scene entirely, goes back several years to the persecution that killed Stephen, and picks up a thread he had left lying in chapter 8: those who were scattered travelled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch — speaking the word to no one except Jews.

Read that immediately after verse 18 and it lands like a cold draught. The council has just agreed, in Jerusalem, in principle, with praise, that God has granted repentance to the Gentiles. And Luke's very next sentence reports that for years believers had been carrying the gospel across three provinces and telling nobody but their own kind.

It is not an accusation and Luke makes no comment. But he has put the two sentences side by side, and the gap between them is the honest measurement of how long it takes a settled conviction to reach the street. The principle was conceded in a meeting. The practice changed in Antioch, some time later, by accident, in the hands of men whose names nobody wrote down.

One small but useful lesson in how to read the Bible lies in that phrase, 'God has granted repentance.' Notice that only repentance is named here, not faith — yet faith is plainly implied, for these Gentiles had believed the gospel (vv. 17, 21). Scripture constantly speaks this way, naming one part of a thing to stand for the whole (a figure of speech called synecdoche). Repentance and faith are simply the two sides of one single turning to Christ: repentance is turning from sin, faith is turning to the Saviour, and you cannot truly do one without the other. So Scripture sometimes names both — 'repent and believe in the gospel' (Mark 1:15), 'repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus' (Acts 20:21) — sometimes only repentance (here; Luke 24:47; Acts 3:19), and sometimes only faith ('believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved,' Acts 16:31; John 3:16). Whichever one is mentioned, the other comes with it. The whole gospel response can be summed up under any of its facets — 'call on the name of the Lord' (Rom. 10:13), 'confess... Jesus is Lord' (Rom. 10:9) all mean the same conversion.

Two cautions follow. First, never build a doctrine on the absence of a word: it would be a serious mistake to read this verse as though faith were unnecessary, or to read Acts 16:31 as though repentance were. Each statement is to be read in the light of the whole of Scripture, which everywhere joins the two. Second, savour what the verse actually says: God granted repentance. The very turning is his gift — as faith is also called 'the gift of God' (Eph. 2:8; cf. 2 Tim. 2:25; Phil. 1:29). So when you read 'repent' or 'believe' standing alone, you should hear the whole: turn to Christ, from sin and unto the Saviour — and give thanks that even the turning was granted you from above.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Everything that matters in the second half of Acts starts here, and Luke introduces it by going backwards. Verse 19 returns to the persecution that killed Stephen and follows the refugees north — as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch — noting, without comment, that they spoke the word to nobody but Jews.

And then some of them did not. Men of Cyprus and Cyrene, whose names Luke either did not know or did not record, arrived in Antioch and started talking to Greeks. There was no vision, no angel, no instruction from the Spirit and no apostolic authorisation. They simply told the people who were in front of them, and the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed. The theological revolution that took an apostle a rooftop vision, three messengers and a hearing in Jerusalem was carried out in Antioch by anonymous men who appear to have thought it was the obvious thing to do.

Jerusalem hears and sends Barnabas — and the choice of man decides the outcome. He arrives, sees the grace of God, and is glad; and then he does the thing that makes him one of the most consequential figures in the New Testament. He goes to Tarsus to look for Saul, who has been out of the story for the best part of a decade, finds him, and brings him back. They teach the church there for a year, and somewhere in that year the neighbours coin a nickname for these people: Christians.

The chapter ends with money going the other way. A prophet named Agabus warns of famine, and the Gentile church at Antioch — the newest and least established congregation in Christendom — takes up a collection for the believers in Judea and sends it by the hand of Barnabas and Saul. The church that Jerusalem had been arguing about whether to admit is the church that feeds it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Antioch and the Shape of a Sending Church

Antioch is the model the New Testament actually gives us for a missionary congregation, and almost nothing about it was planned. It began with unnamed laymen doing the obvious thing; it was recognised rather than authorised; it was established by a year of ordinary teaching; and its first corporate act was to send money to a church that had been suspicious of people like them. Reformed missiology has drawn the pattern out: rooted in the word, generous beyond its own borders, and willing to give away its best men — for within two chapters Antioch will send Barnabas and Saul off on the first missionary journey, which is to say it exported its two finest teachers and kept none of them. A church is not measured by what it gathers. It is measured by what it is prepared to lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The single most important barrier in Christian history was crossed by men from Cyprus and Cyrene whose names nobody recorded. Luke knows their home towns and not their names, which tells you they were never anybody's leadership. Now: The work that turns out to have mattered most in any generation is very often done by people who will not appear in an account of it — who simply spoke to whoever was in front of them, because it did not occur to them to check first whether they were allowed.

verseByVerse.quote: But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything turns on a small word at the start of the sentence: but. Verse 19 said the scattered believers spoke to nobody except Jews. But there were some of them — and the whole future of the church is in that exception.

Luke tells us where they came from and not who they were. Men of Cyprus and Cyrene: Diaspora Jews, Greek-speaking, from an island and from North Africa, used to living among Gentiles and presumably rather less scandalised by them than a man raised in Judea would have been. That is as much as we know. The most consequential thing any believer did in the first century was done by people whose names were not thought worth recording, and Luke, who is a careful historian and names dozens of minor figures elsewhere, evidently could not find out.

Cyrene is worth a second look. Men of Cyrene had a synagogue in Jerusalem and were among those who argued with Stephen and could not withstand him. Luke does not say these are the same men and it would be wrong to assert it. But the city that supplied some of Stephen's opponents also supplied some of the men who first did the thing Stephen had been killed for pointing toward, and that is at least worth noticing.

What they did was not a strategy. They spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. There is a genuine question about the word here — the manuscripts divide between Hellenists, Greek-speaking Jews, and Greeks, meaning Gentiles proper, and your Bible probably has a footnote. The sense of the passage requires Gentiles: verse 19 has just said to no one except Jews, and this sentence is the contrast to it. Whatever the copyists made of the word, Luke's argument is unmistakable.

And notice what is absent. No vision. No angel. No word from the Spirit, no instruction from Jerusalem, no debate, and no record that anybody asked permission. Peter needed a sheet let down from heaven three times before he would enter a Gentile house. These men arrived in a Greek city and started talking to Greeks, apparently because there were Greeks there.

And the hand of the Lord was with them — an Old Testament phrase for God's power actively at work — and a great number who believed turned to the Lord. Heaven's verdict on an unauthorised initiative by unnamed men was to bless it enormously.

verseByVerse.quote: The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem hears, and Jerusalem sends somebody. It is the second time in four chapters that news of an irregular advance has reached the mother church and produced a delegation — they sent Peter and John down to Samaria, and now they send a man to Antioch.

And the man they choose settles the outcome. It is worth pausing on how differently this could have gone. There were men available in Jerusalem who would have arrived at Antioch with the circumcision party's questions in their pocket; the reader has met them at the start of this very chapter. Send one of them, and the first Gentile congregation in history has its foundations examined by somebody looking for a fault. They sent Barnabas.

When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad.

Stop on that. What did he actually see? A room full of Greeks, uncircumcised, with pagan backgrounds and no synagogue training, worshipping the God of Israel in a Syrian city, taught by nobody in particular. There was plenty there for a careful man to be concerned about, and a great deal that would need sorting out, and Barnabas saw the grace of God. He had the eye for it. He looked at an untidy, unauthorised, doctrinally unformed crowd of new Gentile believers and identified the one thing that was actually going on.

And he was glad. Not relieved, not cautiously satisfied — glad, which is the same root as the joy that runs through this book. His name meant son of encouragement and he had earned it twice already, selling a field for the poor and vouching for Saul when nobody else would go near him. Here he does it a third time, simply by being pleased.

Then he does the work: he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose. The Greek is warmer and more physical than that — with the purpose of the heart, a settled inward intention. He does not begin by correcting them. He tells a young church in a pagan city the one thing it will most need, which is to stay put, and he tells them to do it from the inside out.

A great many things in church history have turned on which man was sent, and this is the clearest instance of it in Scripture. The Gentile mission survived its inspection because the inspector was a man capable of being delighted.

verseByVerse.quote: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke stops the narrative to explain why the previous verse happened, and the explanation is a character reference: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.

Take the first word on its own, because it is easy to skim and it is not a small thing. Good. Not brilliant, not strategic, not a powerful preacher, not well connected — Luke had all those words available and did not reach for any of them. He was a good man. It is the plainest commendation in the New Testament and one of the rarest, and it is offered as the reason an entire city came to Christ.

And notice where Luke has placed the sentence. It sits between Barnabas being glad at what he found and Barnabas going to fetch Saul — that is, in the middle of an account of a man rejoicing over somebody else's work and then going to get somebody better at teaching than himself. Luke's portrait of goodness is not abstract. It is a man with no jealousy in him.

And a great many people were added to the Lord. Added to the Lord, not to the congregation — Luke keeps the phrasing careful, as he did at Pentecost. The register that matters is not the one Barnabas was keeping.

'Full of the Holy Spirit' — a description we rarely hear on people's lips today, yet it is one of the loveliest things Scripture ever says of anyone. (On how such fullness shows itself, and how the early church could actually recognise it, see the fuller treatment at 6:5.) In brief, Luke uses the phrase not for a momentary 'filling' for a single task — Acts has those too, a sudden filling for boldness or speech (4:8, 31; 13:9) — but for a settled, habitual condition: a man so yielded to the Spirit that the Spirit pervades and governs his whole life, his character and words and deeds. It is the same thing said of Jesus himself ('full of the Holy Spirit,' Luke 4:1) and of Stephen (6:5) — so to be full of the Spirit is simply to be deeply like Christ. And notice how concrete it is in Barnabas: it is paired with 'a good man... and of faith,' and we have watched it in action — the generous giver who sold his field (4:36–37), the big-hearted man who vouched for the feared new convert Saul when others would not (9:27), the encourager who 'was glad' to see God's grace in Antioch (11:23). That is what a Spirit-full life looks like: goodness, faith, generosity, courage, and an eye quick to rejoice in grace.

And it is not meant to be a rare distinction reserved for a Barnabas. The New Testament commands every believer, 'be filled with the Spirit' (Eph. 5:18) — a continuous filling, sought by yielding to him: letting the word of Christ dwell richly (Col. 3:16), praying, obeying, walking in step with the Spirit rather than grieving or quenching him (Gal. 5:16; Eph. 4:30; 1 Thess. 5:19). It is a phrase worth recovering, and a thing worth coveting — for the highest compliment that could be paid to you is not that you are clever or capable, but that those who meet you meet something of God, because you are full of the Holy Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul.

The verb means to hunt out, to search for something that takes finding, and it implies that Saul was not simply sitting at an address. It had been the best part of a decade since the brothers put him on a boat at Caesarea; he had been working somewhere in Syria and Cilicia and nobody in Antioch knew exactly where. Barnabas made a journey of a hundred miles or so on the strength of remembering a man, and then had to go and look for him.

This is the second time Barnabas has done this for Saul, and the two acts between them are the reason there is a Pauline half to the New Testament. The first was in Jerusalem, when every Christian in the city was frightened of the man and Barnabas took him by the arm and walked him in to the apostles. The second is this: a hidden decade ended because one man could not leave him out there.

And consider what Barnabas is doing to himself. He is the recognised leader of the most promising church in the world, sent by Jerusalem, and he goes and fetches a teacher who will eclipse him entirely. Within two chapters Luke's phrase has changed from Barnabas and Saul to Paul and his companions, and Barnabas moves to the back of the story. He must have known it was likely. He went anyway.

For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. A year in one place, with one congregation, teaching. Not a campaign. It is worth noticing that the church which becomes the launching point for the entire Gentile mission was built by twelve months of ordinary instruction from two men who stayed put.

And then the sentence everybody remembers: in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.

The word is a Greek stem with a Latin ending — the form Romans used for the followers or partisans of somebody, as they said Herodians of Herod's men. So it is a nickname, coined by outsiders, in the street, on a Roman pattern, and it means Christ's lot. There is no suggestion the church chose it; the two other times it appears in the New Testament it is in the mouth of a king who is being sarcastic, and in a letter about suffering for the name.

What it tells you is what the neighbours in Antioch had concluded. Not that these people were generous, or strange, or Jewish, or a philosophy — but that they were somebody's. They were named after a person, by people watching from outside, who could not describe them without using his name.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prophets travel from Jerusalem to Antioch, and Luke mentions them without explanation, which tells you they were a familiar feature of church life rather than a curiosity.

It is worth saying briefly what such men were doing, since the word carries freight it did not then have. New Testament prophecy of this kind is not the writing of Scripture and it does not compete with it. What Agabus supplies is not doctrine but information — a specific, checkable, dated warning about something coming, given so that the church could act. He tells them there is going to be a famine. He does not tell them what to think about God.

Then Luke adds a parenthesis, and it is the sort of thing that makes him worth trusting: this took place in the days of Claudius. He is telling his reader that the prophecy came true and giving the reign in which to look for it. Claudius ruled from the early forties to the mid fifties, and his years were notorious for repeated grain shortages across the empire; a severe famine struck Judea in the mid to late forties, severe enough that a foreign queen who had become a convert to Judaism bought grain in Egypt and had it shipped in to keep Jerusalem alive. Luke is not asking anyone to take his word for it. He is dating the thing.

And notice what the warning is for. God does not tell the church at Antioch about the famine so that they can be impressed, or so that they can prepare their own storehouses. Read on: the next two verses are a collection. The foreknowledge is given so that a church can get money to people who are about to be hungry, before they are hungry.

That is a very characteristic piece of divine economy. A revelation is given about the future, and its entire practical content turns out to be an opportunity to be generous earlier than would otherwise have been possible.

A reader will reasonably ask whether men like Agabus exist now, and it is worth answering plainly rather than leaving it hanging. Christians differ about it, and the difference is real and held in good faith on both sides — some hold that gifts of this kind ceased with the apostolic foundation, others that they continue in some form. The fuller discussion belongs at 5:12, where the question of the signs is worked out.

What can be said here, and what both sides agree on, is the boundary. Whatever Agabus was, he was not adding to Scripture and nobody treated him as if he were; his contribution was a piece of practical information which the church then acted on with its own judgement. Any claim in any century that would correct, supplement or override what is written is a different thing altogether, and the church has always known how to name it.

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch which way the money goes.

Antioch is the new church — Gentile, recently converted, taught for a single year, and still the subject of some anxiety in Jerusalem, where a party had been arguing not long before about whether people like this could properly be admitted at all. Judea is the mother church, the apostolic centre, the place all of this came from. And it is Antioch that sends relief to Judea.

The church that had been argued about is the church that pays for the food.
