Nobody instructed them to. There is no request from Jerusalem in the text, no appeal, no apostolic circular. A prophet said there would be a famine, and the Antioch believers worked out for themselves who would be worst hit and did something about it before it arrived.

Every one according to his ability. Not a flat rate and not an equal share — each person gave in proportion to what he had, which is the New Testament's settled pattern for giving and is a good deal more searching than a fixed figure. A tenth from a man with nothing and a tenth from a man with everything are not the same act, and this arrangement knows it. It also means nobody in that congregation was exempt: the poorest members are included in every one, giving according to an ability that was small and real.

And then the two men who carry it: by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.

Sit with that for a moment. The money is being taken to the believers in Judea — the church in Jerusalem, the very people who had been dragged out of their houses, imprisoned and in some cases killed under the direction of a young man from Tarsus. Saul is walking into Judea carrying famine relief for the families he had broken up. Whatever conversations happened when he handed it over, Luke does not record them.

It is also the first joint mission of the partnership that will take the gospel across the empire, and it is not a preaching tour. Barnabas and Saul's first work together was delivering money to hungry people.

And the collection never really stopped. Paul spends years of his later ministry organising exactly this — a fund gathered from Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem — and he explains the theology of it in a sentence: if the Gentiles have come to share in the Jews' spiritual blessings, they owe it to them to be of service in material blessings. That whole enterprise, which occupies large parts of three of his letters, began here, with a famine warning and a young church that did not wait to be asked.

11.theology: Repentance as Gift. Acts 11:18 contains one of the clearest biblical statements of the Reformed doctrine of monergism in conversion: “God has granted repentance that leads to life.” Repentance is not a human achievement that God rewards with salvation; it is itself a divine gift, granted by God to those he is drawing to himself. This does not eliminate human responsibility — the Gentiles in Cornelius’s house genuinely repented, genuinely believed, genuinely turned to Christ. But behind their turning was God’s giving. This is the grammar of all true conversion: God grants, the sinner turns, and God receives the glory. Antioch is not merely a sociological phenomenon — it is a theological one: God giving repentance to people who had no claim on him, because he is the God of all grace.
11.examples:
Then: Anonymous men from Cyprus and Cyrene, whose names are not recorded in Scripture, who crossed the ethnic boundary no one else had thought to cross, and started the church in Antioch. The hand of the Lord was with them. History turned on their obedience.

Now: The church at Antioch is the model of a healthy sending church: multi-ethnic, Spirit-filled, taught by gifted teachers, responsive to need (the famine collection), and willing to send its best people out on mission. Every local church must ask whether it looks more like the fearful circumcision party in Jerusalem or the glad, generous, outward-facing church at Antioch.

12.title: The Prison and the Providence
12.text: <sup>1</sup>About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. <sup>2</sup>He killed James the brother of John with the sword. <sup>3</sup>And when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. <sup>4</sup>And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. <sup>5</sup>So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. <sup>6</sup>Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentinels before the door were guarding the prison. <sup>7</sup>And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his hands. <sup>8</sup>And the angel said to him, “Dress yourself and put on your sandals.” And he did so. And he said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.” <sup>9</sup>And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision. <sup>10</sup>When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him. <sup>11</sup>When Peter came to himself, he said, “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting.” <sup>12</sup>When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying. <sup>13</sup>And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. <sup>14</sup>Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate. <sup>15</sup>They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, “It is his angel!” <sup>16</sup>But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed. <sup>17</sup>But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place. <sup>18</sup>Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter. <sup>19</sup>And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentinels and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there. <sup>20</sup>Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food. <sup>21</sup>On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them. <sup>22</sup>And the people were shouting, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” <sup>23</sup>Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last. <sup>24</sup>But the word of God increased and multiplied. <sup>25</sup>And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
12.overview:
Herod Agrippa is playing to the crowd. He has killed James the son of Zebedee with the sword — the first of the twelve to be martyred — and it pleased the Jews, so he arrests Peter. The calculation is purely political. Herod is not a theological opponent; he is a man who will do whatever secures his power. And in the background, the church is praying.

The contrast Luke draws in this chapter is stark and deliberate: Herod’s power on one side, God’s providence on the other. Sixteen soldiers, chains, iron gates, maximum security — and Peter sleeping so peacefully that the angel has to strike him on the side to wake him. The man who is about to be executed is asleep. This is the peace that passes understanding — the peace of a man who knows that his life is in hands that Herod cannot reach.

The liberation is almost comic in its details: Peter thinks he is dreaming, Rhoda is too astonished to open the gate, the praying church refuses to believe their prayers are answered. But the most important moment in the chapter may be the shortest sentence: “But the word of God increased and multiplied.” Herod is dead, eaten by worms, and the Word is alive and growing. This is the verdict of history on every power that has set itself against the gospel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Herod's Persecution and God's Deliverance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two apostles are arrested in this chapter. One is executed and one walks out through an iron gate, and the church was praying either way. Luke puts them four verses apart and offers no explanation at all, and any honest reading has to begin there.

Herod Agrippa kills James the brother of John with the sword — half a verse, no speech, no last words, no vision of heaven. Then, finding it popular, he arrests Peter during Passover week and posts sixteen soldiers on him, because the authorities in this city had lost prisoners before. The church prays through the night. An angel arrives, strikes Peter awake, drops the chains off his wrists, walks him past two guard posts and out through a gate that opens by itself, and leaves him standing in an empty street.

What follows is the most human scene in Acts. Peter knocks at the door of the house where they are praying for him; a servant girl recognises his voice and is so overjoyed that she leaves him outside; and the prayer meeting tells her she is out of her mind and then produces a theological explanation for why the answer to their prayers cannot possibly be the answer to their prayers. Nobody in this chapter believes what God is doing while he is doing it — not the church at the door, and not Peter, who thought he was having a vision.

Then the reckoning. Herod executes his own guards, goes down to Caesarea, and on a public occasion in his royal robes accepts a crowd's shout that he is a god and not a man — and is struck down by an angel of the Lord and dies. The same word Luke used of the angel striking Peter awake he uses of the angel striking Herod down: one blow to wake a prisoner, one to end a king. And then, over the body of a man who claimed to be divine: but the word of God increased and multiplied.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Praying Church, the Sovereign God, and the Grave of James

This chapter is where a theology of prayer either becomes honest or becomes cruel. The church prayed earnestly and Peter was delivered; the church had prayed for James too, and James was buried. Luke gives no reason, and the Reformed tradition has been right to refuse to supply one. Prayer is not a mechanism that produces outcomes in proportion to fervency — if it were, the only conclusion available about James would be an obscene one. What prayer is, is the appointed way a dependent people bring their case to a sovereign God who answers according to his own purposes and does not explain them. And notice that Luke reports the failure of the church's expectation in the same breath as the success of its prayer: God answered a request offered by people who did not believe it would be answered, which settles for ever the question of whether the power lies in the praying or in the God prayed to.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Rhoda's announcement was met with you are out of your mind from the very people who had been up all night asking for exactly this. Luke records it without a word of rebuke, and the deliverance stood. Now: A great many Christians pray for things while quietly not expecting them, and then feel like frauds. This chapter is unusually kind to that condition. The answer arrived and stood knocking at the gate while the intercessors argued about whether it could be him.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. He killed James the brother of John with the sword,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He killed James the brother of John with the sword.

Eight words, and one of the Twelve is dead. There is no speech, no trial scene, no defence, no vision of heaven opened, no prayer for his killers, no last words of any kind. Luke gave Stephen — a man appointed to hand out food — a chapter and a half, a sermon of fifty verses, a shining face and a dying prayer. He gives James, one of the inner three who went up the mountain at the transfiguration and into the garden at Gethsemane, half a sentence.

The brevity is not carelessness. It is the shape of the thing, and Luke wants the reader to feel it.

Because four verses later the church is praying for Peter, and Peter walks free. And the question that raises has to be asked out loud rather than stepped around, because every reader asks it: was nobody praying for James?

Of course they were. This is the same church, in the same city, in the same weeks, and James was an apostle they had known for a decade. They prayed for James as earnestly as they prayed for Peter, and James was executed and Peter was delivered, and Luke offers not one syllable of explanation for the difference.

That silence must be respected rather than filled. There is no suggestion anywhere in the text that the prayers for James were less fervent, or that his faith was weaker, or that God had a lesson for him that Peter did not need. Every one of those explanations has been offered to grieving people at some point, and all of them are inventions, and this passage does not license any of them.

What can be said is smaller and truer. First, that Jesus had told James this was coming. When he and his brother asked for the two best seats, Jesus asked whether they could drink the cup he was about to drink, and they said they could, and he said they would. James drank it first, in about the year 44. John drank it slowly, over sixty years, and died old. The same question, the same answer, and two utterly different lives.

Second, that Peter's deliverance is the exception Luke records, not the rule he is teaching. Peter himself was executed in the end, in Rome, and no angel came to that cell. The book of Acts contains two prison rescues and a great many funerals.

And third — this is the point of putting them in one chapter — that a book which recorded only the deliverances would be a lie, and would be useless to most of the people who read it. Luke tells us about the angel and the falling chains. He also tells us, in eight words and without comment, that the church buried an apostle that spring and God did nothing to stop it.

verseByVerse.quote: and when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also.

There is the motive, stated by Luke without embarrassment. Herod did not kill James out of theological conviction, and he did not arrest Peter because he had assessed the Christian claim and found it dangerous. He killed an apostle because it went down well, and moved on to a second for the same reason. It is one of the coldest sentences in the New Testament, and it describes a kind of man every generation recognises.

This is Herod Agrippa the First, and the family record is worth having in front of you. His grandfather was the Herod who tried to kill the child at Bethlehem. His uncle was the Herod who beheaded John the Baptist and put a robe on Jesus to mock him. He himself now executes an apostle and imprisons another. Three generations of one family, three attempts on the same movement, and in this chapter the family runs out.

Agrippa had been raised in Rome among emperors and knew exactly how to play Jerusalem; he was scrupulous about the law in Judea and considerably less so elsewhere. Arresting Peter during the days of Unleavened Bread and holding the execution until after the feast is a piece of religious tact — he will not spoil Passover, and he will have a larger crowd afterwards.

Which produces an irony Luke expects his reader to catch. It is Passover week: the festival commemorating the night God brought his people out of a house of bondage — and the king is holding an apostle in one, waiting for the celebrations to finish before killing him.

Then the security, and the detail tells you something. Four squads of soldiers — four groups of four, sixteen men, one squad on each of the four night watches. Two chained to the prisoner, two at the door, relieved every three hours. That is an extraordinary allocation for one middle-aged Galilean, and there is a reason for it: the authorities in this city had put these men in prison before, and had come in the morning to find the cell locked, the guards at their posts and the prisoners gone.

Herod is not being paranoid. He is being careful, on the basis of evidence. And Luke sets out the sixteen men and the two chains and the rotating watch in careful detail, so that the reader knows precisely what was in place before the chains fell off.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in this chapter hangs on the smallest word in the verse. So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. Everything turns on that but.

On one side, sixteen soldiers, two chains, a locked door and a king. On the other side, a conjunction. Luke sets the entire apparatus of the state against a prayer meeting and joins them with but, and by the end of the chapter one of the two is dead and eaten by worms.

The word for earnest is worth having. It means stretched out, extended at full reach — the word for a muscle under strain or a runner at full stride. It is not the vocabulary of a routine intercession got through before bed. And the praying is corporate: not friends of Peter, but the church, which had already buried James and knew perfectly well what a Herod does with an apostle.

Then Luke turns to the cell, and the sentence he writes there is one of the quietly extraordinary things in Acts. On that very night — the night before the execution, the last night — Peter was sleeping.

Take in the arrangements first. He is chained by each wrist to a soldier, so that he cannot turn over without waking two men. There are sentries at the door. In the morning he is to be brought out to a Passover crowd and killed, and everybody in the building knows it. And he is asleep — soundly enough that in the next verse an angel has to hit him to wake him up.

Luke does not explain that either, and it does not really need explaining. This is a man who had already been in a cell once and walked out, who had been told by his Lord how he would eventually die and knew it involved being old, and who had spent something like fifteen years discovering that the outcome was not his department. Whatever it cost him earlier in the evening, by the small hours he had put it down.

It is the same peace, in a harder place, that a great many Christians have longed for at three in the morning over something far smaller. And it is worth noticing where it comes from in this chapter. Not from confidence about the outcome — Peter had no reason whatever to expect an angel, and James had not got one. From somewhere else entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, "Get up quickly." And the chains fell off his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four things happen in one verse and each of them is worth its own look.

An angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. Luke does not say the angel appeared or descended: he stood next to him, as though he had been there for some time. And a light in a cell in the middle of the night, with two soldiers chained to the prisoner and two more at the door, and none of them wakes.

Then: he struck Peter on the side and woke him.

Hold on to that verb, because Luke uses it exactly twice in this chapter. Here, an angel of the Lord strikes a man to wake him. At verse 23, an angel of the Lord strikes a man and he dies. Same word, same order of being, sixteen verses apart — one blow to rouse a sleeping prisoner and one to end a king who thought he was a god. Luke never draws attention to it. He simply uses the word twice and lets the chapter do the arithmetic.

There is also something almost comic in the detail, and Luke, who could have written this scene reverently, chose not to. An angel from the presence of God, in a blaze of light, in a maximum-security cell — and his first act is to give Peter a dig in the ribs, because the man is asleep and the light has not worked.

Get up quickly. Two words, no explanation.

And then: the chains fell off his hands. Not were unlocked, not were struck off — they fell. Whatever was holding them simply stopped holding. Luke has spent the previous verse itemising Herod's arrangements with some care, and he now disposes of the first of them in five words, without any suggestion of effort.

It is worth registering the order, because it is the order God generally works in. The chains come off first, before the guards are passed and before the gate opens, and before Peter has any idea what is happening — while he is, on his own account two verses later, still under the impression that he is dreaming. He is free before he knows it, and he is walking on the strength of somebody else's certainty.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to him, "Dress yourself and put on your sandals." And he did so. And he said to him, "Wrap your cloak around you and follow me." And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the angel's instructions and notice how small they are. Dress yourself. Put on your sandals. Wrap your cloak around you. Follow me.

A being from the presence of God has just dissolved Roman iron, and he is now telling a middle-aged fisherman to put his shoes on.

It would be easy to hurry past that and it is one of the most characteristic things in the chapter. Peter is about to walk out into a Jerusalem street in the small hours of a spring night with nowhere to go and no idea where he is going, and somebody has thought about the cold. The same providence that stopped the chains working also wanted him properly dressed. There is no suggestion anywhere in Scripture that God finds the practical beneath him; the risen Christ cooked breakfast on a beach, and an angel of the Lord in this verse is concerned about footwear.

Then the sentence that makes this the strangest rescue in the book. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision.

Peter is not being obtuse. He had every reason for the mistake: two chapters ago he had gone into a trance on a roof and seen something let down out of heaven, and had been badly wrong-footed by it, and had then had to explain to Jerusalem what it meant. Visions were a category he now had. So when a light fills a cell and the chains come off and a figure tells him to get dressed, he assumes it is happening in his head, and goes along with it, and walks out of a maximum-security prison in a state of complete confusion.

Which is the thread running through this entire chapter and it is worth watching for. Peter does not believe what God is doing while God is doing it. In a few verses the church will not believe it either, and will tell a servant girl she is raving. The angel is real, the chains are on the floor, the gate is about to open by itself, and every single human being involved is either asleep, dreaming, or arguing.

God did it anyway. That is the comfort of the passage, and it is not a small one: the deliverance was not waiting on anybody's grasp of what was happening.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke walks the reader out of the prison in the order Peter walked it, and dismantles Herod's arrangements one at a time. The chains went in the previous verse. Now the first and the second guard, passed without incident and without explanation — Luke does not say the soldiers were blinded or asleep or struck dumb; he simply reports that two guard posts were passed and says nothing about how.

Then the last obstacle, and it is a serious one. The iron gate leading into the city. This is the outer door of the fortress, the barrier between the prison and the street, and it is the one thing in the building that no amount of quiet walking gets you through.

It opened for them of its own accord. The Greek word is the one our word automatic comes from, and the New Testament uses it only twice — here, and of the earth in the parable that produces a crop by itself. Nobody touched it. There is no lock picked and no guard overpowered; the gate simply behaves as though it had been asked.

And then the detail that is easy to miss and is the most instructive thing in the verse. They went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him.

One street. The angel stays exactly as far as is necessary and not a step further, and then he is gone — no farewell, no instructions, no accompaniment to a safe house, no explanation of what to do next. Peter is standing alone in the dark in a city where a king wants him dead, with his cloak on, entirely free and entirely on his own.

That is worth having in mind by anybody who has watched God do something remarkable and then found the extraordinary help withdrawn while the situation was still difficult. The angel was not sent to look after Peter. He was sent to get him through a gate, and the moment the gate was behind them the errand was finished. God is not sparing with his help; he is exact with it. He gives what the moment requires, and it very often stops at the point where ordinary walking will do.

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter came to himself, he said, "Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting." When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Peter came to himself. The phrase is Luke's, and he had used it once before — of a young man sitting among pigs in a far country who suddenly saw his situation for what it was. It means the moment the fog clears. Peter has been moving through this entire episode convinced he was dreaming, and standing in an empty street with the prison behind him he understands, all at once, that it happened.

Now I am sure. Which is an admission that until this moment he was not.

And notice how he describes what has occurred: the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting. He does not say he escaped. He does not describe his own part in it, because he did not have one — he was asleep for the beginning and confused for the rest. The whole sentence has one subject and it is not Peter.

Then he goes to a house, and Luke tells us whose. The house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark.

Several things are packed into that. Mary owns a house substantial enough to have a gateway and a servant, and she is named in her own right rather than as somebody's wife, which suggests a widow of means who had put her property at the church's disposal — a great many early congregations met in rooms belonging to women like her. Many have thought this is the same house with the upper room in it, where the hundred and twenty had waited for Pentecost; it cannot be proved and it is a reasonable guess. And her son is John Mark, who will join the first missionary journey in the last verse of this chapter, will desert it, will cause the sharpest quarrel in the New Testament, and will end up writing a Gospel.

What matters most, though, is what was happening in that house at the time. Many were gathered together and were praying. It is the middle of the night in Passover week. Peter is under sentence and James is freshly buried, and being known to associate with either of them is demonstrably dangerous. And the church is in a house in the dark, in numbers, praying — which took nerve, and which is the reason Peter knew exactly which door to knock on.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. Recognizing Peter's voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke names her. That is the first thing to notice about this scene, and it is not a small thing.

He does not give us the names of the sixteen soldiers, or of the two men chained to Peter, or of most of the church praying in that room. He gives us the name of a slave girl who answered a door: Rhoda, which means rose. Somebody remembered it, and told him, and it has been read aloud in churches for two thousand years — a servant of no standing whatever in a house she did not own, whose one recorded action was to make a mistake.

Recognising Peter's voice. She knew it through a closed door, without seeing him, at night. That tells you she had heard him a great deal — that a household slave had been in the room often enough while the apostle taught to know his voice from anyone else's. The church that met in Mary's house evidently did not send the staff out.

And then: in her joy she did not open the gate.

It is the most human sentence in the book of Acts and one of the very few in Scripture that is straightforwardly funny. She is so pleased that she forgets the one thing she has actually been sent to do. The most wanted man in Jerusalem, fresh out of a maximum-security cell in the middle of the night, with a search about to start at dawn, is left standing in the street outside a locked gate — because the girl who found him was too happy to let him in.

Luke reports it with obvious affection and not a word of criticism. Nobody in the passage tells Rhoda off, and the narrative does not treat her as the failure of the scene; the people who actually come off badly in the next verse are the ones who were praying.

There is something worth keeping in her, all the same. Joy that forgets the practical step is a real thing and it is not the worst fault a person can have. She is the only one in the entire chapter who both believed it was Peter and was glad — the prayer meeting managed neither — and her error was one of excitement. Of all the things to get wrong on the night God answered, hers is the one to be caught doing.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "You are out of your mind." But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, "It is his angel!" But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are out of your mind. The word means raving; it is what you say to somebody who is not making sense. And it is said by a room full of people who have spent the night asking God for precisely the thing the girl has just announced.

Then it gets worse, and Luke's tenses are merciless. She kept insisting — she would not be put down, and stood her ground against a room of her betters. And they kept saying — imperfect, over and over — it is his angel.

That was a current belief and Luke reports it without endorsing it: the idea that a person had a guardian spirit which might appear looking and sounding like them, and which might turn up at the moment of a death. So the prayer meeting has produced, on the spot, a theological explanation for why the answer to their prayers cannot be the answer to their prayers. It is easier to believe in a spectral double than in a released prisoner.

And while the argument continues — this is the detail Luke will not let go of — Peter continued knocking. Imperfect again. He is still out there. The church is inside debating angelology and the apostle they are praying for is standing in the street in the dark, knocking, and knocking, and knocking.

It would be very easy to be contemptuous about this and it would be a mistake, because these were not casual people. They had buried James. They were meeting at night, in numbers, during Passover week, at genuine risk, to pray for a condemned man. Whatever was wrong with their faith, it was not that they could not be bothered.

Their problem is the one most Christians have and very few will admit to: they prayed without expecting. The asking was sincere and the anticipation was absent, and the two had been running on separate tracks for so long that when the answer knocked they had a category for everything except that.

And here is the thing to take from the passage, which is far kinder than the rebuke this scene usually gets turned into. God answered anyway.

The deliverance did not wait on the quality of their expectation, was not proportioned to their confidence, and was not withdrawn when they told the messenger she was mad. Peter was already out before the debate began. Anyone who has prayed for years about something while privately suspecting nothing will come of it — and has felt a fraud for it — should notice what this chapter does with such people. It does not shame them. It puts the answer on their doorstep and lets them be amazed.

verseByVerse.quote: But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, "Tell these things to James and to the brothers." Then he departed and went to another place. Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Motioning to them with his hand to be silent. The room has erupted, and a fugitive standing in a courtyard at two in the morning has to quieten a houseful of astonished people before somebody in the street hears them.

Then he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison — and the subject of that sentence is the point of it. He does not tell them how he got out. He tells them what the Lord did, which is the only version of the story he is in a position to give, since he slept through the start of it and thought the rest was a dream.

Tell these things to James and to the brothers. This is not the James who was killed fifteen verses ago; that one is dead. This is James the Lord's brother — the man who did not believe in Jesus during his lifetime, and who is now, without any explanation from Luke, the man you send word to when something happens in Jerusalem. Peter's instruction is the quiet marker of a change of leadership. From here on it is James who presides at the council and James to whom Paul reports.

And then five words that shut a door on half the book: then he departed and went to another place.

Luke does not say where. He never does. Peter appears once more, at the council in chapter 15, and after that he leaves the narrative of Acts entirely — no death scene, no farewell, no account of the years in which he wrote two letters and, by every early tradition, died in Rome. The man who has been the leading figure for eleven chapters walks off into an unnamed place at two in the morning, and Luke's spotlight swings away and follows somebody else.

It is a strange piece of authorship and it is deliberate. This book is not the story of Peter. From chapter 13 it will not even be mainly the story of Jerusalem.

Then daylight, and Luke's driest sentence: there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter. He means there was uproar. Sixteen men, a locked cell, an untouched door, two chains lying on the floor, and a prisoner due before the king in a few hours.

verseByVerse.quote: And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse has a shadow in it that ought not to be hurried past, because Luke does not hurry past it and neither should a reader.

He examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death.

Roman military law held a guard answerable for his prisoner: a man who lost one could expect the penalty the prisoner would have received. So Herod, having failed to find Peter, does the thing the system provided for, and men die because an angel opened a gate.

Luke reports it in half a sentence and offers no comment, and it would be dishonest to supply the comfort he withholds. Peter's deliverance cost other men their lives. That is in the text, and a reading of this chapter which celebrates the falling chains and skips verse 19 has read half of it.

Two things can be said, and neither is a resolution. The first is where the moral weight actually sits. God opened a door; Herod gave the order. The king who had already killed an apostle because it was popular now executes his own soldiers to cover an embarrassment, and Luke has arranged this chapter so that four verses later God deals with him about it. The blood of those guards is on the account of the man being carried out of Caesarea in the twenty-third verse.

The second is that this is what the world is like, and Scripture will not pretend otherwise. Deliverances happen inside a fallen system, and the system exacts a price somewhere. The Bible reports it rather than tidying it, which is one of the reasons it can be trusted about the rest. A book written to encourage the church would have ended verse 19 after the word find him.

And then the last clause, which reads like an administrative detail and is in fact the end of a man. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there. Herod leaves Jerusalem, and never comes back. His final recorded act in the holy city, the place where he had been so careful to appear devout, was to have his own men executed for something none of them had done.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king's country for food. On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke now turns to a piece of provincial diplomacy, and the reason he includes it becomes apparent two verses later.

Herod is angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon — the two Phoenician ports up the coast. The quarrel itself is not explained, but the leverage is: their country depended on the king's country for food. Those cities sat on a narrow strip between mountains and sea with almost no farmland, and had imported their grain from the fields of Galilee since Solomon's day. Herod could not conquer them. He could starve them, and they knew it.

So they come to terms, and Luke records how it was arranged: having persuaded Blastus, the king's chamberlain. The chamberlain controlled access to the royal bedchamber and therefore to the king, and persuaded is doing a certain amount of work; men in that position were not usually persuaded by argument. Two ancient cities had to buy a courtier in order to get permission to eat.

Then the day itself. Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them.

It is worth knowing that we have a second account of this occasion from outside the New Testament. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing for a Roman audience some fifty years later and with no interest whatever in defending Luke, describes Agrippa at Caesarea at a festival, coming into the theatre at daybreak in a robe woven entirely of silver, so that when the early sun struck it the garment blazed and the onlookers were dazzled — and then flatterers in the crowd calling out to him as a god. He records that the king was seized almost at once with violent internal pain, was carried out, and died after five days.

Two writers, working independently and for different readerships, describe the same king, in the same city, on the same public occasion, in the same royal display, receiving the same acclamation and dying of the same sudden illness. Luke says an angel of the Lord struck him and Josephus does not, which is exactly the difference one would expect between the two. On everything a historian can check, they agree.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were shouting, "The voice of a god, and not of a man!" Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice of a god, and not of a man.

It is flattery from men who had just bribed a courtier and needed the grain to keep coming, and Herod knew exactly what it was worth. That is not the point. The point is what he did with it, which was nothing. He did not correct it.

Set that beside a scene two chapters earlier in this same city of Caesarea. A Roman centurion fell at Peter's feet, out of genuine reverence rather than calculation, and Peter reached down and pulled him up and said stand up; I too am a man. Same town, same kind of moment, and the two men in it do opposite things. Luke has put them a few pages apart on purpose, and only one of them is alive at the end of this chapter.

Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down.

And there is the verb again — the one Luke used at verse 7, when an angel of the Lord struck Peter on the side to wake him. Two blows in one chapter from the same order of being: one to rouse a prisoner who was about to die, and one to end a king who thought he was a god. Luke never remarks on it. He simply uses the word twice.

Now the reason given, and it is not the one a reader expects. Because he did not give God the glory.

Not because he executed James. Not because he imprisoned Peter, or killed his own guards, or played politics with people's lives to keep a crowd happy. All of that stands on the record and none of it is cited. The charge God brings against Herod Agrippa is that a man let himself be called divine and did not hand the honour back.

That is worth sitting with, because it rearranges most people's instinctive scale of sins. The murders were real and will be dealt with. But the thing named in the indictment is the theft of something that belongs to God alone — which is, when you think about it, the sin underneath the other ones. A man who is willing to be worshipped will do anything at all to the people underneath him.

He was eaten by worms and breathed his last. Josephus, independently, records five days of agonising internal pain. Luke gives it six words. The last of the Herods, in silver, on a platform, with a crowd calling him a god — and a fortnight later a burial.

One guard is needed and it matters. This is not a template for reading illness or sudden death as divine judgement, and it has been misused that way with great cruelty. Luke tells us the reason here because it was disclosed to him. In almost every other case nobody has been told anything, and the man who claims to know why somebody is ill has appointed himself to a bench he has not been called to.

verseByVerse.quote: But the word of God increased and multiplied. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the word of God increased and multiplied.

Put that sentence immediately after the one before it and feel the size of the contrast. A king in cloth-of-silver, hailed as divine by two cities, is dead and buried. And the next thing Luke writes is a sentence about a message spreading — with a but in front of it, as though the death of a king were the sort of thing that might have been expected to slow it down and did not.

The verbs are the ones used of living things. The word grew and multiplied, which is the language Genesis uses of creatures filling the earth. Luke has used this formula twice before, at the end of the Jerusalem years and after the conversion of Saul, and each time it marks the close of a movement and the opening of the next. Here it is doing something more pointed. Herod Agrippa is remembered by most people today for exactly one thing: he appears in this chapter. The movement he set out to destroy wrote him into its records as an illustration.

Then the last verse, which is housekeeping and is also the assembling of a team. Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service — the famine money from Antioch has been delivered, and the two of them turn for home.

Bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.

He is Mary's son, and Mary's house is where the prayer meeting was. Which means that on the night Rhoda left Peter standing at the gate, this young man was almost certainly in that house. He had watched the church pray all night for a man, and had watched it refuse to believe the man was at the door.

He is now going to Antioch, and from Antioch he will go out on the first missionary journey, and at Pamphylia he will lose his nerve and go home — which will cause the sharpest quarrel recorded between two Christians in the New Testament and split Paul from Barnabas. And decades later Paul will write from a prison cell asking for him, because he is useful. And somewhere in those years he wrote down the recollections of Peter, and the church has been reading them as the Gospel of Mark ever since.

All of which is in front of a young man who, at the end of this chapter, is simply a name added to somebody else's luggage. Luke closes an account of an executed apostle, a miraculous deliverance and the death of a king by mentioning, almost in passing, a boy going along with his cousin — and it turns out to be the most consequential sentence in the paragraph.

12.theology: Providence, Prayer, and the Sovereignty of God over Kings. Acts 12 is a meditation on what it means to live under the providence of a God who governs kings and councils, who opens prison gates and strikes down tyrants, and who is not moved by the calculations of the powerful. James dies; Peter lives — both by divine appointment. The church prays; the answer comes — and still takes them by surprise. Herod grasps at divine honour; he is given worms and silence. This is the world the New Testament describes: not a world where God occasionally intervenes, but a world where God is always governing — every chain, every gate, every angel, every worm. The appropriate response is not to explain his ways, but to pray, to trust, and to keep speaking the Word that outlasts every king.
12.examples:
Then: A church under a murderous king, with no political recourse, no legal protection, and no army — meeting in a house and praying with everything they had. Their prayers opened a prison door thirty miles from where they sat. They did not know it would happen that way. They prayed because there was nothing else to do, and because the God they prayed to had not changed.

Now: The church in every hostile political environment must learn the same calculus: Herod has soldiers; God has angels. Herod has chains; God has the Word. The appropriate response to power arrayed against the gospel is not despair and not political calculation — it is earnest, persistent, expectant prayer to the Sovereign Lord who made heaven and earth. And then, when the knock comes at the door, to open it.

13.title: The First Missionary Journey Begins
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. <sup>2</sup>While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” <sup>3</sup>Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off. <sup>4</sup>So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. <sup>5</sup>When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them. <sup>6</sup>When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. <sup>7</sup>He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God. <sup>8</sup>But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. <sup>9</sup>But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him <sup>10</sup>and said, “You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? <sup>11</sup>And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. <sup>12</sup>Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord. <sup>13</sup>Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup>but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. <sup>15</sup>After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.” <sup>16</sup>So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: “Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. <sup>17</sup>The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it. <sup>22</sup>And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, ‘I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’ <sup>23</sup>Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised. <sup>26</sup>Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation. <sup>27</sup>For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. <sup>28</sup>And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed. <sup>29</sup>And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>But God raised him from the dead, <sup>31</sup>and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people. <sup>32</sup>And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, <sup>33</sup>this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you.’ <sup>38</sup>Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, <sup>39</sup>and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. <sup>40</sup>Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: <sup>41</sup>‘Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.’” <sup>42</sup>As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. <sup>43</sup>And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. <sup>44</sup>The next Sabbath almost the whole city came together to hear the word of the Lord. <sup>45</sup>But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him. <sup>46</sup>And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. <sup>47</sup>For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’” <sup>48</sup>And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. <sup>49</sup>And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region. <sup>50</sup>But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. <sup>51</sup>But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium. <sup>52</sup>And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
13.overview:
The first missionary journey begins not with a committee decision but with the Holy Spirit speaking in a worship service: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” The church at Antioch is worshipping and fasting — attending to God — and God speaks. This is always the order: first the consecration, then the commission. The church that is too busy to fast and pray will miss what God is saying. The church that waits on him will find that he is the one who sends.

Paul’s sermon at Pisidian Antioch is his great synagogue address — the same structure as Peter’s sermon at Pentecost: the sweep of Israel’s history, the fulfilment in Jesus, the resurrection, the call to repentance. But Paul adds something Peter did not stress: “by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses.” The law cannot save. The law could never save. It was never designed to save. Only Christ can do what the law could only demand.

Then verse 48, which has caused theologians to argue for twenty centuries and which the text itself presents without apology: “as many as were appointed to eternal life believed.” Election precedes faith. The believing is real; the appointment is prior. Both are true. Luke sees no contradiction.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The First Missionary Journey Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The mission that will occupy the rest of the New Testament begins in a prayer meeting, and Luke lists the men who were in the room. A Cypriot Levite, a black African, a North African, a man who had grown up in Herod's household as the tetrarch's boyhood companion, and a converted persecutor from Tarsus. That is the leadership of the church at Antioch: five men from four countries and two continents, and not one of them from Jerusalem.

While they are worshipping and fasting the Spirit speaks, and what he asks for is the two best men they have. Antioch fasts again, prays, lays hands on them, and lets them go — which is the whole of what a sending church does and is a great deal harder than it reads.

They sail to Cyprus, Barnabas's home island, and work it end to end. At Paphos, the Roman capital, they run into both the highest authority on the island and the sharpest opposition of the journey in the same room: the proconsul Sergius Paulus wants to hear them, and a Jewish magician attached to his household tries to stop it. Paul — and Luke changes his name to Paul in this very verse and never uses Saul again — looks straight at the man and calls him a son of the devil, and he goes blind, and gropes for a hand to lead him.

Which is the detail to hold, because Paul had once been led by the hand into Damascus after a light he could not look at. He is watching a man become what he himself had been, and the blindness is for a time.
verseByVerse.theology:
Missionary Call and Corporate Discernment

The Spirit does not speak to Barnabas and Saul privately and send them to inform the church. He speaks in the assembly, to the assembly, about two men who are standing in it — and the church then fasts, prays, and lays hands on them before letting them go. Reformed ecclesiology has taken this as the pattern: an individual sense of call confirmed by a congregation, and a congregation's judgement confirmed by the Spirit, with neither operating alone. Notice also what the sending cost. Barnabas had founded that church and Saul was its finest teacher, and Antioch gave away both on the strength of one sentence in a prayer meeting. A church's seriousness about mission is not measured by what it collects for it but by whom it is willing to lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The list in verse 1 is the most cosmopolitan leadership team in the New Testament, and it was assembled by a persecution. Every man on it was in Antioch because something had gone wrong somewhere else. Now: Congregations tend to produce leaders who resemble each other, and to regard that as normal rather than as a symptom. Antioch did not set out to be diverse; it set out to preach to whoever was in front of it, and this is what the room looked like a few years later.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the list of names slowly, because Luke did not have to give it and it tells you what had happened to the church in about fifteen years.

Barnabas — a Levite from Cyprus, the man who sold a field and vouched for Saul. Simeon who was called Niger — and Niger is Latin for black, which is almost certainly a description rather than a family name. Lucius of Cyrene — North Africa, and men of Cyrene were among the unnamed pioneers who first preached to Greeks in this very city. Manaen, a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch — the word means he was brought up with him, a foster-brother at court; this man had shared a nursery with the Herod who beheaded John the Baptist and mocked Jesus. And Saul, last on the list, who had gone through Jerusalem dragging believers out of houses.

Five men, four countries, two continents, an African, an aristocrat and a former persecutor, and not one of them from Jerusalem. Nobody designed that. It is what a church looks like when it has been assembled out of a scattering and has stopped asking who is allowed in.

And then, while they are worshipping the Lord and fasting, the Spirit speaks and asks for the two best men in the room.

Set apart for me. The verb is the one behind the word Pharisee — to separate, to mark off — and Paul uses it of himself when he writes to Rome, saying he was set apart for the gospel. He had been a separated man before; he is being separated again, for the opposite purpose.

'Fasting' — worth pausing on, since many believers today have never done it. To fast is voluntarily to go without food (for part of a day, a day, or longer) to seek God. It is not dieting, nor a hunger strike to twist God's arm, nor the self-punishment Scripture warns against (Col. 2:23). The empty stomach drives the soul to God — saying with the body what the heart means: 'Lord, I want you more than my daily bread.' In Scripture it goes with earnest prayer and attends the great seekings of God: guidance and the sending of missionaries (here; 13:3; 14:23), repentance (Joel 2:12; Jonah 3), grief (2 Sam. 1:12), crisis and intercession (Esther 4:16; Ezra 8:21–23), and steady devotion (Anna, Luke 2:37). Jesus himself fasted forty days (Matt. 4:2).

Is it commanded of Christians — and is it in the Epistles? Honestly, no: fasting is nowhere laid on believers as a law, and the letters mention it barely (2 Cor. 6:5; 11:27 may even be involuntary hunger). So no one sins by not fasting, and no one earns anything by it. And yet Jesus plainly assumed his people would fast: 'WHEN you fast' (not if), warning only against doing it for show (Matt. 6:16–18); and asked why his disciples did not fast, he said the wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is with them, 'but the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away... and THEN they will fast' (Matt. 9:15) — this present age between his ascension and return. So fasting is not a rule to keep under compulsion, but a privilege and means of grace the Lord expects his church to use.

So should you fast? Gently, yes — not from guilt or to score points, but as a gift worth taking up; you are missing a help your Master meant you to have. Why? Because in some seasons — a weighty decision, a heavy burden in prayer, sorrow over sin, a longing to seek God afresh — setting aside even food to give that time and hunger to God focuses and humbles the heart and intensifies prayer; and the very hunger preaches that 'man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word... from the mouth of God' (Matt. 4:4). How? Start small — skip a meal or a day, and spend the time in prayer and the Word; always tie the fast to a purpose and to prayer (fasting without praying is merely going hungry); keep it secret, never paraded (Matt. 6:17–18). Two cautions: guard against pride — the Pharisee boasted, 'I fast twice a week' (Luke 18:12), and Isaiah 58 shows God despising a fasting joined to hard-heartedness; and use ordinary wisdom about health (the unwell, pregnant, or medicated should take care, and abstaining from water is only ever brief). Fasting earns nothing; but as a humble, hungry way of seeking the God who satisfies, it is worth recovering — for out of one such fast at Antioch the Spirit launched the gospel to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four verbs, and the whole of a sending is in them: they fasted, they prayed, they laid hands on them, and they let them go.

Notice that they fast again. They had been fasting when the Spirit spoke; now, having heard him, they fast a second time. There is no suggestion that the word settled the matter and the rest was administration. Between the call and the departure there is another season of going without food and asking God about it — which is not doubt, and is what serious people do before an irreversible step.

The laying on of hands here is not ordination to an office and does not confer anything Barnabas and Saul did not have; the Spirit had already called them, and both had been in ministry for years. It is the congregation's public act of identification — these are our men, this is our work, and we are putting our hands on it in front of everybody. Whatever happens in Cyprus and Galatia, Antioch has signed for it.

And then the last two words, which are the costly ones: sent them off. Literally, they released them, let them go.

Consider the arithmetic from Antioch's side. Barnabas is the man Jerusalem had sent to establish them, who had seen the grace of God among them and been glad, and who had then travelled to Tarsus to fetch the teacher. Saul is that teacher, who had spent a year instructing them. They are the two most valuable men the congregation possesses, and the church has had them for perhaps two years, and it lets them both walk out of the door at once.

Every church knows how to pray for missions and most know how to fund it. The thing this verse describes is rarer and is the actual test: a congregation giving away the people it can least afford to lose, to work it will not see, on the strength of a conviction that God has asked for them.

verseByVerse.quote: So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit — and Luke has just told us in the previous verse that the church sent them off. Both are true and he sets them side by side without the slightest awkwardness. The congregation released them and the Spirit sent them, and it is one act described from two sides.

They go down to Seleucia, the port for Antioch, sixteen miles down the Orontes, and take ship for Cyprus — which is a hundred miles across open water and, on a clear day, visible from the Syrian coast. It is worth registering how modest the first stage is. The first missionary journey in the history of the church begins with a day's sail to an island you can see from the beach, in the direction of the place one of the two men grew up.

That is not a criticism; it is how sensible mission usually starts. Barnabas was a Cypriot with family and contacts there, and the island had a substantial Jewish population and a settled community of believers already, since some of the refugees of chapter 8 had gone there. They begin where they have a reason to begin.

And at Salamis they establish the pattern that will govern the next fifteen years: they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. Plural — Salamis was large enough to have several. Paul will do this in every city he enters, right through to the end of the book, and he will do it in cities where the synagogue has already thrown him out of the last one.

Then the last sentence, dropped in without emphasis: and they had John to assist them. The word is the one for a subordinate who does the practical work — the man who handles the arrangements, the money, the baggage, the copies of the Scriptures. John Mark is not on the platform. He is carrying things.

Luke mentions him here so that the reader will notice his absence eight verses later.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos — a hundred miles on foot, coast to coast, town by town. Luke covers it in a clause. There is a great deal of ordinary walking in the missionary journeys and almost none of it gets a sentence.

Paphos is the Roman administrative capital, so this is the seat of government, and what they find there is a study in contrasts that Luke sets out with some care.

On one side, a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. Note the combination, because it is a peculiarly ugly one: a Jew, with access to the Scriptures, trading in the magical arts that those Scriptures forbid absolutely, attached to a Roman household as a resident specialist in the supernatural. His name means son of Joshua, or son of salvation — which is about to become one of the bleaker ironies in the New Testament.

On the other side, the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence. Luke's word means shrewd, perceptive, a man who understands things. And what this shrewd man does is send for two travelling Jewish preachers because he sought to hear the word of God.

It is worth pausing on the title, because it is one of the small marks of Luke's accuracy that has been tested and held. Cyprus had been an imperial province governed by a legate, and was transferred to the senate in 22 BC, after which its governor was a proconsul. Luke uses the correct term for the correct decade in the correct province — a thing he does repeatedly, and which has been vindicated by inscriptions again and again. The fuller defence of Luke as a historian is set out at 5:37-38 and need not be repeated; it is enough to note that this is another instance.

And the human situation is one every evangelist recognises. There is an intelligent man who genuinely wants to hear, and there is somebody at his elbow whose whole position depends on his not hearing it.

verseByVerse.quote: But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them.

Luke gives us two names for this man in three verses — Bar-Jesus in the Aramaic and Elymas in whatever language the parenthesis is explaining — and then tells us plainly what he was: a magician. The trade has been described at Samaria in chapter 8, and it was not entertainment; it was the sale of access to power, and it paid well when the customer was a Roman governor.

Which is exactly what is at stake, and it is worth naming without pretending the man's motives were purely theological. Elymas has a position. He is the resident authority on the invisible in the household of the most powerful man on the island, and two Jewish preachers have just been invited in to talk about God. If the proconsul believes them, Elymas is finished — not damned, merely unemployed. A great deal of opposition to the gospel has looked exactly like this, and very little of it has ever announced itself in those terms.

Note also his method, because it is the shrewd one. He does not challenge Paul to a debate and he does not attack the doctrine. Luke says he was seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith — the work is done sideways, in private, through the relationship he already has. A man with the governor's ear does not need to win an argument. He needs only to keep the argument from being properly heard, and he has all the time in the world to do it.

That is worth recognising because it is still the commonest shape of the thing. The gospel is rarely refuted in front of the person who was about to believe it. It is undermined afterwards, quietly, by somebody they trust, who says nothing that could be written down and answered.

And the last phrase tells you how close the man was to being lost: away from the faith. Sergius Paulus was not on the edge of an interesting conversation. He was on the edge of believing, and Elymas could see it.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, "You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Saul, who was also called Paul.

It happens in the middle of a sentence and Luke never explains it. From this verse to the end of the book the man is Paul, and the name Saul appears again only when he is retelling the Damascus road and quoting the voice that used it.

The change is not a conversion souvenir; converts in the New Testament do not get new names, and he had been a Christian for well over a decade by now. Like a great many Jews of the Diaspora he simply had two — a Hebrew name for the synagogue and a Roman one for everywhere else, and Paulus was a common Latin family name. What changes here is not the man's name but his world. He has walked into the household of a Roman proconsul, and from this point onward his life is spent among Gentiles, and Luke starts calling him what those Gentiles called him.

There is one further touch, and it is either a coincidence or a very dry joke: the proconsul's name is Sergius Paulus. Luke introduces the Roman Paulus and switches to the Jewish Paul in the space of three verses.

Then the confrontation, and it is ferocious. You son of the devil — which is an exact and deliberate reply to the man's own name, since Bar-Jesus means son of Joshua. You are not the son of salvation; you are the son of the other one. You enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy.

And then the charge itself, which is quoted Scripture. Will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? The prophet's cry was to make straight in the desert a highway for our God; Elymas has been doing the reverse, putting bends in a road God was building toward a man's soul.

It should be said that this is not a model for how to talk to opponents generally, and Paul elsewhere instructs Timothy to correct with gentleness. Luke is careful to tell us where the words came from: Paul was filled with the Holy Spirit when he said them. This is not temper. It is a prophetic sentence, and the man it was spoken to had a governor's ear and was using it to shut a door.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time." Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time. Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand.

Read that last clause and then remember who is watching it.

Some fifteen years earlier a man had been travelling to Damascus, certain he was doing God's work and standing between the gospel and everybody he could reach, and a light had struck him blind, and he had gone into the city groping, led by the hand — Luke's phrase in chapter 9 and his phrase again here. Paul is looking at a man going through the exact thing that happened to him. He is not enjoying it. He is recognising it.

Which explains the three words that turn the whole judgement round: for a time.

It is a sentence with an end date. Paul had been blind for three days, and at the end of them a man had come and put hands on him and called him brother. There is no suggestion anywhere in this passage that Elymas is beyond hope, and the one man in the room who knew what that darkness was like is the one who set a limit on it. Luke never tells us what became of him. Given who is speaking, the silence is not a bad sign.

And notice what Luke says actually converted the proconsul. Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred — the sign got his attention — for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord.

Not astonished at the miracle. Astonished at the teaching. The blindness cleared the obstruction; what a shrewd Roman administrator actually found overwhelming was the content of what these men were saying. Luke has been careful about this all through his book, and he is careful here: the sign opens the door and the word does the work, and a man who believes because he was impressed has not yet believed anything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–52 — Paul's Sermon in Pisidian Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The synagogue sermon in Pisidian Antioch is the first major speech of Paul's missionary career in Acts and a theological masterpiece. Luke preserves it as the representative example of Paul's apostolic preaching, structured identically to Peter's Pentecost sermon: a recital of God's redemptive history with Israel (vv. 17–25), the proclamation of Jesus's death and resurrection as the fulfillment of that history (vv. 26–37), and a call to response with warning (vv. 38–41). But Paul's sermon has characteristic emphases that distinguish it: the prominent place of David, the explicit statement of justification by faith apart from the law of Moses, and the citation of Habakkuk as warning against unbelief.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith in Paul's First Sermon

Paul's climactic statement in vv. 38–39 is the first explicit statement of justification by faith in Acts: 'let it be known to you that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses.' The law cannot justify; faith in the crucified and risen Jesus frees from everything the law could not free from. This is the heart of Paul's theology, already fully formed in his first recorded sermon — the gospel that will generate the letters to the Galatians and Romans.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: 'The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God.' The widespread hunger for the gospel was met with jealousy from the Jewish leaders, who spoke against Paul. Their opposition drove the explicit turn to the Gentiles. Now: The pattern repeats whenever the gospel meets institutional religion: those who should be most receptive are sometimes least so, while those outside the religious establishment respond with open hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia.
verseByVerse.commentary: John Mark's departure at Perga — without explanation in Luke's account — will become a source of serious conflict between Paul and Barnabas (15:36–41). Paul will regard the departure as desertion from the work; Barnabas will see it as a recoverable failure. The journey from Perga to Pisidian Antioch crosses the Taurus Mountains — a difficult and dangerous route. The missionaries' willingness to make this crossing after John Mark's departure shows their commitment to the mission regardless of reduced team size. The mission's difficulty does not deter them; it refines them.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, "Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sabbath synagogue service is the natural platform: after the readings from Torah and the Prophets, visiting teachers were invited to speak. The rulers' invitation — 'if you have any word of encouragement' — is gracious and open; they do not know what they are inviting. Paul will give a 'word of encouragement' that reads everything they have just heard from the Law and the Prophets in light of the risen Jesus — a word that will divide the congregation by the next Sabbath.

A word on 'the reading from the Law and the Prophets,' since it shaped the scene. The service centred on two readings: one from the Law (the five books of Moses) and one from the Prophets (a chosen passage, the Haftarah — the reading Jesus stood to give from Isaiah, Luke 4:16–20). After them came a 'word of exhortation,' open to any competent man present — exactly the door opened to Paul.
