Its roots run to Moses, who commanded the Law be read aloud to the people (Deut. 31:10–13), and to Ezra, who read it to the gathered nation 'and gave the sense, so that the people understood' (Neh. 8:8). The synagogue itself (the word means 'gathering') grew up during and after the Babylonian exile: with the temple gone and the people scattered, Jews met locally to hear and study God's Word. The Law was read in order over a fixed cycle, the prophetic reading chosen to match, often with an Aramaic paraphrase for those who no longer spoke Hebrew.

And do Jews still do this? Yes, with striking continuity. To this day the Torah is read aloud from a handwritten scroll on the Sabbath (and Mondays, Thursdays, and festivals), on the annual cycle that ends and begins again each year at Simchat Torah ('rejoicing in the Torah'), still paired with a prophetic reading and a teaching — the very practice Luke describes, kept now as two thousand years ago. And it is the church's inheritance too: the public reading of Scripture followed by exposition is the pattern Paul charged Timothy to keep — 'devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching' (1 Tim. 4:13) — the shape of Christian worship ever since. The deep irony here: the Law and the Prophets had just been read aloud, and Paul rises to show that every line was pointing to the Jesus he is about to preach (Luke 24:27, 44). The reading set the table; Paul served Christ from it.

verseByVerse.quote: So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: "Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's address to both constituencies — born Jews and Gentile God-fearers — frames the gospel from the beginning as inclusive: both communities are addressed as potential recipients of the salvation that follows. His survey of Israel's history begins with divine election and the exodus: the 'uplifted arm' (Exodus 6:6) is the image of God's powerful intervention on Israel's behalf. Paul is establishing that the story he is about to tell is not a departure from Israel's story but its climax — the same God who parted the sea has now raised Jesus from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: "And for about forty years he bore with them in the wilderness. And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'He bore with them' — God's patient endurance through forty years of murmuring, idolatry, and rebellion in the wilderness. The exodus generation gave him every reason to abandon them; he bore with them, sustained them, and brought them to the border of the land. The conquest — 'destroying seven nations' and giving Israel their land 'as an inheritance' — is compressed into one verse to make the point: God's faithfulness overcomes Israel's faithlessness, and divine promise achieves what human obedience alone never could.

'Destroying seven nations' — Paul passes over it in a phrase, but it is one of the hardest things in Scripture, and an honest reader feels its weight: how could a good God order the destruction of the Canaanites? We must not be glib — the loss of life is real and grievous. But several truths, held together, show this is not the arbitrary cruelty it is often imagined to be.

It was judgment, not ethnic hatred. Israel had no general warrant to harm Gentiles — she was even to offer peace to distant cities (Deut. 20:10). This was a bounded act of justice on particular nations for particular, appalling sin. God said so: four centuries earlier he told Abraham his descendants would wait, 'for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete' (Gen. 15:16) — holding back judgment four hundred years. And the sin? Among other things, burning their own children alive in sacrifice (Deut. 12:31; Lev. 18:21), with entrenched idolatry and cultic prostitution — until the land itself, defiled, 'vomited out its inhabitants' (Lev. 18:24–25). This is the wrath of a holy God against great and violent evil, long endured.

And it was not favouritism toward Israel. God twice tells them this is 'not because of your righteousness... but because of the wickedness of these nations' (Deut. 9:4–6), warning that if Israel does the same, the land will vomit them out too (Lev. 18:28) — and centuries later it did, in the exile. The standard is God's holiness applied impartially, not ethnic preference; that dismantles the charge of 'tribal genocide.' And mercy stood open throughout: Rahab the Canaanite was spared through faith and stands in the Messiah's own bloodline (Josh. 6:25; Matt. 1:5). The issue was never race but allegiance.

And underneath lies a question the objection skips. We assume the Canaanites had a right to life that God violated. But Scripture holds that God is the Author and rightful Lord of all life (Deut. 32:39), and that every one of us has already forfeited life through sin (Rom. 6:23). On that reckoning, what needs explaining is not that God judges sin, but that he is so patient, and that anyone is spared at all. The Canaanites were not innocents struck down by a capricious deity but guilty people under the just sentence of a Judge who had waited centuries. (On the hardest part, the children, Scripture gives no glib answer; we rest in the One of whom Abraham asked, 'shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?' (Gen. 18:25), trusting his mercy toward little ones — as David did for his own child, 2 Sam. 12:23 — and refusing to pretend we see more than we do.)

And finally, most importantly for a Christian. This was a unique, one-time event — Israel as a covenant nation executing God's judgment in a particular land. It is emphatically not a model for today. Jesus refused the sword ('my kingdom is not of this world; if it were, my servants would fight,' John 18:36); the church's weapons 'are not of the flesh' (2 Cor. 10:4); we love our enemies and leave vengeance to God (Matt. 5:44; Rom. 12:19). No one may invoke Joshua to justify violence in Christ's name. Rather, the conquest is a sober, localized preview of the final judgment. And here the gospel speaks its deepest word: at the cross the judgment we all deserve fell on Jesus — the same holy God who judged Canaan 'did not spare his own Son' (Rom. 8:32) but laid our condemnation on him, so that wrath and mercy met. The only refuge from judgment, as for Rahab, is faith in the God of Israel, now revealed in Christ. That is just where Paul's sermon is heading: all this history runs to a Saviour (v. 23).

verseByVerse.quote: "All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary: The 450-year span covers the patriarchal sojourn in Egypt, the wilderness wandering, and the period of conquest — the entire pre-monarchic history of Israel compressed into a number that conveys the patience and persistence of divine faithfulness across generations. 'He gave them judges' — each judge was God's provision for Israel's need in a specific crisis; the pattern of Israel's need and God's provision is the rhythm of the book of Judges. Samuel stands at the threshold of the monarchy, preparing Israel for the king who will prepare the way for the King.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified, 'I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's mention of 'Saul' (his own Hebrew name, the tribe of Benjamin) may carry conscious self-awareness — the rejected king, replaced by the one after God's heart. David's description ('a man after my heart, who will do all my will') comes from 1 Samuel 13:14 and Psalm 89:20 combined. It is the highest possible royal commendation: not a man after his own heart (as Saul was) but one whose heart was aligned with God's. The Davidic covenant is the bridge Paul is building toward Jesus, and David's character is the theological foundation of that covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: "Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised' — the thesis of the entire sermon in one sentence: the promise to David (2 Samuel 7:12–16) has been fulfilled in Jesus. 'As he promised' — the resurrection of Jesus is not an unexpected event but the fulfillment of covenantal promise. 'Savior' — the title that encompasses the entire gospel: Jesus saves his people from their sins, from the law's condemnation, from death, from the wrath of God. The saving that the exodus prefigured, the kingdom of David anticipated, the prophets foretold — has arrived in the person of Jesus of Nazareth.

verseByVerse.quote: "Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. And as John was finishing his course, he said, 'What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: John the Baptist is the hinge between the prophetic preparation and the messianic fulfillment: his baptism of repentance prepared Israel to receive the greater one. His explicit self-denying witness — 'I am not he... I am not worthy to untie his sandals' — is the model of authentic ministry. The Baptist understood his role as preparatory and himself as secondary: every element of his ministry pointed away from himself toward the one who was coming. The measure of a ministry's authenticity is the consistency with which it directs attention toward Christ rather than toward itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'To us has been sent the message of this salvation' — Paul's application is personal and inclusive. Both the Jewish 'sons of Abraham' and the Gentile God-fearers are addressed as recipients of the same salvation: 'to us.' The message has been sent — divine initiative, not human discovery. 'This salvation' — the specific, historical, embodied salvation accomplished in Jesus of Nazareth, the message that distinguishes Christianity from philosophy: not a theory about salvation but the news of what God has done to accomplish it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. And though they found in him no guilt deserving death, they asked Pilate to have him executed."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets' — the tragedy of fulfilled prophecy unrecognized. The Jerusalem authorities had the prophets read to them every Sabbath and fulfilled those very prophecies by rejecting the one they foretold. The blindness is not moral failure alone but spiritual incapacity: without the Spirit's illumination, even the closest proximity to Scripture does not produce recognition of the one Scripture proclaims. The sermon is simultaneously an explanation of why the Messiah was rejected and an implicit warning against repeating the error.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When they had carried out all that was written of him' — every detail of the passion narrative was the fulfillment of prophetic Scripture (Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, Zechariah 12, etc.). The crucifixion and burial are presented as complete: 'the tree' (Deuteronomy 21:23 — the curse of the law) and 'the tomb' together constitute the depth of the descent. Jesus bore the curse, died, and was buried — the completeness of his death is essential to the completeness of his resurrection. You cannot have a resurrection without a genuine, verifiable death and burial.

Why 'the tree' here, and not 'the cross'? The word is xylon, which means simply 'wood' or 'timber' — a beam, a stake, a tree. The apostles use it of the cross on purpose (also 5:30; 10:39; Gal. 3:13; 1 Pet. 2:24), to sound a deliberate echo of the Law: 'if a man... is hanged on a tree... a hanged man is cursed by God; you shall bury him the same day' (Deut. 21:22–23). To call the cross a 'tree' is therefore to load the word with meaning: Jesus hung where the accursed criminal hung, bearing the curse of God in our place — as Paul spells out, 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree' (Gal. 3:13). And notice the precise fit right here: they 'took him down from the tree' and buried him at once, fulfilling that very command not to leave the body on the tree overnight. The word is no loose synonym; it preaches the heart of the cross — he took our curse. (Some also hear a quiet echo that the curse which entered the world by a tree in Eden was undone on a tree at Calvary — a lovely thought, though the plain reference is Deuteronomy's curse.)

verseByVerse.quote: "But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'But God raised him from the dead' — the divine reversal that transforms every element of the passion narrative. God's 'but' is the hinge of all history. The resurrection appearances are grounded in eyewitness testimony: 'for many days,' 'to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem,' 'who are now his witnesses.' The continuity from Galilee to Jerusalem to the present ('who are now') grounds the resurrection proclamation in living, accessible witnesses — people the audience can in principle speak with.

verseByVerse.quote: "And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'We bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled' — the resurrection is presented as promise-fulfillment, not innovation. The citation of Psalm 2:7 ('you are my Son, today I have begotten you') is applied to the resurrection as the moment of the public declaration of Jesus's divine sonship: the resurrection is God's formal pronouncement that this crucified man is his eternal Son. The 'today' of Psalm 2 is the day of resurrection, when what was always true was publicly declared by the Father's act of raising the dead Son.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.' Therefore he also says in another psalm, 'You will not let your Holy One see corruption.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Two Old Testament texts converge on the resurrection. Isaiah 55:3 — 'the holy and sure blessings of David' — speaks of the eternal covenant with David that will be fulfilled in the resurrection of his ultimate Son. Psalm 16:10 — 'you will not let your Holy One see corruption' — speaks of one who will not decompose in the tomb. Both texts require a fulfillment that David himself could not provide: his own body saw corruption. Therefore both texts must be prophetically pointing to the one who actually rose without corruption: Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'David served the purpose of God in his own generation' — the highest possible summary of a godly life: purpose-driven service to the God of one's generation, within the specific scope of one's calling. But even such a life ends in death and decomposition: 'he fell asleep and saw corruption.' The contrast with Jesus is absolute: Jesus 'did not see corruption' because God raised him. The one who serves not just his generation but all generations forever is the one whose body the grave could not hold. David's purpose was fulfilled; Jesus's purpose is eternal.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary: The sermon's application: forgiveness through Jesus, justification by faith, freedom from what the law could not provide. 'Everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses' — the law could not justify because no one kept it perfectly; Jesus's death bears the law's condemnation, his resurrection vindicates his righteousness, and faith receives the benefit. This is the seed of the theological argument that will fill the letters to the Galatians and Romans — already fully formed in Paul's first recorded sermon, because it is the gospel itself. (cf. Rom. 3:21–24; Col. 2:13–14)

verseByVerse.quote: "Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: 'Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.'" As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary: Habakkuk 1:5 provides the warning that frames the sermon's application: the resurrection of Jesus is God's 'incredible work' in these days, and those who refuse to believe it — who hear it and scoff — are fulfilling the same prophecy that forewarned Israel about God's incredible works they could not believe. The crowd's response is enthusiastic: 'they begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath.' The hunger for the gospel is genuine; the word has found its mark. What happens next Sabbath will reveal which hearts are merely curious and which have genuinely received it.

verseByVerse.quote: And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they talked with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas' — the word 'followed' implies attachment, discipleship, the beginning of a community. This is not a polite request for more information but the beginning of the congregation. Paul and Barnabas' response is pastoral: they urge these new believers 'to continue in the grace of God.' The first pastoral instruction to the first converts in Pisidian Antioch is not a command to do more but an exhortation to remain in what they have received. The Christian life begins in grace and continues in grace; the danger is always drifting out of it.

What does it mean 'to continue in the grace of God'? 'Grace' is God's free, undeserved kindness to sinners in Christ — salvation as a gift, never a wage, never earned. To continue in it (the word means to remain, to abide, to hold fast) is to go on living every day on that same footing of free grace on which you first came in. You were welcomed home freely, with empty hands; continuing in grace means staying there — not slipping back onto the treadmill of trying to make God love you by being good enough, and not despairing when you fail, as though grace had run out. It is the very thing Paul urges on the Colossians: 'as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him' (Col. 2:6). The way in is the way on.

Picture the prodigal son. He came home expecting to earn his keep as a hired servant, and instead the father ran to him, put the robe on him, and welcomed him as a beloved son — sheer grace. Now imagine that son, a week later, quietly slinking off to the servants' quarters to start earning his place after all. That is exactly what it looks like to drift out of grace. 'Continue in the grace of God' means: stay at the Father's table as a freely-loved child. Keep coming to Christ with empty hands; keep drawing on his daily mercy for strength, forgiveness, and growth (grace is not just the door you enter by but the room you live in — 'grow in the grace... of our Lord Jesus Christ,' 2 Pet. 3:18). And keep going — persevere, do not give up. Lest this make you anxious about whether you can hold on, remember what was said at Colossians 1:23: the call to continue is real, yet the God who began this grace is the one who keeps us in it; we persevere because he preserves us. Even our continuing is grace.

verseByVerse.quote: The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Almost the whole city' — the week between the first and second Sabbath has been busy: word has spread throughout Pisidian Antioch that something extraordinary is being proclaimed in the synagogue, and the city turns out. The Jewish leaders' response to this success is jealousy — the same motivation that drove Herod's persecution of the church (12:1) and the Sadducees' arrest of the apostles (5:17). When the gospel's popularity threatens the institution's authority, the institution often responds with opposition rather than participation. 'Reviling' — the argument has given way to abuse: they cannot refute Paul, so they attack him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The explicit turn to the Gentiles is here given its theological foundation: Isaiah 49:6, the Servant Song in which the Servant is given 'as a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth.' The mission to the Gentiles is not a contingency plan prompted by Jewish rejection; it is the fulfillment of Israel's prophetic calling, now carried by those who receive the Servant's mission. 'You judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life' — the rejection of the gospel is self-judgment; the missionaries do not condemn, they declare the consequence of the hearers' own choice. (cf. Isa. 49:6; Rom. 1:16)

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As many as were appointed to eternal life believed' — Luke's most explicit statement of election in Acts. The believing is real and free; the appointment is divine and prior. Both stand together, and Luke does not explain the philosophy of how. And 'the word of the Lord spread throughout the whole region' — the gospel multiplied through the new believers far beyond the city, in ways the missionaries could not track.

Why this is one of the strongest verses for election. Three things give it force. 'Appointed' (tetagmenoi) is a perfect passive participle — a completed action done to them by another, and the unnamed agent, as so often, is God (the 'divine passive'): 'as many as had been appointed [by God] to eternal life believed.' The order is decisive: the appointment comes first and the believing follows — faith is the fruit, God's prior choice the root. And the context sharpens it: two verses earlier the unbelieving Jews 'judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life' (v. 46) — rejection at their own door — while the believing Gentiles are those 'appointed to eternal life.' Luke sets the two side by side without embarrassment: responsibility in unbelief, grace in belief. It fits a steady pattern — 'all that the Father gives me will come to me' (John 6:37); 'you do not believe because you are not among my sheep' (John 10:26); 'the Lord opened her heart' (Acts 16:14); Eph. 1:4–5; Rom. 8:29–30.

How our non-Reformed brothers read it. Godly, Bible-loving Christians who are not Calvinist honour this verse and read it mainly two ways. First, some take the participle as middle voice, 'as many as had disposed themselves toward eternal life' — describing the people's own receptivity rather than a prior decree. (The form can be middle or passive; Reformed readers answer that, given Luke's usage and the contrast with v. 46, the passive with God as agent is far more natural — but the middle is honestly held.) Second, the classic Arminian reading affirms a genuine appointing grounded in God's foreknowledge: foreseeing who would freely believe, God appointed those to eternal life (Rom. 8:29). Election is real, but conditioned on foreseen faith, so free will is preserved. A few read it corporately — the destiny of the believing people as a body, entered by faith.

Held in charity. What unites us comes before what divides: every side believes salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone, that God is sovereign and good, that sinners are truly responsible, and that the gospel must be freely offered to all — exactly what Paul is doing here. The difference is over how God's sovereignty and our believing fit together. In honesty, many even non-Calvinist scholars grant the plain passive is the most natural sense of the Greek; but this is an in-house disagreement among brothers who love the same Lord and Bible, to be carried with humility, not point-scoring. And note what the verse does not do: it does not make God the author of anyone's unbelief (v. 46 lays that on the rejecters), nor does it dampen evangelism — in Acts, election runs right alongside the most tireless preaching the world has seen. Rightly held, it humbles the believer, banishes boasting, and turns assurance into worship: if I believe, it is because grace appointed me, sought me, and opened my heart.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.
verseByVerse.commentary: The persecution is organized through the most influential channels: devout women of high standing and the leading men — the religious and civic establishment working together to expel the missionaries. Paul and Barnabas shake the dust from their feet — the symbolic gesture of prophetic rejection (Matthew 10:14) — and move on. The gesture is not vindictive but declaratory: the responsibility has been transferred. They do not stop the mission; they relocate it. The expulsion from one city is the introduction of the gospel to the next.

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit' — the community left behind in Pisidian Antioch is not abandoned; it is Spirit-filled. The missionaries' departure does not leave the congregation spiritually impoverished; the Spirit who was poured out at Pentecost remains with every community he has filled. The joy that marks them is the same joy that marked the Samaritans after Philip's preaching (8:8) and the eunuch after his baptism (8:39): the Spirit-given gladness that no persecution can extinguish, because it is rooted in the risen Lord who cannot be killed again.

13.theology: Election and Evangelism. Acts 13:48 is the Reformed doctrine of election stated with apostolic directness: the believing of the Gentiles in Pisidian Antioch is grounded in their prior appointment to eternal life. This is not fatalism — it does not prevent preaching; it undergirds it. Paul and Barnabas preach with everything they have, to everyone who will listen, in the synagogue and in the streets. They do not know who is appointed; they preach to all. And God, through the preaching, brings to faith those he has appointed. Election is the guarantee that the mission will not ultimately fail: there are sheep in every flock that God is calling, and the voice of the gospel will reach them. This is the ground of missionary confidence in every hostile city.
13.examples:
Then: Barnabas and Saul, sent out from a worshipping, fasting, praying church, arriving in city after city with nothing but the word and the Spirit — and the word going out, and the appointed ones believing, and the disciples filled with joy even when expelled. The first missionary journey is a portrait of how the kingdom advances: through weakness and proclamation and sovereign grace.

Now: The church sends when it worships. Mission flows from the presence of God, not from strategic planning. The Antioch church was not looking for a missionary project; they were seeking God — and God spoke. The question for every congregation is not “what is our mission strategy?” but “are we in the kind of sustained, attentive, fasting prayer in which the Spirit can speak?” When he speaks, we must be ready to send our best.

14.title: Suffering and Strengthening
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. <sup>2</sup>But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers. <sup>3</sup>So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace by granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. <sup>4</sup>But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. <sup>5</sup>When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat and to stone them, <sup>6</sup>they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, <sup>7</sup>and there they continued to preach the gospel. <sup>8</sup>Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. <sup>9</sup>He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well, <sup>10</sup>said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.” And he sprang up and began walking. <sup>11</sup>And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” <sup>12</sup>Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker. <sup>13</sup>And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds. <sup>14</sup>But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, <sup>15</sup>“Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them. <sup>16</sup>In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. <sup>17</sup>Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness.” <sup>18</sup>Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them. <sup>19</sup>But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. <sup>20</sup>But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe. <sup>21</sup>When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, <sup>22</sup>strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. <sup>23</sup>And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. <sup>24</sup>Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. <sup>25</sup>And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia, <sup>26</sup>and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled. <sup>27</sup>And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. <sup>28</sup>And they remained no little time with the disciples.
14.overview:
The pattern of the first missionary journey is by now familiar: the Word is proclaimed, some believe, others oppose, the apostles are driven out, and they preach in the next city. At Lystra, the pattern intensifies. Paul heals a lame man and the crowd, speaking in Lycaonian, decides that the gods have come down. They want to sacrifice oxen to Barnabas and Paul. The apostles tear their garments — the Jewish gesture of horror at blasphemy — and push back into the crowd to preach the living God who made heaven and earth. They scarcely hold back the sacrifice.

And then the same crowd stones Paul. The speed of the reversal is breathtaking: one moment they are bringing garlands and oxen; the next, stones. The crowd that wanted to worship Paul drags his body out of the city, supposing him dead. And Paul gets up and walks back into the city. He does not leave the region; he does not change his message; he goes on to Derbe and comes back through Lystra and Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the disciples.

What he tells them on the return journey is the sentence that threads through the whole of Acts: “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” Not may — must. Suffering is not the exception for the follower of Jesus; it is the road. The kingdom does not come without the cross — not for the King, and not for those who follow him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — The First Journey Continues and Returns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final leg of the first missionary journey takes Paul and Barnabas through Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe — a sequence of proclamation, opposition, suffering, and stubborn continued witness. At Lystra, the healing of a man lame from birth triggers a near-catastrophe: the crowd concludes that Paul and Barnabas are gods (Zeus and Hermes) and prepares to offer sacrifice to them. The missionaries' response — ripping their garments, running into the crowd, insisting they are 'men of like nature with you' — is the most explicit natural theology in Acts, but it cannot prevent the sacrifice attempt. When Jewish opponents arrive from Antioch and Iconium, the mood shifts instantly: the crowd that was about to worship Paul stones him and drags him out of the city for dead.

The summary of the return journey is the most important missiological passage in Acts for the church's ongoing life: Paul and Barnabas retrace their steps, strengthening every church they had planted, 'saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God,' appointing elders in every church, praying with fasting, and committing the new communities to the Lord. The pattern is established here — plant, strengthen, appoint leadership, entrust to God — and it will be the pattern of every missionary effort that follows.
verseByVerse.theology:
Suffering as the Path into the Kingdom

Paul and Barnabas's declaration in v. 22 — 'through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God' — is not pessimism but theology: the path of the crucified Lord is the path of his followers. Reformed theology insists that suffering is not a sign of God's absence but often a sign of his presence and approval: the servant who shares his Lord's cross shares his Lord's resurrection. The 'must' (dei) is the divine necessity — the same 'must' applied to Christ's suffering in Luke 24:26. The pattern of dying and rising is the pattern of life in the kingdom.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul was stoned and dragged out of Lystra for dead, then got up and went back into the city the next day. The courage required to re-enter the city where you were nearly killed is the courage of the man who has nothing to fear from death. Now: The willingness to re-enter dangerous territory — to continue faithful witness after suffering for it — is the distinctive quality of those whose security is not in this world's preservation of their lives but in Christ's resurrection that awaits them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Iconium pattern mirrors Pisidian Antioch: great success (both Jews and Greeks believing), followed by organized opposition (unbelieving Jews stirring up the Gentiles). The word 'poisoned' (ekakōsan) — made wicked or bitter — captures the deliberate character of the opposition: this is not honest disagreement but the intentional corruption of the community's perception of the missionaries. When the word cannot be refuted on its merits, the strategy shifts to character assassination and social pressure.

verseByVerse.quote: So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They remained for a long time' — the opposition does not determine the mission's length; the Spirit does. Paul and Barnabas stay despite the stirred-up Gentiles because the Lord is bearing witness to the word through signs and wonders. 'The word of his grace' — the gospel is named for its essential character: grace, unmerited favor, the good news that God gives what human beings cannot earn. The Lord's authentication of this word through miracles is his endorsement of its content: this grace is real, and he will confirm it with power.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat and to stone them,
verseByVerse.commentary: The gospel always produces division before it produces unity, because it requires a decision. Iconium is divided: some with the Jews (maintaining the status quo), some with the apostles (following the new word). When the opposition hardens into a formal conspiracy — 'both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers' — the alliance of religious and civil authority against the missionaries mirrors the alliance that condemned Jesus. The attempt to stone them is the same impulse that stoned Stephen: silence through violence what cannot be silenced through argument.

verseByVerse.quote: they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, and there they continued to preach the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul and Barnabas exercise prudence: they flee when the plot becomes known. Jesus had modeled this wisdom himself (Luke 4:30; John 10:39), and commanded it in Matthew 10:23: 'when they persecute you in one town, flee to the next.' The flight is not cowardice but mission-wisdom: preserve the missionaries to continue the mission in the next city. And they do continue — immediately, in Lystra and Derbe and 'the surrounding country.' The geographical expansion driven by persecution mirrors the pattern established in chapter 8: opposition becomes mission strategy.

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well,
verseByVerse.commentary: The lame man at Lystra parallels the lame man at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3) and the healing of Aeneas (Acts 9): crippled from birth, never walked, healed by an apostle's word in the name of Jesus. But the context is entirely different — this is Gentile territory, outside the synagogue, in a community with no prior exposure to the God of Israel. Paul 'looked intently' — the Spirit-given perception that sees the faith the word has produced. The man's listening to Paul's preaching has generated faith that his healing will manifest. Faith precedes the miracle; the miracle confirms the faith.

verseByVerse.quote: said in a loud voice, "Stand upright on your feet." And he sprang up and began walking.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Stand upright on your feet' — the command of the risen Lord spoken through his apostle, producing what it declares. 'Loud voice' — the healing is public, undeniable, visible to all. 'He sprang up and began walking' — the immediacy and completeness of the restoration: not cautious first steps but leaping movement, the exuberance of a body that has never known what it is now experiencing. The crowd's response will show how differently a Gentile audience with no Scriptural framework interprets a miracle: where Jerusalem saw the power of the God of Abraham, Lystra will see the gods of Olympus.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, "The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!" And Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Lystran crowd's response reveals the interpretive framework of Gentile polytheism: extraordinary events are explained by divine visitation. The identification of Barnabas with Zeus (the chief deity, perhaps because of his dignified bearing or senior status) and Paul with Hermes (the messenger-god, because he spoke) shows how deeply the Gentile mind was shaped by a divine-human continuum — the gods were always potentially walking among humans in disguise. Luke's detail that they spoke 'in Lycaonian' explains why Paul and Barnabas did not immediately understand what was happening: the acclamation was in a language they may not have known.

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds.
verseByVerse.commentary: The priest of Zeus responds with institutional enthusiasm: oxen (expensive sacrificial animals), garlands (the decorative festive wreath used in sacrifice), and the full priestly apparatus. The temple of Zeus at the entrance to the city places the divine presence at the city's threshold — exactly where the gods would appear if they were coming in. The scene is about to become a theological crisis requiring immediate, desperate action: the crowd that seconds ago witnessed a healing is about to worship the healed man's benefactors.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, "Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Tore their garments' — the Jewish gesture of horror at blasphemy, completely instinctive in this moment. The apostles run toward the crowd, not away from it, to stop the sacrifice before it begins. Their counter-proclamation is the most basic natural theology: 'turn from these vain things to a living God, who made everything.' 'Vain things' — idols, whose vanity was a prophetic theme (Psalm 31:6; Jeremiah 2:5; 10:15). 'A living God' — categorically different from idols: not a projection of human imagination but the creator of everything, including the humans doing the imagining.

verseByVerse.quote: "In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways' — the divine patience with Gentile ignorance is acknowledged, but the emphasis falls on 'past': that era of divine accommodation is now ending. Paul will develop this point in Athens (17:30): 'the times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent.' The coming of Christ marks the end of the period when the nations could walk in their own ways without direct divine summons to the gospel. The arrival of the missionaries in Lystra is the arrival of that summons, and the Lystrans are now accountable to it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness." Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'He did not leave himself without witness' — natural revelation: rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness testify to the Creator's goodness even where the gospel has not yet come. Paul develops this in Romans 1:19–20 and 2:14–15 — the knowledge of God through creation is enough to leave humanity without excuse, though not enough to save. 'Scarcely restrained the people' — redirecting devotion from idols to the living God is the missionary challenge in every culture.

This verse is one of Scripture's clearest windows onto common grace. 'Common' means not cheap but given to all in common — the goodness God shows every creature, believer and unbeliever alike: the rains and fruitful seasons, the food and gladness here; and beyond, life and breath (Acts 17:25), the restraint of evil, the skill and kindness and beauty found even among those who do not know God, and the patience that delays judgment to leave room for repentance. Jesus grounds it in the same gifts: God 'makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust' (Matt. 5:45; cf. Ps. 145:9; James 1:17). The astonishing thing Paul presses on these idolaters is that God had been feeding them, gladdening them, and watering their fields all along — lavishing kindness on people building altars to other gods.

Two things must be kept clear. First, common grace is not saving grace: genuinely grace, undeserved kindness, but it blesses this life without, by itself, reconciling anyone to God — the redeeming grace given in Christ is a greater thing, granted to those who believe. (To confuse them is to imagine everyone is saved because everyone enjoys God's sunshine.) Second, see what it is for: it is a 'witness' (v. 17) — daily goodness testifying that God is real and kind, leaving people 'without excuse' (Rom. 1:20) and meant 'to lead you to repentance' (Rom. 2:4). The tragedy is to take the gifts and ignore the Giver (Rom. 1:21). And the lesson is warm and practical: every good thing you enjoy — the rain on your garden, the harvest, the meal on the table, the laughter of friends, the sun on your back — is a gift from the open hand of a good God, a daily knock pointing past the gift to the Giver. It teaches you to give thanks for everything, see God's hand everywhere, and love even your enemies as God does, doing good to all (Matt. 5:44–45).

verseByVerse.quote: But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe.
verseByVerse.commentary: The reversal is breathtaking: the crowd that was about to offer sacrifice to Paul now stones him at the instigation of his Jewish opponents. Paul is dragged out of the city 'supposing that he was dead' — the stoning is intended to be lethal. When the disciples gather around him, he rises — whether miraculously preserved or simply not as dead as supposed, Luke does not say. But the fact that 'on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe' is extraordinary: the man who was nearly stoned to death re-enters the city that nearly killed him, then continues his mission the next morning. 2 Corinthians 11:25 confirms Paul was stoned once.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The return to the planted churches is as essential as the planting — the missionaries are not just church-starters but church-builders. 'Strengthening the souls' is pastoral care: the new disciples face the same opposition their founders did, and need the theology to survive it. 'Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God' — the 'must' (dei) is a divine necessity for all who follow the crucified Lord: the disciple's path mirrors his Lord's, suffering before glory. This is not bad news; it is the theology that makes suffering survivable. (cf. Rom. 5:3–4; 2 Tim. 3:12)

'Made many disciples' — worth pausing on, because we easily lose the very idea of a disciple. The word (mathētēs) means a learner, an apprentice — not one who collects information but one who attaches his whole life to a master, learns his teaching and his way of living, and sets out to become like him: 'everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher' (Luke 6:40). Jesus made it costly and total — 'let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me' (Luke 9:23) — yet also the ordinary identity of every believer: 'disciple' was the word for a Christian before the name 'Christian' existed (Acts 11:26).

That is where the modern church stumbles. We can reduce the faith to a single decision — getting people 'converted' — and forget that the commission is to 'make disciples... teaching them to observe all that I have commanded' (Matt. 28:19–20). A disciple is not an optional upgrade for keen Christians; it is simply what a Christian is — a lifelong apprentice of Jesus. Paul and Barnabas did exactly this: not counting converts and moving on, but returning to strengthen the disciples and appointing elders to watch over them (vv. 22–23). The reminder is bracing and freeing: you were not saved to make one decision and drift, but to follow — to walk after Jesus as a learner, for the rest of your life.

'We must enter the kingdom of God' — and you may be puzzled: did we not already enter it? Paul says God 'has transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son' (Col. 1:13, past tense) — yet here entering is still future. Both are true; this is the 'already and not yet.' God's saving reign in King Jesus comes in two stages. It already arrived at his first coming — 'the kingdom of God has come upon you' (Matt. 12:28) — and every believer is already under its reign, enjoying its blessings (forgiveness, the Spirit, sonship). And it is not yet consummated: its full glory waits for his return, when he reigns openly and makes all things new, and in that sense we will yet 'enter' or 'inherit' it (Matt. 25:34; 1 Cor. 15:50; 2 Tim. 4:18). Same kingdom, two stages — the 'already' real but partial, the 'not yet' full and final. (See on Col. 1:13; 4:11.)

So Paul speaks both ways as his point requires: to assure us of what is already ours by grace, he says we have been placed in the kingdom; to press us on in hope — as here — he points to the kingdom we have yet to enter. Picture a decisive battle already won, the outcome settled, while the victory parade still lies ahead; or dawn — the sun truly risen, the full blaze of noon still to come. And notice why he raises the future entrance here: to frame the 'many tribulations' as the appointed road home. The trials are not a sign we have lost the kingdom; they are the path into its fullness — 'provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him' (Rom. 8:17).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The appointment of elders 'in every church' is what makes the churches sustainable without the missionaries. Local leadership, raised from within, is the mechanism of the church's ongoing life. 'With prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord' — not organizational promotion but prayerful entrustment: handing the churches over to the Lord whose they are.

The mandate. That they appointed elders 'in every church' shows it was fixed practice, and the rest of the New Testament confirms it: Paul left Titus in Crete to 'appoint elders in every town' (Titus 1:5), a church without them being 'not yet in order.' Every church we meet has them — Ephesus (Acts 20:17), Peter's readers (1 Pet. 5:1), James's (James 5:14), Philippi's 'overseers and deacons' (Phil. 1:1). Two things. First, three words name the same office from different angles: elder (presbyteros, maturity), overseer/bishop (episkopos, oversight), and pastor/shepherd (poimēn, care) — all used of the same men (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5, 7; 1 Pet. 5:1–2). Second, it is always elders, plural — a team, not a lone ruler. Shared leadership is the apostolic norm.

The authority they have — and don't. Elders have real, God-given authority: to lead or 'rule' (1 Tim. 5:17), to teach and guard sound doctrine (Titus 1:9), to shepherd and watch over souls (Acts 20:28); and the flock is to 'obey your leaders and submit to them' (Heb. 13:17). But it is strictly bounded. It is derived: they are under-shepherds serving the Chief Shepherd (1 Pet. 5:4), tending 'the church of God,' not their own (Acts 20:28). It is Word-bound: they minister Scripture's authority, so they may not bind consciences with rules God has not given (the error of Col. 2) — they declare God's Word, they do not legislate. And it is not the right to dominate: 'not domineering... but being examples' (1 Pet. 5:3); they lead as servants, not lords (Mark 10:42–45), and will 'give an account' to God (Heb. 13:17). Real authority, but servant-authority — Christ-derived, Scripture-limited, accountable, never tyrannical. The elders are no little popes.

The qualifications. The two lists (1 Tim. 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9) stress character, not talent. The umbrella is 'above reproach' — a life giving no just handle for accusation. Under it: faithful in marriage (a 'one-woman man'), self-controlled, sober-minded, gentle and not violent, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, hospitable, upright, holy, 'not a recent convert' (mature, lest he be puffed up). He must manage his own household well — 'if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?' (1 Tim. 3:5) — and be 'well thought of by outsiders.' Only one item is an ability, not a trait: he must be 'able to teach,' holding firm to sound doctrine 'to give instruction... and to rebuke those who contradict' (1 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:9) — the chief thing distinguishing an elder from a deacon. The lesson humbles: an elder is not the most gifted or successful man in the room, but a man of proven Christlike character who knows and can teach the truth — nearly everything on the list is simply the mature Christian life, on display in one fit to model it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia,
verseByVerse.commentary: The return through Pisidia and Pamphylia adds Perga — where they had landed at the journey's beginning (13:13) and where John Mark had departed — to the list of cities that have heard the word. Speaking the word in Perga on the return is characteristic of the missionaries' consistency: no city is passed through without proclamation. The descent to Attalia (the port city of Pamphylia, modern Antalya) prepares for the sea voyage home to Antioch. The geography of mission is the geography of the word spreading from city to city across the region.

verseByVerse.quote: and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled' — the work commissioned by the Spirit through the Antioch community has been completed. The missionaries return to the community that sent them, accountable to the community's prayer and the Spirit's call. 'The grace of God' is the resource in which they were placed and from which they have operated throughout: grace is not merely the message they preached but the environment in which they worked and the power by which they accomplished what they were given to do. The first journey is done; the reporting begins.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they remained no little time with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'All that God had done with them' — the mission report is theocentric: it is what God has done, not what the missionaries accomplished. 'Opened a door of faith to the Gentiles' — the metaphor of the opened door will recur in Paul's letters (1 Corinthians 16:9; 2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3); here it captures the Gentile mission's breakthrough: God has opened the way. The extended stay in Antioch ('no little time') is the rest and refreshment of the returning missionaries and the joyful celebration of the sending community. The next crisis — the question of Gentile circumcision — is about to arrive. (cf. 1 Cor. 16:9; Col. 4:3)

14.theology: Suffering as the Path of the Kingdom. Acts 14:22 is the New Testament’s clearest statement that suffering is the appointed means by which the people of God enter the kingdom. This is not peripheral; it is structural. The cross was not a detour on the way to the resurrection; it was the way. And the church that follows a crucified Lord is called to the same road. Paul writes later that he fills up in his flesh “what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body” (Colossians 1:24) — not that Christ’s atoning work was incomplete, but that the suffering of Christ is reproduced in his body, the church, as the gospel goes forth into the world. The church that suffers for the name is the church that looks most like its Lord. And it is the church that the watching world cannot ultimately explain away.
14.examples:
Then: Paul, stoned and left for dead outside Lystra, rising and walking back into the city, going on to Derbe the next morning. Returning through Lystra and Iconium and Antioch — the cities that had tried to kill him — to strengthen the believers he left behind. Appointing elders, committing them to God with prayer and fasting, and sailing home to report everything God had done. This is what faithful looks like.

Now: The Western church has largely lost the theology of suffering. We expect the Christian life to be comfortable, and when it is not, we assume something has gone wrong. Acts 14 says the opposite: tribulation is the appointed road, and the God who walked it first walks it with his people. The suffering church is not the failing church; it is often the most faithful church — and, in God’s strange economy, the most fruitful.

15.title: The Jerusalem Council
15.text: <sup>1</sup>But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” <sup>2</sup>And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question. <sup>5</sup>But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.” <sup>6</sup>The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. <sup>7</sup>And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe. <sup>8</sup>And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, <sup>9</sup>and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith. <sup>10</sup>Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? <sup>11</sup>But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.” <sup>12</sup>And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. <sup>13</sup>After they finished speaking, James replied, “Brothers, listen to me. <sup>14</sup>Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name. <sup>15</sup>And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, <sup>16</sup>‘After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it, <sup>17</sup>that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things <sup>18</sup>known from of old.’ <sup>19</sup>Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, <sup>20</sup>but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood. <sup>22</sup>Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. <sup>28</sup>For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements. <sup>36</sup>And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.” <sup>37</sup>Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. <sup>38</sup>But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work. <sup>39</sup>And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, <sup>40</sup>but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. <sup>41</sup>And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
15.overview:
The first great theological crisis of the church comes from within. Men from Judea arrive in Antioch teaching that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. This is not a secondary issue — it is the gospel itself at stake. If Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved, then Christ alone is not enough. The cross is not sufficient. Grace is not free. Paul and Barnabas see this immediately and oppose it with everything they have.

The Jerusalem Council is the church’s first great doctrinal assembly — and what it produces is not a compromise but a clarification. Peter says it most plainly: neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear the yoke of the law. Why lay it on the Gentiles? We believe we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus — just as they will. The playing field is level at the foot of the cross. There is one way of salvation for Jew and Gentile alike: grace through faith in the Lord Jesus.

James confirms with Amos: God always intended to take a people for his name from the Gentiles. This is not deviation from the old covenant; it is its fulfilment. The letter goes out. The Gentile churches are freed from the burden of circumcision. The gospel is clarified, codified, and sent. And then, quietly, Paul and Barnabas fall out over John Mark, and the mission continues in two streams — which means God uses even the sharp disagreements of his servants to multiply the advance of his kingdom.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Jerusalem Council is the most important ecclesiastical event in the New Testament outside of Pentecost. The question it answers will determine the character of the church for every subsequent generation: must Gentiles become Jews (through circumcision and Torah observance) to be saved, or is faith in Jesus Christ alone sufficient? The question is not peripheral but central: it concerns the nature of the gospel itself. If circumcision is added to faith as a condition of salvation, then Christ's death is insufficient, and the gospel has become something other than grace.

The council's process is itself instructive: extended testimony (Paul and Barnabas reporting what God had done among the Gentiles), apostolic deliberation, and finally James's ruling grounded in Scripture (Amos 9:11–12). The decision is remarkable for what it does not require: no circumcision, no full Torah observance, only abstentions from idolatry, sexual immorality, and what was strangled and blood — practical requirements that would allow Jewish and Gentile believers to share table fellowship. The Gentiles are welcomed into full membership in the people of God on the sole condition of faith in Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith Alone — the Council's Theological Verdict

Peter's speech in vv. 8–11 is the clearest statement of justification by faith alone in the book of Acts: 'God made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith... we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.' The Gentiles are saved the same way the Jews are — by grace through faith, not by law observance. This is the verdict that Paul will develop in Galatians and Romans. The Jerusalem Council is the communal confirmation of what the Spirit had demonstrated in Cornelius's house.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem Council produced a letter of pastoral decision rather than a theological treatise — practical guidance that allowed Jew and Gentile to live together in one community. Now: The church continues to face questions about what is required for full membership in the people of God. The council's method — testimony, Scripture, deliberation, pastoral wisdom — remains the model for ecclesial discernment on divisive questions.

verseByVerse.quote: But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved." And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, it was decided that Paul and Barnabas and some of the others should go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Judaizing teachers' claim — 'unless you are circumcised... you cannot be saved' — is the addition that Paul will call 'a different gospel, which is not another' (Galatians 1:6–7). The issue is not circumcision as a cultural practice but circumcision as a condition of salvation: if physical rite is required for justification, then Christ's death alone is insufficient. Paul and Barnabas engage in 'no small dissension' — the dispute is fierce because the stakes are ultimate. The resolution to seek the Jerusalem council's judgment reflects both the seriousness of the question and the church's commitment to apostolic accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: "So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them."
verseByVerse.commentary: The mission report as worship: Paul and Barnabas describe in detail — word by word — what God had done with them, and the response is great joy. The phrase 'all that God had done with them' is Luke's theological signature: it is God who acts; the missionaries are instruments. Welcome by 'the church and the apostles and the elders' signals the full community of Christ receiving what God has accomplished among the Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: "But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, 'It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The Pharisee party within the church represents the most serious theological challenge the early church faces: not persecution from outside but distortion from within. Their demand — circumcision plus Torah observance — is not malicious; it flows from sincere conviction that God's covenant people must be marked as God's covenant people. But the gospel hangs in the balance, and the Council must address it directly.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, "Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Much debate' — the Jerusalem Council is not a rubber stamp; it is a genuine deliberative assembly where competing positions are stated, argued, and weighed. Peter's opening reference to 'the early days' points to the Cornelius episode (ch. 10–11) as the precedent that governs the current question: God himself chose to use Peter's mouth to bring the gospel to Gentiles, and God himself confirmed the genuineness of their reception by pouring out the Spirit on them without circumcision. The precedent is divine, not human — it cannot be overridden by a subsequent human requirement.

verseByVerse.quote: "And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'God, who knows the heart' — the divine heart-knower does not look at circumcision; he looks at faith. His testimony to the genuineness of the Gentile believers' faith was the gift of the Spirit, given 'just as he did to us' at Pentecost. 'He made no distinction' — the same word used in 10:20 when the Spirit told Peter to go with the Cornelius messengers 'making no distinction.' God has declared there is no distinction between Jewish and Gentile believers; to add circumcision as a requirement would be to impose a distinction that God has explicitly removed. (cf. Rom. 10:12–13; Gal. 3:14)

verseByVerse.quote: "Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A yoke... that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear' — the law, as a system of salvation, has never worked: Israel's entire history is the story of the covenant people's failure to keep the covenant they received. To impose on Gentile believers a yoke that Jewish believers themselves have never been able to bear is to impose on them what is both impossible and unnecessary. 'We believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will' — the gospel of grace is the same for Jew and Gentile. The Jewish believers are not saved by law plus Christ; they are saved by grace through faith. So are the Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: "And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. After they finished speaking, James replied, 'Brothers, listen to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The assembly falls silent — the weight of the missionary testimony commands attention. Signs and wonders are not proofs of truth in themselves, but Luke deploys them as evidence of divine authentication: God himself has been at work among the Gentiles. James, presiding as the leader of the Jerusalem church, now speaks with authoritative finality. The silence followed by 'Brothers, listen to me' marks a pivotal moment.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: James uses Peter's Hebrew name — Simeon — grounding the apostle in his Jewish identity even as he testifies to Gentile inclusion. The language 'a people for his name' is covenant language drawn from Exodus 19 and Deuteronomy 7: the Gentiles are now being constituted as God's covenant people, named by his name. This is not ethnic assimilation into Israel but the eschatological ingathering the prophets foresaw.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, "After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it, that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord,"'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
James cites Amos 9:11–12 as the hermeneutical key to the entire council debate. The rebuilt tent of David — the restored Davidic dynasty — is fulfilled in Jesus, the son of David raised from the dead. This restoration is not merely national but cosmic: its purpose is that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord. The Gentile mission is not an improvisation in response to Jewish rejection; it is the fulfillment of prophetic expectation embedded in Israel's own scriptures.

Here too brothers read the prophecy differently, and it is worth noting kindly. On the amillennial / Reformed reading taken above, the 'rebuilding of David's fallen tent' is being fulfilled now in the risen Son of David and the ingathering of the Gentiles into his church — which is exactly why James cites it to settle the question. Our dispensational friends, by contrast, generally take Amos's rebuilt tent of David to await a future, literal restoration of national Israel and the Davidic throne in the millennial kingdom; on their reading James is not declaring the prophecy fulfilled today but showing that the present Gentile ingathering is in harmony with the prophets ('after this I will return and rebuild'), the church age being a foretaste of what Christ will yet establish at his return. Both honour the prophets and rejoice that Gentiles are saved by grace, apart from becoming Jews — the very point of the council; the difference belongs to the larger, family conversation between amillennial and dispensational readings of God's future for Israel, and should be carried with charity.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things known from of old.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The Gentiles called by God's name — bearing the covenant name of the Lord — are the fulfillment of Israel's prophetic hope, not its replacement. Amos saw this from within Israel's own worship. 'Known from of old' grounds the council's decision in divine eternity: God has known this from before the foundation of the world. The council is not innovating; they are recognizing what God has always intended, now becoming visible in history.

verseByVerse.quote: "'known to God from of old are all his works.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The capstone of James's argument: God has known this from eternity. The inclusion of the Gentiles is not a plan B, not an afterthought, not a concession to circumstance. It is the ancient purpose of God unfolding in history. This grounds the council's decision in divine sovereignty: they are not innovating; they are recognizing what God has always intended.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
James's ruling is not a compromise of the gospel but a pastoral measure to make table fellowship possible between Jewish and Gentile believers. The four abstentions map roughly onto the Noahide laws — binding on all who dwell among Israel — and the concerns of Leviticus 17–18. Gentiles need not be circumcised or keep the Mosaic Torah; but they must separate from the practices most bound up with idolatry and sexual immorality that would fracture the community.

If the food laws are abolished, why forbid blood and strangled meat? First, hold on to what the council had just decided: Gentiles are saved by grace, not by keeping the law (15:11) — so these are not kosher rules smuggled back in, nor conditions of salvation. Why ask them, then? For love and unity. Jewish believers were revolted by these things — meat offered to idols, and the eating of blood (which strangled meat retains). Scripture had forbidden blood since Noah, long before Moses (Gen. 9:4; Lev. 17), out of reverence for the life in it. For Jew and Gentile to sit at one table and be one church, the Gentiles — free in conscience — were asked to surrender a few things that would deeply wound their brothers: liberty limited by love (Rom. 14). And all four cluster around the pagan temple — idol-meat, blood, strangled animals, ritual immorality were the stuff of idol-feasts — so the decree also keeps new converts clear of their old idolatry. It is not 'back to the law'; it is 'love your brother, and stay clear of idols.'

But doesn't Paul later allow food offered to idols (1 Cor. 8–10)? No contradiction, once two questions are distinguished. (1) Eating as an act of worship, at a temple feast — Paul forbids it as flatly as the council: 'flee from idolatry... you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons' (1 Cor. 10:14, 21). On idolatry, Paul and James are identical. (2) Eating meat that merely happened through a temple and is now sold in the market or served at a private meal — this Paul treats as neutral ('an idol has no real existence,' 8:4; 'eat whatever is sold in the meat market,' 10:25), permitted, governed only by love: do not eat if it would wound a weaker brother (8:9–13). So Paul is not overturning the decree but applying its same two principles — flee idolatry, let love limit liberty — with more nuance.
