The Areopagus sermon is the model for engagement: begin where people are, affirm what is true in their searching, and then announce the resurrection without apology. The resurrection is still the scandal. It is also still the only answer to the altar inscribed “To the unknown god.”

18.title: Corinth
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. <sup>2</sup>And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them, <sup>3</sup>and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade. <sup>4</sup>And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. <sup>5</sup>When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” <sup>7</sup>And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue. <sup>8</sup>Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized. <sup>9</sup>And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, <sup>10</sup>for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.” <sup>11</sup>And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. <sup>12</sup>But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, <sup>13</sup>saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.” <sup>14</sup>But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. <sup>15</sup>But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things.” <sup>16</sup>And he drove them from the tribunal. <sup>18</sup>After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. <sup>24</sup>Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. <sup>25</sup>He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. <sup>26</sup>He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. <sup>27</sup>And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, <sup>28</sup>for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.
18.overview:
Corinth is the last place a fastidious missionary would choose. It is the Las Vegas of the ancient world — a great port city famous for commerce, vice, and the worship of Aphrodite. Paul arrives from Athens, where the reception was mixed, and he comes, as he later writes, “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3). He finds Aquila and Priscilla, works with them at their trade, preaches every Sabbath, and waits.

Then the Lord speaks in the night: “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you… I have many in this city who are my people.” This is the doctrine of election turned into pastoral comfort. God already has people in Corinth — people who are his, who will be gathered by the proclamation of the gospel. Paul does not need to manufacture a harvest; he needs to be faithful, and God will bring in what is his. He stays a year and a half. The church at Corinth — with all its chaos, all its gifts, all its problems — is born.

The chapter closes with Apollos — eloquent, fervent, scripturally competent, but knowing only the baptism of John. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside privately and explain the way of God more accurately. They do not embarrass him publicly; they instruct him privately. And Apollos, genuinely humble, receives the teaching and goes on to powerfully confute the opponents of the gospel. The church grows not only by addition but by the deepening of those already in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Corinth and the Return to Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Corinth is the unlikely setting for one of the most fruitful and sustained periods of Paul's missionary work. A prosperous, cosmopolitan, morally notorious Roman colony — the Las Vegas of the ancient Mediterranean — Corinth would seem to be the least promising soil for a gospel community. But God tells Paul in a vision: 'I have many in this city who are my people.' The sovereignty of election precedes the labor of mission: there are people in Corinth whom God has appointed for salvation, and Paul's task is to preach to them until they come to faith. He stays eighteen months.

The divine encouragement to Paul in the night vision (vv. 9–10) is the theological heart of the Corinthian mission: 'Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.' The promise of divine protection, the command to speak, and the assurance of predetermined harvest together give Paul the perseverance the Corinthian mission will require. Every new congregation faces the challenge of whether to trust the promise or to succumb to discouragement; the vision at Corinth is the answer to that challenge.
verseByVerse.theology:
Tent-Making Ministry and the Support of Proclamation

Paul's tent-making partnership with Aquila and Priscilla is the first explicit mention of Paul's manual labor as a means of supporting his missionary work. Reformed theology has often discussed whether 'tentmaker ministry' (self-supported missionary work) is a normative apostolic pattern or a situational adaptation. Paul's own letters suggest the latter: he worked with his hands to avoid being a burden on new churches and to model the dignity of labor, but he accepted support from established communities (Philippians 4:15–16). The Corinthian mission itself was eventually supported by the arrival of Silas and Timothy from Macedonia (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Gallio decision — the Roman proconsul's dismissal of the Jewish charge against Paul — established a legal precedent protecting Christian preaching as an internal Jewish dispute. Now: God continues to use civil authorities and legal processes to protect the gospel's proclamation, even when those authorities have no understanding of or sympathy with the gospel. Providence works through the decisions of those who know nothing of its purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: "After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them,"
verseByVerse.commentary: Corinth is the commercial capital of Greece — wealthy, cosmopolitan, morally notorious, strategic. The expulsion of Jews from Rome (under Claudius, c. AD 49 — likely related to disturbances 'at the instigation of Chrestus,' possibly about Christ) has brought Aquila and Priscilla to Corinth, where they will become Paul's most significant co-workers. Providence works through imperial edicts: the very persecution that uprooted this couple placed them exactly where the mission needed them.

verseByVerse.quote: "and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's tentmaking is both economic necessity and theological principle: he does not burden the new churches financially, and he maintains the dignity of manual labor against the cultural prejudice of the Greco-Roman world, which looked down on artisans. The shared trade creates the bond that becomes a missionary partnership. Aquila and Priscilla will travel with Paul, plant churches, and instruct Apollos — all from this tentmaker's workshop in Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, devoting himself completely to testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The arrival of Silas and Timothy from Macedonia — apparently bringing financial support from the Philippian and Thessalonian churches (Philippians 4:15) — frees Paul from tent-making and allows him to focus entirely on proclamation. 'Occupied with the word, devoting himself completely' — the whole-person investment in proclamation that Paul will later describe as his primary calling (1 Corinthians 9:16). The arrival of team members and material support is itself a providential provision: the mission intensifies when the missionary's practical needs are met by the community behind him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.' And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary: The shaking out of garments is a prophetic gesture of dissociation — Paul's version of the 'shaking the dust off feet' of Luke 9:5. 'Your blood be on your own heads' is Ezekiel's language (Ezek. 33:4) for individual moral responsibility: Paul has warned them, and the rejection is theirs. 'From now on I will go to the Gentiles' is not a permanent abandonment of Jewish mission but a local pivot — and the next gathering point is right next to the synagogue, maximally visible to the rejected community.

verseByVerse.quote: "Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized."
verseByVerse.commentary: Crispus — the ruler of the very synagogue that has just rejected Paul — believes with his whole household and is baptized (Paul baptized him himself, 1 Cor. 1:14). The gospel penetrates the institution that has just opposed it, through its own leader. Many Corinthians believe and are baptized. The turn to the Gentiles does not mean the end of Jewish response; it means the widening of the river of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, 'Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vision comes at a moment of vulnerability — Corinth's opposition, Paul's aloneness before Silas and Timothy arrived, the weight of the mission. The Lord's word is threefold: do not be afraid, keep speaking, I am with you. Then a remarkable promise: 'I have many in this city who are my people.' These people are not yet Christians; they are the elect whom God has fore-known. The mission will find them because God has already claimed them. This is the Calvinist confidence that fuels missionary boldness: the preacher goes to find those God has already chosen to save. (cf. Isa. 41:10; Matt. 28:20)

'I have many in this city who are my people' — spoken of Corinthians who had not yet believed. Notice how God's election here does not cool evangelism but fires it: because God has a chosen people in Corinth who will come to faith through the preaching, Paul can keep speaking, unafraid, certain his labour will not be wasted. Election does not make sowing pointless; it makes the harvest sure, for the Lord gathers his own through the gospel preached (cf. 13:48; 2 Tim. 2:10, 'I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain salvation'). It is the discouraged evangelist's deepest comfort: somewhere in your 'city' are people God means to save, and your faithful witness is the means he will use.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them."
verseByVerse.commentary: Eighteen months — the longest single stay in Paul's missionary career to this point. The vision gave him permission to put down roots, and he did. The church in Corinth is the most troubled of Paul's churches, as his letters reveal, but it is also the most deeply formed — eighteen months of sustained teaching. Depth of formation and subsequent struggle are not contradictory; the Corinthian letters are evidence that even deep teaching requires ongoing pastoral attention.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, saying, 'This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gallio's proconsulship is historically datable (c. AD 51–52 from the Delphi inscription), giving Acts one of its most secure chronological anchors. The Jewish charge is carefully legal: persuading people to worship contrary to the law — hoping Gallio will interpret this as a violation of Roman law governing religious practice. If they can get a Roman ruling against Paul's mission, it becomes legally binding throughout the province.

A quick word on 'proconsul' (Greek anthypatos). Rome's provinces came in two kinds: the settled, peaceful ones governed on behalf of the Senate by a proconsul, and the frontier ones governed by the emperor's own appointees. Achaia (southern Greece, capital Corinth) was a senatorial province, so its governor was a proconsul — usually a senior senator sent out for about a year, holding supreme civil and judicial authority, which is why Paul is hauled before his 'tribunal' (the bēma, the judgment seat) for a ruling. In modern terms he was something like a centrally-appointed regional governor who was also the province's chief judge — combining in one man the executive and judicial powers our democracies usually keep apart, answerable not to local voters but to Rome. (Luke's precise title here is also a quiet mark of his accuracy: Achaia's status shifted over the years, and he names it correctly for this moment — the same Gallio whose term the Delphi inscription dates to c. AD 51–52.)

verseByVerse.quote: "But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, 'If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Gallio's ruling is one of the most important legal decisions in Acts: the dispute about Jesus is an internal Jewish religious matter, not a Roman legal concern. Gallio refuses jurisdiction — inadvertently protecting the Pauline mission from provincial suppression. The charge of teaching people to worship contrary to the law is dismissed as an intramural Jewish debate about 'words and names and your own law.' Providence works through the disinterest of a proconsul who does not care about theological questions.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I refuse to be a judge of these things.' And he drove them from the tribunal."
verseByVerse.commentary: The driving away from the tribunal — Gallio physically dismisses the case and the crowd — functionally extends the legal protection of Judaism (religio licita) to Christianity, at least in this moment and province. This ruling will not last forever, but it creates a window for the mission. The gospel's legal vindication before Roman authority is a recurring theme in Acts: wherever fair procedure is applied, the gospel is declared innocent of criminal charges.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sosthenes's beating by the crowd (Gentile frustration at the failed prosecution) may explain why 'Sosthenes the brother' co-sends 1 Corinthians (1:1) — the synagogue ruler who bore the cost became a believer. Gallio's indifference confirms his neutrality. And Paul's Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), the hair cut at Cenchreae marking its close, shows the shape of his practice: free from the law as a means of salvation, still glad to engage its disciplines as devotion.

Paul's vow raises a real question: now that Christ has come, may a believer still keep the law, or parts of it? The Reformed answer distinguishes three strands in the law of Moses. The moral law (the Ten Commandments, summed up as loving God and neighbour) reflects God's unchanging character and abides always; we are not saved by it, but the believer gladly obeys it as the Spirit-enabled pattern of a thankful life. The ceremonial law (sacrifices, priesthood, temple, feasts, clean-and-unclean foods, circumcision as rite) was the shadow that pointed to Christ and is fulfilled in him (see on Col. 2:16–17) — no Christian is bound to keep it. The civil law that governed Israel as a nation expired with that nation, though its underlying justice still instructs. So: the moral law stands; the ceremonial and civil are not binding as obligations.

But notice the careful line Paul walks — here a Jewish vow, later a temple purification (21:23–26), and Timothy's circumcision (16:3), yet a flat refusal to circumcise Titus (Gal. 2:3–5) and thunder against anyone who made law-keeping a condition of salvation (Gal. 5:2–4). The difference is always why. Made a means of being right with God, or imposed on others as necessary, a practice denies the gospel and is forbidden. Kept freely — as heritage, devotion, conscience, or love that wins a hearing ('to the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might win Jews,' 1 Cor. 9:20) — it is Christian liberty. Paul kept his vow not to earn anything but as free devotion; that is the model.

So, the two cases. A Jewish believer may in liberty keep ancestral customs — feasts, food traditions, even a vow — as heritage, devotion, and witness among his people, as Paul did, provided he never makes them the ground of his standing nor binds them on others. A Gentile believer is under no obligation to the ceremonial law at all (the whole verdict of Acts 15); he may find devotional value in some Old Testament root — 'one esteems one day above another... let each be fully convinced in his own mind' (Rom. 14:5) — but must heed Galatians' warning never to put himself under the law as a system, which is to fall from grace (Gal. 4:10–11; 5:1). The test in every case: am I doing this to be saved or accepted, or imposing it as necessary? — then stop. Is it a free, loving, Christ-honouring practice that binds no one? — then you are free. Christ alone for salvation; liberty in the rest, governed by love. (Where the Lord's Day and Sabbath fit is one place Reformed and other believers differ — for another verse.)

verseByVerse.quote: "They came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The brief visit to Ephesus is a reconnaissance: Paul reasons in the synagogue, the Jews respond positively and want him to stay, but he cannot — he has a vow to fulfill in Jerusalem and a church network to report to in Antioch. He promises to return if God wills, and he will — for three years. Ephesus is the future, not the present. The gospel's advance requires both the willingness to plant briefly and the discernment to know when to stay.

verseByVerse.quote: "but he said farewell to them, saying, 'I will return to you if God wills,' and he set sail from Ephesus. When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'If God wills' — Paul's consistent acknowledgment that the mission's itinerary belongs to God, not the planner. The return to Jerusalem ('went up' is the technical term for ascending to the holy city) and Antioch closes the second missionary journey. Antioch is home base: the church that sent him receives him back. The apostle is accountable to his sending community, not merely to his own vision.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Apollos's appearance in Acts is brief but significant. He is introduced as 'an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures,' who 'taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.' His knowledge is genuine and considerable; it is also incomplete. Priscilla and Aquila's response to Apollos's preaching is the model of wise, humble theological correction: they 'took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.' Not a public rebuke, not a formal confrontation, but a private, respectful completion of what was missing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Importance of Thorough Gospel Formation

Apollos's incomplete knowledge — accurate as far as it went but stopping before the resurrection — is the permanent challenge of theological formation. Every generation needs to receive not just the part of the gospel that resonates with its existing categories but the complete gospel that the Scriptures teach. Priscilla and Aquila model the ministry of theological completion: receiving those who are partially formed, honoring what is genuine, and filling in what is absent. This is the ministry of discipleship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Apollos went to Achaia and was of great help to those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. Now: The church continues to be built by ministers whose gifts complement each other — some plant (Paul in Corinth), some water (Apollos in Corinth, 1 Corinthians 3:6), and God gives the growth.

verseByVerse.quote: "After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary: The third missionary journey begins with the same pastoral work that marked the second: strengthening the disciples. The word means making firm what is already standing. Paul is not always planting; he is also watering, supporting, reinforcing. The churches planted on earlier journeys need ongoing formation, and Paul understands that apostolic ministry includes the long work of consolidation.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Apollos is introduced as a remarkable figure: eloquent, Scripturally competent, fervent in spirit, teaching accurately about Jesus — and yet his knowledge stops at John's baptism, before Pentecost. He knows the Messiah but not the fullness of what has been given in the Spirit. This is not a defect of character but of catechesis — he teaches what he has been taught. The church's response to his incompleteness is instructive.

What does 'he knew only the baptism of John' mean? John the Baptist's baptism was a preparatory one — 'a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins' (Luke 3:3), in which people confessed their sins, turned to God, and got ready for the Messiah who was coming. John pointed beyond himself: 'I baptize you with water... but he who is coming after me... will baptize you with the Holy Spirit' (Matt. 3:11). So it looked forward to Jesus; it was the 'getting ready' baptism, not yet the full Christian one. To say Apollos 'knew only John's baptism,' then, is to say his grasp of the gospel reached accurately up to that preparatory point — he knew and proclaimed Jesus as the Messiah truly, as far as it went — but had not yet been brought up to the fuller apostolic message that followed: Pentecost, the outpouring and gift of the Holy Spirit, and baptism in the name of Jesus. His faith was real but incomplete, the fault of his teaching, not his heart — he taught what he had been taught, probably away from the centre in Alexandria before the fuller news reached him.

(He is the cousin of the Ephesian 'disciples' of 19:1–7, who also knew only John's baptism — though note the difference: Apollos, already fervent in the Spirit and teaching accurately, is simply taught 'more accurately' by Priscilla and Aquila (v. 26) and is never re-baptized, whereas those men, who had not even heard the Spirit was given, are baptized into Jesus and receive the Spirit; see on 19:1–2.) And the lovely lessons here: even a brilliant, eloquent, fervent Bible teacher still had more to learn — and humbly received it from a tentmaking couple (Priscilla named first). None of us has arrived; we keep growing. And the way to help someone whose understanding is incomplete is Priscilla and Aquila's way: not to attack him publicly, but to 'take him aside' and explain the way of God more accurately — gently, privately, helpfully.

verseByVerse.quote: "He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately."
verseByVerse.commentary: Priscilla and Aquila — Paul's tentmaking co-workers from Corinth — model the right response to incomplete but sincere teaching: they take him aside privately and explain more accurately. Not public correction, not dismissal, but patient, careful, private instruction. The woman is named first — unusual in antiquity — suggesting she was the primary teacher. The church grows in understanding through this kind of generous, accurate, humble correction of those who teach imperfectly.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary: The fully catechized Apollos is a force: he greatly helps those who have believed and powerfully refutes the Jews in public — the same activity Paul did, now done by one trained more fully in the apostolic faith. The chain of teaching — Paul to Priscilla and Aquila, Priscilla and Aquila to Apollos, Apollos to Achaia — is how the gospel multiplies. Every teacher who teaches accurately creates new teachers who teach accurately. (cf. 1 Cor. 1:17–18; 2 Tim. 2:15)

18.theology: Election as the Ground of Courage in Mission. “I have many in this city who are my people” (v. 10) is the doctrine of election functioning as a promise to a frightened missionary. Paul is afraid — he says so later. And God’s answer to his fear is not “it will go well” or “people will respond positively” — it is “I have my people here.” The ground of missionary perseverance is not optimism about human receptivity; it is confidence in divine election. God has sheep in every city, in every culture, in every hostile context — sheep who will hear the shepherd’s voice when it is proclaimed through his servants. This is not a reason for laziness; it is a reason for courage. Preach. His people will come.
18.examples:
Then: Paul in Corinth, afraid, working as a tentmaker, preaching every Sabbath, sustained by a vision and a promise, staying eighteen months because God told him to stay. The church that emerged from that eighteen months will cause him more trouble than any other — and will receive his most profound letters about the cross, the resurrection, and love.

Now: Every city has people who are God’s — people the Spirit is already preparing, already drawing, already making ready to hear. The task of the church is to be in the city, to preach the word, to stay when the Lord says stay, and to trust that the harvest belongs to him. The missionary who preaches in the hardest city is not alone. God is already there, and his people are waiting.

19.title: Ephesus and the Power of the Word
19.text: <sup>1</sup>And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. <sup>2</sup>And he said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” And they said, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” <sup>3</sup>And he said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” <sup>4</sup>And Paul said, “John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.” <sup>5</sup>On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. <sup>7</sup>There were about twelve men in all. <sup>8</sup>And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. <sup>9</sup>But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus. <sup>10</sup>This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks. <sup>11</sup>And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, <sup>12</sup>so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them. <sup>13</sup>Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.” <sup>14</sup>Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this. <sup>15</sup>But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?” <sup>16</sup>And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. <sup>17</sup>And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. <sup>18</sup>Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices. <sup>19</sup>And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. <sup>20</sup>So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily. <sup>21</sup>Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” <sup>23</sup>About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. <sup>24</sup>For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen. <sup>25</sup>These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, “Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. <sup>26</sup>And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. <sup>27</sup>And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship.” <sup>28</sup>When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>34</sup>But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>41</sup>And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.
19.overview:
Ephesus is Paul’s most sustained ministry in any single city: three months in the synagogue, then two years in the hall of Tyrannus — reasoning daily, so that all the residents of Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord. Not all of Ephesus came to hear Paul; the word went out through those who heard and carried it. Two years. Daily. All of Asia. This is what sustained, patient, Word-centred ministry produces.

The power of the word in Ephesus is confirmed by two vivid episodes. The sons of Sceva attempt to use the name of Jesus as a formula — and the evil spirit recognises the difference between the name wielded by authority and the name borrowed without relationship: “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognise, but who are you?” The name of Jesus is not magic; it is the delegated authority of the living Lord, available only to those who are his. And the new believers burn their magic books — fifty thousand pieces of silver worth — in a public bonfire of repentance that is one of the most vivid pictures of genuine conversion in the New Testament.

Then the riot. Demetrius the silversmith has done the economic analysis: if people stop worshipping Artemis, the shrine-making trade is finished. His complaint is one of the most honest in Acts: it is not primarily about theology but about money. The Word of God is economically disruptive. When people stop giving themselves to idols, the industries built on those idols suffer. The gospel always costs someone something.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Ephesian ministry is the climax of Paul's third missionary journey and the most sustained and fruitful period of his missionary career. Over two years of daily lectures in the hall of Tyrannus, 'all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.' Ephesus was the commercial and religious capital of the Roman province of Asia — home of the temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, and a center of magical arts and occult practice. The gospel's victory in Ephesus is therefore the gospel's victory over the most formidable concentration of spiritual opposition in Paul's experience.

The Ephesian episode contains three defining moments: the disciples of John who receive the Holy Spirit through Paul's ministry (completing what Apollos had begun teaching), the seven sons of Sceva whose attempt to exploit the name of Jesus results in their violent expulsion, and the riot of Demetrius the silversmith whose economic interests are threatened by the gospel's displacement of Artemis worship. Each moment illustrates a different dimension of the gospel's power: its completion of incomplete faith, its sovereignty over demonic opposition, and its economic disruption of idolatry.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Word of the Lord Prevailing Over Magic and Idolatry

The burning of the magical books — fifty thousand pieces of silver worth — is one of the most dramatic acts of new-believer repentance in Acts. The magicians do not gradually reduce their practice; they make a clean, costly, public break. Reformed theology sees in this the pattern of genuine repentance: the thoroughgoing abandonment of what the gospel has displaced, at whatever cost. The summary in v. 20 ('So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily') is the theological verdict on the entire Ephesian episode: the word wins, over magic, over economics, over riot.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Demetrius the silversmith's complaint — 'there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing' — is the most honest statement of why people oppose the gospel: it costs them something they value. Now: The gospel continues to threaten economic arrangements built on idolatry, and the opposition it meets is often economic before it is theological.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. And he said to them, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' And they said, 'No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's diagnostic question is immediate: Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed? The question presupposes that receiving the Spirit is the normal, expected experience of Christian initiation. These twelve men are disciples — followers of some form of Jewish teaching about the coming one — but they have not heard of the Pentecostal Spirit. Their honest answer reveals the frontier of the mission: there are people sincerely seeking God who have not yet received the fullness of the gospel.

This passage is the cousin of Acts 8, and is read the same several ways (see there). These men knew 'only the baptism of John' and had not even heard the Spirit was given (v. 2) — so the Reformed reading sees them not as ordinary Christians awaiting a second blessing, but as disciples still standing at the old, pre-Pentecost stage of John the Baptist, who on hearing of Jesus believe fully, are baptized into him, and receive the Spirit — their deficiency being in the gospel they had yet to hear, not a missing 'stage two' for already-complete believers. (Pentecostal brothers read it, with Acts 8, as evidence of a Spirit-baptism subsequent to conversion.) Note that Paul's question, 'did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?', naturally ties the receiving of the Spirit to believing, not to a later experience — which is how the letters speak of it (Eph. 1:13; Rom. 8:9). Said, as ever, with respect for those who differ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he said, 'Into what then were you baptized?' They said, 'Into John's baptism.' And Paul said, 'John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: John's baptism was preparatory — pointing forward to one who was coming. These disciples have received the preparatory sign but not the fulfillment. Paul's catechesis is swift: John's baptism was a baptism of repentance toward one coming after him, and that one is Jesus. The bridge from John to Jesus is the bridge from anticipation to fulfillment, from the forerunner to the king. Every aspect of John's ministry finds its completion in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary: Christian baptism — 'in the name of the Lord Jesus' — follows immediately upon hearing. These disciples do not resist or delay; they receive what they have been taught and are baptized. The simplicity of their response is the model of all Christian initiation: hearing, believing, receiving the sign. The church grows by this simple, repeated pattern of proclamation and response.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. There were about twelve men in all."
verseByVerse.commentary: The laying on of hands and the coming of the Spirit mirrors Pentecost and Samaria. The twelve — a number resonant with the twelve apostles and the twelve tribes — receive the Spirit with visible manifestations: tongues and prophecy. This is the Ephesian Pentecost, completing the geographic mandate of Acts 1:8. The Spirit is poured out at the frontier of the mission, authenticating the extension of the gospel to this outpost of Asia.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three months in the synagogue, then withdrawal — Paul's Ephesian pattern follows Corinth's. When the synagogue becomes hostile, he does not leave the city; he relocates the school. The hall of Tyrannus is a lecture hall where Paul rents space during off-hours (a Western text adds 'from the fifth to the tenth hour' — 11am to 4pm, during the afternoon siesta when the hall is otherwise unused). The mission moves from sacred space to secular space without missing a beat.

What is Paul doing when he 'persuades them about the kingdom of God'? In plain terms, he is making the case for King Jesus. The 'kingdom of God' is God's kingly rule, and the great news is that the King has come: Jesus, crucified and risen, now reigns and will one day return to reign in full. So to 'persuade about the kingdom' is to show people from the Scriptures who Jesus is and to urge them to bow to him as Lord — and so enter his kingdom, which a person does the moment he repents and trusts the King. (For what 'the kingdom of God' means, and why the phrase fills the Gospels but is rarer in the letters, see on 8:12; for the 'already, but not yet' of it — we are brought into it now, yet await its full coming — see on 14:22.)

And notice how he does it: 'reasoning and persuading.' He did not merely announce; he argued (the word means to discuss, to dialogue) and sought to convince, patiently, from the Scriptures, for three whole months. The faith is reasonable and invites the mind; commending Christ can mean kindly, patiently making the case and answering objections over time, not just a single quick pitch. You need not be a clever debater — but you can take heart that to 'persuade about the kingdom' is, at bottom, simply to help people see and trust the King.

verseByVerse.quote: "This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two years of daily teaching in Tyrannus's hall — and the result is that all of Asia hears. Ephesus is the hub: travelers, merchants, pilgrims, students all pass through the commercial capital of Asia Minor, hear Paul in the lecture hall, and carry the word back to their home cities. The seven churches of Revelation — Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea — likely trace their origins to this period. The strategy of Ephesus is to teach in the center and let the word radiate outward.

A little more on this 'hall of Tyrannus.' The word is scholē — our 'school' — a lecture hall where a teacher or rhetorician would hold his discourses and discussions. 'Tyrannus' (the name means 'ruler' or 'tyrant') was either the owner of the building or the lecturer who normally taught there; we know nothing more of him, save that his hall outlived his name by housing the gospel. As an early manuscript tradition notes, Paul used it 'from the fifth hour to the tenth' — roughly 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., the heat of the day, the afternoon siesta when the hall stood empty and most people rested. Picture it: Paul at his tent-making bench in the cool early hours (20:34), then teaching through the sweltering midday while the city slept, and his hearers giving up their own rest to come and learn — labour and sacrifice on both sides. And note the move: shut out of the synagogue (sacred space), Paul carried the gospel straight into a public lecture hall (secular space), the open marketplace of ideas, where any Jew or Greek could wander in. The encouragement is plain: the gospel needs no grand temple. A rented room, used in the leftover hours of the day, by a man who also worked a trade, became the hub from which 'all Asia' — Colossae, Laodicea, the cities of Revelation — heard the word of the Lord. Ordinary, borrowed, off-peak means, and a whole province reached.

verseByVerse.quote: And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Extraordinary miracles' — Luke signals that even by Acts's standards, the Ephesian miracles are exceptional: handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched Paul's skin conveying healing power. Luke does not explain the mechanism; he records the result. The point is not a theology of physical objects but the demonstration that God's healing power through Paul extended even beyond direct contact — appropriate in a city saturated with magical arts that claimed to channel power through physical objects. The miracles authenticate the word being proclaimed and demonstrate that the power behind the gospel exceeds any competing power the city has to offer.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, 'I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.' Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons of Sceva represent the ancient pattern of magical appropriation of divine names: if Paul's Jesus-invocations produce results, perhaps the name can be used as a formula by those who do not know Jesus. This is magic thinking, not faith — using sacred language as a tool rather than as address to a person. The name of Jesus is not a spell; it is the name of a living Lord who knows those who are his.

A word on these 'Jewish exorcists.' Exorcists were people who tried to drive evil spirits out of the afflicted — and in the ancient world it was a common, and often paid, trade, a kind of spiritual technician or magician-for-hire. They worked by technique: incantations and spells, secret formulas, herbs and charms, and above all the reciting of powerful names believed to compel the spirits to obey. Jewish exorcists were especially sought after, precisely because they could invoke the name of the one true God and the sacred names of Scripture, which were thought to carry unusual power over the dark world (Josephus describes them, and legend traced their arts back to Solomon). The point to grasp is that it was all about harnessing power by the right words, not about knowing God — they treated a holy name as a magic word.

That is exactly their fatal mistake here. Seeing Paul cast out demons in Jesus' name, the sons of Sceva simply added 'the Jesus whom Paul proclaims' to their list of power-words, as one more spell to try — and it ended in disaster (vv. 15–16), the evil spirit answering, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' before the man fell on them and beat them. The lesson is sharp and freeing: the name of Jesus is not a magic formula anyone can wield. It carries authority only on the lips of those who truly belong to him by faith. Real power over the powers of darkness is not a technique to be mastered but a gift that flows from being united to Christ — you cannot borrow Jesus' authority while keeping Jesus himself at arm's length.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the evil spirit answered them, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded."
verseByVerse.commentary: The demonic response is withering: Jesus I know, Paul I recognize — but you? The spirit distinguishes between the Lord himself, his authorized apostle, and these unauthorized imitators. The violent repulse is both judgment on the magical appropriation and a demonstration that the name of Jesus is not a power that can be harnessed by anyone who speaks it. The authority belongs to Jesus and extends to those he sends; it cannot be borrowed.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices."
verseByVerse.commentary: The failure of the magical exorcism does not discredit the gospel — it glorifies it. The name of Jesus is extolled precisely because it cannot be hijacked. The believers' response is striking: many come to confess and divulge their magical practices. The word for 'divulging' suggests a full disclosure of secrets — this is public, costly repentance from the occult practices that were woven into Ephesian religious life. The gospel does not coexist with magic; it displaces it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. And the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fifty thousand silver pieces — an enormous sum, representing the economic cost of full repentance from the lucrative trade in magical formulae. The public burning is an act of worship and a witness: these believers count the cost and burn the books anyway. This is the radical economic implication of the lordship of Jesus: whatever competes with him must go, whatever its value. The result: the word of the Lord prevails mightily. Obedience and mission are not separate tracks. (cf. Isa. 55:10–11; 2 Thess. 3:1)

Two small phrases worth a word. 'The word of the Lord' is Luke's regular name for the gospel message — the Christian message about and from the Lord Jesus, his own word carrying his own authority (much like 'the word of Christ,' explained at Col. 3:16). It is, in short, the gospel as God's living, authoritative word.

And your instinct about 'increased' is exactly right: it does not mean the gospel grew larger in content, but that it spread, multiplied, and triumphed — more and more people heard and believed, and the message gained ground and overcame opposition ('prevailed mightily' — here, over the magic arts whose books had just gone up in smoke). But why does Luke put it so oddly, making the word itself the thing that grows, rather than simply saying 'more people believed'? On purpose — it is one of his favourite ways of speaking (6:7, 'the word of God continued to increase'; 12:24, 'the word of God increased and multiplied'; 13:49). Two reasons. First, he is deliberately picturing the gospel as a living seed: the very word for 'increase' (auxanō, 'grow') is the language of living, fruitful things, the word of Jesus' parables where the kingdom-seed sprouts and grows of its own God-given life (Mark 4:8, 26–29; the seed is the word, Luke 8:11). The gospel is planted in the world and grows like wheat, and believers are its fruit. Second, and more pointedly, by making the word the actor Luke takes the credit off the preachers and puts it on God: it is not Paul's cleverness or the church's strategy that conquers Ephesus, but the word itself, alive with God's own power (Rom. 1:16; Isa. 55:11, 'my word... shall not return empty'). So the 'strange' phrasing is really a confession of faith: watch the word, not the men — and take heart, for that same living word is still growing and prevailing in the world today.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, "After I have been there, I must also see Rome." And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'He resolved in the Spirit' — the planning is both Paul's decision and Spirit-guided. His itinerary — Macedonia, Achaia, Jerusalem, Rome — is exactly the route Acts follows to the end. 'I must also see Rome' — the divine necessity (dei) that has governed the mission throughout. This is not personal ambition but the Spirit's confirmation that the horizon reaches the imperial capital; sending Timothy and Erastus ahead keeps the network running while Paul finishes at Ephesus.

('Resolved in the Spirit' is slightly ambiguous — 'in his own spirit' (he made up his mind) or 'in the Holy Spirit' (under the Spirit's leading). Given how the Spirit steers Paul throughout, and that the Lord later confirms this very plan — 'you must testify also in Rome,' 23:11 — the Spirit-guided sense fits well.)

But the practical question: how can I know my decisions are Spirit-guided today? First, let the anxiety down. The apostles received extraordinary, direct steering because of their unique founding role (see on 8:26); God's ordinary way is quieter, and he has not promised you a voice in your head for every choice. So how does the Spirit lead? Chiefly through the Word. Spirit and Scripture always go together: he guides by lighting up the Bible he inspired ('a lamp to my feet,' Ps. 119:105; 'equipped for every good work,' 2 Tim. 3:16–17). Most of God's will is already plainly revealed — be holy, love, forgive, flee sin, serve — so the Spirit-led life is, nine times in ten, simply the obedient life. Then through a renewed mind and sanctified wisdom. For what Scripture does not directly settle (which job, where to live), the Spirit leads not by bypassing your thinking but maturing it: 'be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that... you may discern the will of God' (Rom. 12:2); and 'if you lack wisdom, ask God, who gives generously' (James 1:5). Add prayer (Prov. 3:5–6), godly counsel (Prov. 15:22), and the providence of opened and closed doors. Inner promptings and a sense of 'peace' may play a part (Phil. 2:13), but never trusted alone; they must be tested by Scripture and wisdom, for the heart can deceive (Jer. 17:9; 1 John 4:1).

And the most freeing thing of all: the clearest mark of being 'led by the Spirit' is not a feeling about one decision but the shape of a life. 'Those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God' (Rom. 8:14) — led, in context, to put sin to death and live as God's children; and 'the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience...' (Gal. 5:22–23). So a choice made in love, humility, holiness, and faith, by a person walking closely with God, is a Spirit-led choice, even if no special feeling attends it; while one driven by pride, lust, greed, or self-will is not, however 'peaceful' it feels. So your checklist is simple: Does it square with Scripture? Have I prayed for wisdom and sought counsel? Is my heart surrendered, ready to do even the hard thing? Does it flow from love and holiness, or from the flesh? Then decide, and trust him with the outcome — he is sovereign over your steps ('the heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps,' Prov. 16:9), big enough to guide a surrendered, Word-shaped heart, and kind enough to redeem even our wrong turns (Rom. 8:28). A Christian walking with God need not fear 'missing God's will'; the pressure is off, for the Guide is faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: "About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen. These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The riot in Ephesus has an economic trigger: the gospel's conversion of idol worshipers threatens the market for silver shrines of Artemis. Demetrius is not a theological opponent but a businessman whose livelihood is imperiled by the spread of the gospel. Luke's account of the Ephesian riot is one of the most vivid in Acts, and its inciting cause is commercial — the gospel disrupts economic systems built on idolatry.

'The Way' — here is one of the earliest names the Christian movement went by (Luke uses it repeatedly: 9:2; 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). Why 'the Way'? Three roots run together. First and deepest, Jesus said, 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me' (John 14:6) — so to follow the Way is to follow him, the one road home to God. Second, it echoes the Old Testament, where the life of faith is pictured as a road one walks: 'the way of the LORD,' 'the Way of Holiness' (Isa. 35:8; 40:3). Third, it captures that Christianity is not merely a creed to hold but a way of life to walk — a whole road travelled after Jesus (recall 'as you received Christ... so walk in him,' Col. 2:6). It is a humble, vivid name: the faith is a path you travel with the Lord who is himself the Way, not just a box you tick.

And 'Artemis' (the Romans' Diana) was the great goddess of Ephesus — not quite the classical Greek huntress, but a distinctive local mother- and fertility-goddess, patroness and protectress of the city. Her temple at Ephesus, the Artemision, was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world — vast, magnificent, and the heart of a huge pilgrimage and tourist economy. Demetrius and his guild made and sold silver models of the shrine, devotional souvenirs for the pilgrims, a very lucrative trade. So the gospel here collides with a formidable triple alliance — a famous false god, fierce civic pride (Ephesus called itself the goddess's 'temple-keeper,' 19:35), and big money. When people turned from idols to Christ, the idol-souvenir business suffered, and that — not theology — is what lit the riot (19:27). The gospel had already burned the magic books (19:19); now it threatens the idol trade. Wherever Christ truly advances, the kingdoms of money and idolatry feel the tremor.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Demetrius's speech is an unintentional tribute to the gospel's effectiveness: not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia, Paul has turned a great many people away from idolatry. The craftsmen's economic anxiety is the measure of the gospel's success. When the idol market collapses because people are turning to the living God, the mission is working exactly as it should. The gospel's disruption of the economy of idolatry is a sign of its power, not a problem to be managed.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Gods made with hands are not gods' — Demetrius accurately summarizes Paul's preaching (and the Old Testament prophetic tradition, Isaiah 44:9–20). The admission is inadvertent but devastating: the silversmiths know that their silver shrines are hand-made objects, not divine beings. The danger Demetrius identifies — that Artemis 'may be counted as nothing' — is not a distortion of the gospel's effect but an accurate description of what the gospel always does to idols: it reveals them as nothing. The entire religious economy of Ephesus is built on the premise that Artemis is something; the gospel says she is nothing. (cf. Matt. 6:24; 1 Tim. 6:10)

verseByVerse.quote: "When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' And the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's companions in travel."
verseByVerse.commentary: The mob is theological in its outcry — 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians' — but economic in its motive. The confusion fills the city: this is not a controlled protest but a riot. Gaius and Aristarchus are seized as representatives of Paul — Paul himself is not present, but his companions bear the danger of his mission. The theater of Ephesus, seating twenty-five thousand, is the public space where civic passions are expressed at the largest scale.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul wanted to go in among the crowd, but the disciples would not let him. And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's courage tends toward recklessness and his brothers restrain him — including the Asiarchs, the wealthy and politically prominent officials who superintended the imperial cult in Asia. That these figures are Paul's friends, and that they care for his safety, is a remarkable social detail: the gospel has reached into the highest levels of Ephesian society. Their concern is both friendly and prudent — nothing good can come from Paul in a riot of twenty-five thousand.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews put forward. And Alexander, motioned with his hand, wishing to make a defense to the crowd."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chaos of the mob: most do not even know why they have gathered. Alexander — a Jewish representative seeking to distance Judaism from the Christian movement — attempts to address the crowd. The Jews are trying to make clear that they are not associated with this gospel that threatens the idol trade. The irony is that from the mob's perspective, Jews and Christians are equally suspect as monotheists who reject Artemis.

'Most of them did not know why they had come together' — it is indeed a touch of sad comedy, and Luke surely means us to feel the irony: a whole city roaring itself hoarse for two hours (v. 34) over a god, and most of the rioters cannot even say why they are there. But Scripture has a sober teaching that this little scene puts on display. The Bible takes a dim and realistic view of the mob: 'You shall not fall in with the many to do evil' (Exod. 23:2); crowds are fickle and passion-driven, the same Jerusalem voices crying 'Hosanna!' one week and 'Crucify him!' the next (Matt. 21:9; 27:22). And deeper still, this is what idolatry does to a mind. When men exchange the true God for idols, Paul says, 'they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools' (Rom. 1:21–22; Eph. 4:17–18). The psalmist is even more pointed: those who make idols 'become like them' — as deaf, blind, and senseless as the mute images they worship (Ps. 115:8). A senseless god makes for senseless worshippers; the confused babble of the Ephesian theatre is simply idolatry's darkened mind made audible.

Set against it is the gospel, for 'God is not a God of confusion but of peace' (1 Cor. 14:33). The riot is a little Babel — the proud city's voices dissolving into noise, as at the tower where God confused the tongues of the self-exalting (Gen. 11:7–9) — while the gospel is the Babel-reversing word that brings light, sanity, and order (think of Pentecost, Acts 2, undoing the confusion of tongues). It is the Word that gives a man back his right mind, as the delivered demoniac sat 'clothed and in his right mind' (Mark 5:15). For you it is a mirror held up to the world: so much of its frenzy — the crowds roaring for causes, fashions, and outrages — is people swept along without truly knowing why, defending empty things. The Scripture's counsel is plain: do not be carried by the herd, but let the truth of God steady and clear your mind (Rom. 12:2). The gospel does not merely save the soul; it brings the muddled head home to sanity and peace.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they cried out, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Alexander's Jewish identity triggers the crowd's anti-monotheist chanting — two hours of 'Great is Artemis.' The mob does not distinguish between Jewish and Christian monotheism; both reject the goddess. The chant is both religious affirmation and civic identity expression: Ephesus is Artemis's city, and Artemis's greatness is Ephesus's greatness. Two hours of chanting is the last gasp of a religious system losing its grip on the city.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, 'Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The town clerk — the most important civic official in Ephesus, the liaison between the city and the Roman provincial government — steps in to end the riot. His appeal is to civic pride and legal prudence: Ephesus's status as temple keeper of Artemis is unassailable, so there is no need for this disorder. His concern is not theological but political: a riot could bring Roman intervention and cost Ephesus its civic privileges.

'The sacred stone that fell from the sky' — one Greek word, diopetes, 'fallen from Zeus/heaven.' It was almost certainly a meteorite. In the ancient world, before anyone understood such things, a stone that fell flaming out of the sky seemed an obvious gift from the gods — heaven-sent, holy, undeniable proof of the deity; several pagan cults treasured such 'fallen-from-heaven' stones. The Ephesians believed their goddess (or her very image) was bound up with one, and the town clerk waves it as his clinching argument: everyone knows Artemis is real and we are her guardians, so settle down. The quiet irony is sharp: they revered the falling rock and the goddess, while missing the true God who actually made the heavens and flung the stone — worshipping 'the creature rather than the Creator' (Rom. 1:25). A meteorite is a wonder, but it points to its Maker, not to a goddess; 'every good gift comes down from above, from the Father of lights' (James 1:17).

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The town clerk's legal analysis exonerates Paul's mission: not sacrilegious, not blasphemers, no chargeable offense. The proper channels — courts, proconsuls — are available if there are legitimate grievances. This is Roman due process operating correctly, and it vindicates the missionaries. Luke's point is consistent throughout Acts: where Roman legal procedure is fairly applied, the gospel is innocent of the charges leveled against it.

('Proconsul' is explained at 18:12: the Senate-appointed governor of a province like Asia, who held supreme civil and judicial authority — in modern terms, roughly a regional governor who is also the province's chief judge. The clerk's point is simply that lawful channels exist: 'the courts are open, and there are proconsuls' — so let Demetrius take any real grievance to the proper authorities rather than whipping up a riot. There is a quiet wisdom here too: the gospel does not fear due process, and the Christian's way is to seek justice through lawful order, not mob passion.)

verseByVerse.quote: "'But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. For we are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The town clerk's final argument is prudential: the riot itself is the legal danger, not the missionaries' teaching. Ephesus risks losing its civic privileges with the Roman provincial government if it cannot explain why twenty-five thousand people assembled in the theater in disorder. The irony is complete: the city called to defend Artemis against Paul finds itself defending its own riot record. The gospel does not need the mob's suppression; it needs only for the law to work.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly."
verseByVerse.commentary: The dismissal is the gospel's vindication by Roman civic authority. The riot is over; Paul is free; the mission continues. Ephesus has had its encounter with the word of God — three years of daily teaching in Tyrannus's hall, signs and wonders, the burning of fifty thousand silver pieces worth of magic books, and now a riot that proves itself lawless. The word of the Lord has prevailed in Ephesus, and it departs with Paul toward Jerusalem and Rome.

19.theology: The Word of God as the Power of Mission. Ephesus is Luke’s great exhibit of what the Word of God, given time and sustained proclamation, can do. Two years in a lecture hall, and all of Asia hears. The mechanism is not apostolic travel or institutional strategy — it is daily teaching, received by hearers who carry it wherever they go. The Reformation insight that the Word creates the church (“verbum Dei creat ecclesiam”) is visible in Ephesus: the Word goes out, conversions happen, the old life is burned, fear of God falls on the city, new communities form. The Word is not one tool among many; it is the engine of the whole enterprise. This is why Paul will later write to Timothy: “preach the word; be ready in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2). There is no substitute.
19.examples:
Then: All of Asia hears the word from a lecture hall in Ephesus. A bonfire worth a hundred and forty years’ wages lights the night. A silversmith’s trade is threatened by a theological truth. The word of the Lord prevails mightily — not with weapons, not with political power, not with cultural cachet, but with the truth about the living God and the risen Christ.

Now: The church in every generation must resist the temptation to replace sustained Word-ministry with more immediately impressive alternatives — spectacle, experience, technique, programme. Ephesus was not won by any of these. It was won by a man who reasoned daily from the Scriptures for two years. The Word still has this power. It has not diminished. The question is whether we are willing to give it the time and the centrality it requires.

20.title: Farewell to Ephesus
20.text: <sup>7</sup>On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. <sup>8</sup>There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. <sup>9</sup>And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead. <sup>10</sup>But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.” <sup>11</sup>And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed. <sup>12</sup>And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted. <sup>17</sup>Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him. <sup>18</sup>And when they came to him, he said to them: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, <sup>19</sup>serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews; <sup>20</sup>how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, <sup>21</sup>testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>22</sup>And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, <sup>23</sup>except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me. <sup>24</sup>But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God. <sup>25</sup>And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. <sup>26</sup>Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all, <sup>27</sup>for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. <sup>28</sup>Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. <sup>29</sup>I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; <sup>30</sup>and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. <sup>31</sup>Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish everyone with tears. <sup>32</sup>And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. <sup>36</sup>And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. <sup>37</sup>And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him, <sup>38</sup>being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.
20.overview:
The farewell at Miletus is one of the most moving passages in Acts, and the only speech Paul addresses to Christians. It is a pastor’s testament — the account of a ministry offered to its people before the man who gave it disappears from their sight. Paul did not shrink. He did not select the comfortable texts and leave the hard ones. He declared the whole counsel of God — repentance and faith, warning and promise, the cross and the coming judgment — to Jews and Greeks, in public and house to house, with tears, for three years. This is the standard.

And now he commends them to two things: God, and the word of his grace. Not to his successors. Not to an institution. Not to a programme. To God and his Word — the two sources of power that will outlast every pastor and sustain every flock. The Word that built them up will continue to build them up. The God who saved them will continue to keep them. Paul is going to Jerusalem with chains waiting; the Ephesian elders are going home to fierce wolves. Both are in the same hands.

They kneel on the beach and pray together, and then they weep — sorrowing most of all because they will not see his face again. The affection between shepherd and flock is total and mutual. This is what three years of tears and teaching and house-to-house ministry produces: a bond that no departure can finally break, because it is a bond forged in the gospel and sealed in the Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third missionary journey enters its final phase as Paul turns his face toward Jerusalem. The route back — through Macedonia, Greece, and then by sea — is the reverse of the outward journey, and the pastoral quality of the narrative reflects Paul's awareness that he is saying goodbye. At Troas, the young man Eutychus falls from a window during an all-night sermon and is raised by Paul — a miracle that is also a portrait of the community gathered around the word and the table until dawn.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord's Supper as the Community's Center

The gathering at Troas 'on the first day of the week' to 'break bread' (v. 7) is the earliest explicit reference in Acts to the Christian practice of Sunday worship centered on the Lord's Supper. The resurrection day becomes the day of communal gathering; the bread broken in homes is the continuation of what Jesus instituted at the Last Supper. Reformed theology sees here the established pattern of Christian worship: Word and Table together, on the Lord's Day, as the community's defining weekly practice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul walked from Troas to Assos (about 20 miles) while the others sailed — apparently choosing the solitary walk for prayer and reflection as he moved toward Jerusalem and the suffering that awaited him. Now: The disciplines of solitude and prayer that prepare for costly obedience are as necessary for Christ's servants today as they were for Paul on the road to Assos.

verseByVerse.quote: "After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's departure from Ephesus is pastoral: he sends for the disciples and encourages them before leaving — he does not slip away in the night but says farewell, commending them to the grace of God. The journey through Macedonia is similarly characterized by 'much encouragement.' Paul is the pastor who encourages on the way out as surely as he teaches on the way in. The churches are formed not only by his arrival but by the grace of his departure.

verseByVerse.quote: "There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia."
verseByVerse.commentary: The plot against Paul redirects his return route — from a direct sea voyage to Syria, he goes back overland through Macedonia. Providence works through danger: the longer route will allow him to encourage more churches and will be described in verses 4–6 with the carefully listed traveling companions who represent the collection from the Gentile churches for Jerusalem. The plot intending harm becomes an occasion for extended pastoral ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: "Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The list of companions is a catalog of the mission's fruit: delegates from Berea, Thessalonica, Derbe, and Asia — representatives of churches planted on the previous two journeys. They are likely carrying the collection for Jerusalem (2 Cor. 8–9) as delegates of their churches, making this journey both a pastoral tour and an act of inter-church solidarity. The diverse roster — Macedonians, Galatians, Asians — is a living demonstration of the one body of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days."
verseByVerse.commentary: The 'we' resumes — Luke rejoins the party at Philippi, where he has apparently remained since Acts 16:17.
